title: Split-Perception: Measuring Divergence in How Large Language Models Assess Company Credibility

detail.title: Split-Perception: Measuring Divergence in How Large Language Models Assess Company Credibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of VeritasLinks, Inc., the company that operates the measurement platform used to collect the data analyzed in this paper. The longitudinal case study in Section 6 uses the author's own company domain as its subject; this is disclosed in Section 4 of the paper, and all case figures are reproducible from the platform's publicly shared reports. The author has no other financial or personal relationships that could be perceived to have influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human participants and no personal data; the units of observation are model-generated responses about companies.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. All work was conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly the first source consulted when an investor, analyst, or counterparty evaluates a company. Yet different models, asked identical questions about the same firm, routinely return materially different assessments-a phenomenon we term split-perception. Drawing on a dataset of AI-generated assessments covering more than 5,000 companies and several million individual model responses collected between 2025 and 2026, we introduce a structured methodology for scoring AI-mediated company perception on a 300-870 scale modeled on consumer credit scoring, decompose the score into visibility, positioning, and risk components, and quantify cross-model divergence. We find that divergence between models on the same company is large and structured: in the fully instrumented subset, the median gap between the highest-and lowest-scoring models is 100 points, with a 90th percentile of 134, and in the longitudinal case study the single-date split reached 115 points-while four of the five judge models were individually stable across repeated runs, the retrieval-grounded model's verdict on the same firm varied by more than 200 points. We argue that split-perception constitutes an unpriced information risk for M&A due diligence, KYB review, and credit assessment workflows that rely, formally or informally, on AI-assisted research, and we distinguish divergence that is a stable property of the model-evidence pair from volatility imported by live retrieval.

title: The AI Unemployment Myth? Why Four Regression Frameworks Show No Aggregate Job Loss (So Far)

detail.title: The AI Unemployment Myth? Why Four Regression Frameworks Show No Aggregate Job Loss (So Far)

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses aggregated, de-identified administrative records from the Israeli Employment Service, analyzed exclusively at the occupation-by-year level. No individual human participants were recruited, contacted, or subjected to any intervention, and no personally identifiable information was accessed in the analysis. The data were used in accordance with the Employment Service's data-governance and confidentiality rules. Given the exclusive use of aggregated, non-identifiable administrative data, the study did not require research-ethics-committee approval.

detail.abstract: Public debate anticipates imminent, AI-driven job losses concentrated in high-skill software work. We test this claim directly using the complete administrative records of the Israeli Employment Service: 6.2 million person-year observations on 2.4 million distinct job seekers, spanning 277 occupations (32 of them hightech) over eight years (2019-2026). For estimation we aggregate to occupation-by-year cells, each summarizing hundreds to thousands of individual job seekers, forming an unbalanced panel of 1,086 cells across 145 occupations, and we estimate four complementary frameworks: OLS, occupation and year fixed effects, Poisson, and Negative Binomial. The exposure-registration correlation is strong: a one-standarddeviation increase in AI exposure is associated with roughly 17% more registered job seekers (baseline OLS, beta = 0.159). Yet no framework identifies a causal displacement effect. The association predates generative AI and does not intensify after 2023: with occupation-clustered standard errors the general post-2023 interaction is insignificant (p = 0.185), and the exposure coefficient does not grow across successive AI release waves (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude Code), the trajectory genuine displacement would require. Only one model, the Negative Binomial, produces even a partial signal, a software-specific post-2023 term resting on five occupations that is suggestive at best. Consistent with reallocation rather than displacement, the registrant pool shifts toward experienced workers rather than junior entrants. The post-2023 window also coincides with the October 2023 war, which would independently raise high-tech registrations, so the absence of a robust effect further weakens the displacement reading. We do not rule out displacement in other settings or future periods, but in these data no robust aggregate signal is detectable. Policy should accordingly prioritize continuously updated exposure measures, real-time monitoring of registrant composition, and targeted reskilling for experienced workers in high-exposure occupations.

title: Content Moderation Under Competition: Spillovers, Advertising, and Liability
affiliations: and University of Utah - Department of Operations and Information Systems

detail.title: Content Moderation Under Competition: Spillovers, Advertising, and Liability
detail.abstract: We study how competing content platforms (e.g., TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, and X) moderate user-generated content while monetizing attention through advertising. Section 230 of the U.S. Communications Decency Act, enacted in 1996, delegates moderation to market forces on the premise that competition will discipline it. Since then, consumption-side competition has intensified and cross-posting tools have strengthened generation-side complementarity. We examine these shifts in a duopoly where sensitive and insensitive users jointly consume and generate content and platforms simultaneously choose moderation and advertising load. A platform's moderation unambiguously cleans its own content, but its effect on the competitor depends on the relative strength of consumption- and generation-side interactions. When platforms are strong generation-side complements---arguably the case today---moderation is a public good: it cleans the competitor and raises its demand, diluting private returns; platforms under-moderate relative to centralized and welfare-maximizing benchmarks. Under weaker complementarity, moderation is a quasi-public good: it still cleans the competitor but steals its users on net, yet platforms can still under-moderate. When platforms are generation-side substitutes, moderation is business-stealing: it displaces harmful content onto the competitor and steals its demand, and platforms over-moderate. These spillovers can leave harmful-content generators better off and those moderation is meant to protect worse off. Proposed liability amendments to Section 230 (e.g., the SAFE TECH and EARN IT Acts) may improve welfare only up to a point, beyond which they worsen it. Under sufficiently strong generation-side complementarity, coordination on moderation alone, with advertising competition intact, is collectively profitable and raises moderation on both platforms.

title: Comparative Systems Anatomy: Locating Systems and Their Observers in a Common Epistemic Landscape

detail.title: Comparative Systems Anatomy: Locating Systems and Their Observers in a Common Epistemic Landscape

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: Every discipline that deals with complex objects begins with an anatomy. Medicine teaches structure before function, so that a property belonging to an organ is not assigned to the organism. Engineering has no equivalent. It has excellent anatomies of particular classes—load paths, control loops, failure modes—but no common frame in which those are projections of one another. Claims about “the system” are therefore made in private languages: superlatives asserted without a comparison set, mathematics carried across anatomical boundaries without warrant. This essay proposes comparative systems anatomy: the placement of engineered and natural systems in a common characterization space, prior to any account of dynamics. The field is not empty, and its ancestors are conceded—Bertalanffy, Ashby, Simon, Perrow, Rasmussen, Leveson, Woods and Hollnagel, Alderson and Doyle. The claim is that the fragments have never been assembled, and that one element is missing from all of them: the observer, which even the framework that comes closest admits only halfway. Two spaces are distinguished, an anatomy space describing the artifact and a knowledge space describing our relation to it, and the central, empirically testable claim is that they are only partially correlated. The demonstration is a bacterium set beside the human circulatory system, the second more complex and better understood. The operative instrument is a four-part profile—inherent and engineered attenuation, inherent and engineered observability, with a fifth layer governing constraint, motivation, and cost—exhibited on a rooftop chiller. Four results follow: modality is a per-subsystem determination; anatomy licenses mathematics and never the reverse; measurement, interpretation, explanation, and prediction are distinct achievements; and assembled complexes accumulate an epistemic deficit. A speculative appendix sketches, in a directional rather than derived spirit, what a formalization of this deficit would require—information-theoretic and matrix-based candidates, and the latent-state estimation problem that stands between them and any deployed measurement—without claiming that the quantities are yet computable or that an automated pipeline gate follows from them. The costs are paid at the design table, in the automated execution fabric, and in the classroom.

title: A Survey and Tutorial on Autogenic Network Management for AI-Native 6G Communication Networks: Architectures, Control Loops, and Protocol-Aware Operation
affiliations: , Celona Inc. and Chongqing University

detail.title: A Survey and Tutorial on Autogenic Network Management for AI-Native 6G Communication Networks: Architectures, Control Loops, and Protocol-Aware Operation
detail.abstract: This article surveys and provides tutorial guidance on autogenic network management for AI-native 6G communication networks. The focus is data communications and information networking: radio access, core, transport, edge, cloud-native network functions, programmable forwarding, network slicing, mobility, service assurance, telemetry, and control-plane/user-plane coordination. Autogenic management extends self-organizing networks, zero-touch management, intent-based networking, autonomous networks, and agentic control by adding governed self-generation of management logic. Instead of only selecting from predefined actions, an autogenic manager can generate, validate, deploy, monitor, and revise communication-network artifacts such as slice policies, routing and traffic-engineering workflows, RAN xApp/rApp policies, telemetry queries, servicechain repairs, edge-placement rules, and orchestration logic. The paper defines an autogenic lifecycle of understanding, reasoning, generation, verification, execution, observation, reflection, and improvement, and separates a fast inner loop for operational control from a slower outer loop for improving the management system itself. It synthesizes enabling work on SON, ZSM, IBN, O-RAN, SDN/NFV, cloud-native networking, LLM/LAM agents, network digital twins, reinforcement learning, security, and network-utility optimization. The survey contributes a capability taxonomy, reference architecture, agent-role model, selfprogramming pipeline, staged-trust model, deployment ladder, communication-network use cases, benchmark requirements, and research roadmap. The central claim is that safe autogenic management is not unconstrained LLM control; it is protocolaware, policy-bounded, verifiable, reversible, auditable control over communication-network resources.

title: Digital Transformation in Pharmaceutical Commercial Excellence: A Systematic Review of Emerging Technologies, Applications, and Future Directions

detail.title: Digital Transformation in Pharmaceutical Commercial Excellence: A Systematic Review of Emerging Technologies, Applications, and Future Directions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval was not required for this study because it is a systematic review based exclusively on previously published literature. No human participants, animals, or identifiable personal data were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.
declarations.clinicalTrialRegistration: Not applicable. This study is a systematic review of previously published literature and did not involve the registration or conduct of a clinical trial.

detail.abstract: Background: The pharmaceutical sector is moving through a pretty fast digital change, mostly because of tech innovation, higher customer expectations, and also because the way healthcare gets delivered is evolving all the time. In that setting, newer tools like artificial intelligence (AI), customer relationship management, CRM platforms, omnichannel touchpoints, predictive analytics, and big data analytics are quietly (or not so quietly) reshaping commercial work. They do this by making customer engagement better, pushing sales effectiveness forward, and helping people make decisions that feel more evidence based. Objective: This systematic review is meant to look at how digital transformation actually supports pharmaceutical commercial excellence. More specifically, it tries to spot the crucial digital technologies, describe how they're used in commercial activities, weigh the benefits against the hurdles, and also point toward where future research should go. Methods: We carried out a systematic literature review using the PRISMA 2020 approach. Studies from 2015 until 2026 were gathered by searching Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and ScienceDirect. Then eligible papers, meaning those that focus on digital transformation in pharmaceutical commercial roles, were filtered, and afterward the remaining evidence was synthesized in a qualitative way. Results: What the reviewed work suggests is that AI, CRM systems, omnichannel engagement, predictive analytics, and big data analytics are among the most used technologies for pharmaceutical commercialization. In practice, these tools support sales forecasting, help with customer segmentation, enable more tailored engagement, improve marketing performance, and strengthen commercial decision-making. Still, real world implementation problems keep showing up. Things like cybersecurity threats, regulatory compliance pressure, data integration issues, workforce capability gaps, and organizational resistance can all limit the success of digital transformation, even when the intention looks strong. Conclusion: Digital transformation has basically become a strategic enabler for pharmaceutical commercial excellence, since it helps build intelligent, customer centered, and data driven business models. To keep commercial performance sustainable, ongoing investment will matter, plus ethical AI usage, and real organizational transformation not just tool adoption.

title:
Türkiye’s Tripartite Digital Regulation:
A Kantian Deontological Analysis of PDPL, Law No. 5651, and Law No. 4054*
affiliations: Riga Graduate School of Law

detail.title:
Türkiye’s Tripartite Digital Regulation:
A Kantian Deontological Analysis of PDPL, Law No. 5651, and Law No. 4054*
detail.abstract: Türkiye presents itself as a GDPR-aligned digital governance actor, yet simultaneously operates three legally inconsistent instruments: the Law on Protection of Personal Data (PDPL), which partially mirrors EU data protection standards; Law No. 5651, which authorises administrative platform blocking without prior judicial authorisation and criminalises broadly defined online expression; and the draft amendment to Competition Law No. 4054, which adopts Digital Markets Act gatekeeper thresholds while remaining silent on individual rights. No existing scholarship has analysed these three instruments together through a unified ethical framework. This article applies Kantian deontological theory, specifically the categorical imperative and the principle of treating persons as ends in themselves, to evaluate the internal coherence of Türkiye's tripartite digital regulatory framework. It argues that the PDPL partially honours deontological principles, Law No. 5651 structurally violates them, and the draft amendment to Law No. 4054 is deontologically silent in ways that compound the contradiction.in GDPR-adjacent digital regulatory regimes and offer three concrete reform recommendations for Turkish digital governance.

title: Algorithmic Architecture and Consumer Choice: A Strategic Analysis of AI Personalisation and Consumer Purchase Intentions in the UK E-Commerce Sector

detail.title: Algorithmic Architecture and Consumer Choice: A Strategic Analysis of AI Personalisation and Consumer Purchase Intentions in the UK E-Commerce Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no financial support or external funding for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionised consumer decision-making and buying habits in the UK e-commerce sector over the last few years. This study critically analyzes the implications of the impact of AI driven personalization on consumer purchase intention, specifically in the context of recommendation systems, algorithmic architecture, trust building and choice overload. The research is derived from a comprehensive literature review of the latest research and analyzes the impact of AI-driven recommendations on perceived relevance, convenience, engagement, and value, ultimately boosting consumers' intent to purchase. The study utilizes some of the most widely used theories namely the Stimulus-Organism-Response (SOR), Information Overload Theory (IOT), Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) to explain the psychological processes that drive algorithmic consumer behaviour. The results show that using AI to personalise the shopping experience can enhance the efficiency and results of online shopping, but it can also create information overload, decision fatigue, privacy concerns, and algorithm resistance when personalisation is overdone. Trust is found as the key mediator between personalisation and purchase intention, and transparency and consumer autonomy have a significant effect on the acceptance of AI recommendations. The study finds that there is a need for e-commerce companies in the UK to use AI to personalise customer experiences in a responsible way that is transparent, trustworthy and human-centred to create sustainable competitive advantage.

title: Upstream: Where Human-in-the-Loop Goes at Machine Speed

detail.title: Upstream: Where Human-in-the-Loop Goes at Machine Speed

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work presented in this manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This manuscript presents theoretical and conceptual research and does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or identifiable personal data requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was independently conducted and self-funded by the author. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
Software now takes consequential action on its own. It places orders, moves money, approves
claims, and grants access, and it does all of it faster than anyone can review. Governance that
cannot be present at the moment of action has to be settled beforehand, and written so a
machine can apply it without asking. This paper examines what happens when organisations
try to do that at scale.
The usual conclusion is that the human leaves the loop. That conclusion is wrong. The human
does not leave — the loop moves. Judgment that once sat at the moment of action, exercised
case by case and mostly unrecorded, relocates to the moment the rule is settled: earlier, on the
record, attributed, and applied to every case that follows. Human-in-the-loop does not
weaken under machine-speed execution. It becomes more consequential, exercised by fewer
people, at higher altitude, with their names on the result.
Which raises the question of how much of it there is to do, and the answer is that the work
does not end. Governance is produced everywhere at once — by the business, by its
regulators, by its contracts — while translation happens in one place, at the speed of the few
people with the authority to settle what a rule actually means. Production outruns translation
structurally, not temporarily. Every organisation running executable governance therefore
operates in two regions at all times: a Compiled Region, enforced by machine, and an
Uncompiled Region, still held by people. The boundary between them is the Uncompiled
Frontier. It moves. It does not close.
Four structural consequences follow. Human judgment does not shrink; it migrates upstream,
into designing constraints and deciding what cannot be compiled at all. Translation becomes
a standing function rather than a project, and therefore a professional services market with no
natural end date. The failures of compilation — ambiguity, contested authority, dead policy,
undocumented exceptions — are not waste but the principal output, because each one is a
question the institution had never been forced to answer. And enforcement architectures have
to be built for a world where most governance never reaches them.
This is an opportunity rather than a burden. The institutions that build translation capacity
early can launch products their competitors cannot govern, and the knowledge the work
depends on is held by people who will not be there indefinitely. Each proposition here is
independently testable. The paper provides a test for whether a policy can be compiled at all,
a treatment of what should happen when governance is unavailable, and an account of the
work, the roles, and the market the transition creates.

title: From Adoption to Intimacy: Experiential and Emotional Pathways of Digital Customer Intimacy in FinTech
affiliations: , University of Southern Queensland, University of Southern Queensland and University of Southern Queensland

detail.title: From Adoption to Intimacy: Experiential and Emotional Pathways of Digital Customer Intimacy in FinTech

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was approved by the University of Southern Queensland Human Research Ethics Committee (Approval No. ETH2024-1194). Informed consent was obtained from all participants before their participation.

detail.abstract: This study examines how user relationships with FinTech platforms evolve beyond initial adoption, focusing on the formation of Digital Customer Intimacy (DCI) in human–machine interactions. Using a quantitative-dominant design combining survey data from 414 users and thematic analysis of open-ended responses, the study develops and tests a staged-based model linking cognitive evaluations, experiential interaction, emotional connection, and Digital Customer Intimacy (DCI). The findings show that while perceived quality and behavioural intention explain early engagement, emotional connection is the most direct driver of digital intimacy. Trust supports engagement but influences intimacy only indirectly through emotional pathways. By introducing and validating DCI as a distinct relational construct, the study extends digital service research beyond behavioural continuance toward an understanding of how emotionally meaningful interactions shape long-term digital relationships.

title:
Final, but Not Yours

Protocol Finality, Private Law and The Allocation of Digital-Asset Loss
affiliations: University of Groningen, Faculty of Law

detail.title:
Final, but Not Yours

Protocol Finality, Private Law and The Allocation of Digital-Asset Loss

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded researcher

contentType.other: Short jurisprudential working paper / legal essay

detail.abstract: A system for ordering transactions is not a law of ownership, and the Bitcoin protocol was never meant to be the second thing. It settles the sequence in which transactions are recorded. It does not decide who, as between rival claimants, is entitled to what has moved. The distinction is not a technicality. It is the ground on which a growing body of digital-asset litigation now turns. A transfer may answer the consensus rules to the letter and still be unauthorised, mistaken, procured by fraud or made in breach of trust. On a fair reading, ByBit Fintech Ltd v Ho Kai Xin, Fabrizio D'Aloia v Persons Unknown Category A & Ors, Quoine Pte Ltd v B2C2 Ltd and Ping Fai Yuen v Fun Yung Li & Anor are decisions about the legal consequences of transactions that were, in the technical sense, entirely effective. The chain records that value moved. It does not, of itself, prove mandate, consent, notice or title. D'Aloia teaches that a public history of transactions does not spare a claimant the task of proving the route by which value reached the defendant, least of all where exchanges pool their customers' dealings and experts differ over the method of tracing. There is a consequence in this for the distribution of loss. Irreversibility takes away an administrative means of putting matters right and moves much of the cost of error onto the victim, the intermediary and the court. The weight of that cost falls unequally, for the exchange and the custodian hold the private data of attribution and can buy expert help, while the smaller claimant may be unable to turn a visible path of dealings into any relief that is worth having. The Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025 confirms that a digital thing may be the object of property rights, and leaves the questions of remedy and jurisdiction to the common law. Stablecoin regimes restore a regulated counterparty through duties as to reserve and redemption, without making an on-chain transfer immune from legal challenge. The article proposes a modest rule of evidence. A confirmation proves that specified data were included in the canonical chain and given a place in its sequence, subject to the risk of reorganisation; the block time is no better than approximate. Whether a transfer was authorised, who owns the asset and who must answer for its loss are matters to be proved by other means. Commercial parties would do well to allocate what risk remains to whoever controls the signing, holds the customer's information or can insure against the loss.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly constrained by physical infrastructure rather than algorithmic capability alone. This paper develops a conceptual political economy framework that treats compute as strategic infrastructure, linking physical bottlenecks, capital allocation, industrial policy, and geopolitical competition. Using a structured forecasting methodology, the framework is applied to ten medium-term forecasts spanning infrastructure, finance, macroeconomics, and geopolitics. Rather than presenting independent predictions, the paper demonstrates how multiple forecasts emerge from a single causal system. The framework contributes to ongoing discussions on AI economics, strategic competition, and infrastructure investment by providing a unified analytical perspective on the evolving compute economy.

title: The State Waqfs of Ottoman Istanbul, 1453-1923
affiliations: and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The State Waqfs of Ottoman Istanbul, 1453-1923
detail.abstract: Drawing on a quasi-random sample of waqfs from Ottoman Istanbul, this study defines the state waqf as an analytical category, distinguishes it from the private waqf, and identifies its functions. Unlike private waqfs, state waqfs functioned as instruments of governance and delivered urban services at scale. Enjoying operational flexibility unavailable to private waqfs, they could support one another. Prior to reforms of the nineteenth century, religious services, education, potable water, and lodging for visitors were funded almost entirely by state waqfs. Their functions also extended to improving individuals' prospects in the hereafter. Only one-quarter made explicit provisions for the poor.

title: Digital Signal Governance: A Foundational Framework for the Signal Layer of Digital Systems

detail.title: Digital Signal Governance: A Foundational Framework for the Signal Layer of Digital Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Modern digital systems depend on a continuous exchange of signals: transmissions of intent, state, identity, and behavioral information that organizations increasingly rely upon for measurement, compliance, and decision-making. Privacy, information security, data governance, and audit frameworks each engage these signals instrumentally, as a means to governance-external ends, but none treats the digital signal itself as a primary object of governance. This gap leaves the conditions under which signals are generated, admitted, and relied upon largely unaddressed as a distinct governance concern. This paper addresses that gap by introducing Digital Signal Governance (DSG), a governance framework whose primary unit of analysis is the digital signal. The paper establishes DSG’s core definition, scope conditions, boundary conditions, and definitional exclusions; articulates the foundational concepts developed in this paper, including signal integrity, signal lifecycle, signal admission, and governance exposure; and specifies the governance assumptions and principles on which the framework rests. DSG is positioned as an analytically distinct discipline that complements, rather than substitutes for, existing governance frameworks in privacy, information security, audit, and data management. This paper serves as the foundational theoretical statement of a broader Digital Signal Governance research program; subsequent work will develop empirical methods for assessing signal-layer governance conditions and explore applied governance models across signal-dependent environments.

title: Pricing Settlement Priority: Structural Evidence from Bitcoin Transaction Fees
affiliations: University of Saskatchewan - Economics

detail.title: Pricing Settlement Priority: Structural Evidence from Bitcoin Transaction Fees
detail.abstract: Bitcoin fees allocate scarce settlement priority and finance proof-of-work security, but paid fees also contain wallet and payment wedges. Using 18.26 million first-seen mempool transactions, we estimate a structural priority-queue model that maps fee ranks to confirmation outcomes. Structural priority prices are 4.3% of fitted mean paid fees; a re-estimation bootstrap gives a 2.5%-10.1% interval. Capacity expansions lower fees and delays; fee floors raise payments without improving confirmation. Because fees are only 0.56% of current miner rewards, security effects are small today but first-order in fee-only futures.

title: Cost-Aware Spatial Sampling for Private Wireless Network Validation
affiliations: , Celona Inc. and Chongqing University

detail.title: Cost-Aware Spatial Sampling for Private Wireless Network Validation
detail.abstract: Private-network coverage validation is a budgeted spatial-estimation problem: a field campaign must observe enough of a deployment to predict received signal power in unmeasured regions while avoiding redundant measurements along repeatedly traversed routes. This paper develops and evaluates a deployment-specific sampling framework using 2,842 cleaned SigCap measurement events from a distribution center, a supercenter, a healthcare facility, and a corporate headquarters. Each deployment is processed, partitioned, trained, and evaluated independently. Five spatial blocks are constructed per site, and complete blocks are withheld to measure regional extrapolation rather than local interpolation. Four coordinate-only regressors are benchmarked, followed by random, trajectory-preserving, and greedy maximin sampling at budgets from 5% to 100%. Random row splitting understates KNN mean absolute RSRP error by 55.0-116.7% depending on the deployment. At a 5% budget, maximin sampling reduces mean error by 17.2% relative to random selection across folds. The minimum maximin budgets that remain within 10% of full-data spatial error are 20% for the distribution center, 5% for the supercenter, 5% for healthcare, and 10% for headquarters. Continuous estimation and threshold assurance exhibit different operating points: several deployments reach the continuous-error band at low budgets while still producing asymmetric false-good or false-poor risks. The results establish a technical basis for planning site surveys as deployment-specific measurement-allocation problems rather than fixed-density datacollection exercises.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the legal conditions under which environmental obligations may operate as enforceable and sanctionable obligations in Peru’s environmental enforcement system. It argues that the authority’s power to supervise and sanction does not rest solely on the existence of a broad environmental mandate or on a list of formal sources. Environmental enforcement requires obligations that are valid, enforceable, sufficiently determined, and attributable to a regulated entity. In particular, an environmental obligation must identify the subject bound by it, the legal relationship that gives it binding force, the required conduct, and the source from which it derives. The object of the obligation must be possible, lawful, and determined or determinable. Determinability requires that the obligation provide objective criteria to answer basic questions: who must comply, what must be done or avoided, how compliance must occur, when the obligation is triggered or due, and where it must be implemented when location is relevant. The paper further distinguishes between obligations that may be subject to supervision and breaches that may lawfully support an administrative sanction. Not every breach of an environmental obligation is sanctionable; sanctioning requires a typified infringement, prior and valid sanctioning rules, sufficient clarity, and compliance with the principles of legality, typicity, non-retroactivity, legal certainty, and the prohibition of arbitrariness. Although focused on Peru’s OEFA system, the analysis is relevant to environmental enforcement systems that rely on regulatory instruments, permits, environmental management plans, and administrative orders as sources of enforceable obligations.

title: Technological Forecasting & Social Change How Does Big Data Affect Organizational Financial Performance in Turbulent Markets? The Role of Customer-Linking and Selling Capabilities

detail.title: Technological Forecasting & Social Change How Does Big Data Affect Organizational Financial Performance in Turbulent Markets? The Role of Customer-Linking and Selling Capabilities
detail.abstract: The information age provides vast opportunities for organizations to improve their efficiencies by relying on big data-AI empowered analytics (BDA). The purpose of this study is to address the critical question of how BDA-fit affects organizational financial performance, taking into consideration differences between markets and customer change caused by technology turbulence. Using data collected at the firm level and building on Task-Technology Fit Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, empirical results indicate that BDA-fit is important to drive organizational financial performance through the development of customer-linking and selling capabilities. These results vary across markets, with BDA-fit having stronger effects on selling capabilities and organizational financial performance in highly turbulent markets. BDA allows organizations to upturn challenges and hindrances caused by market turbulence into opportunities to increase sales revenues. Based on the findings, theoretical contributions and managerial implications are provided.

title: From Mining to Compute: Site Conversion, Speculative Development, and the Assembly of U.S. AI Infrastructure
affiliations: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign

detail.title: From Mining to Compute: Site Conversion, Speculative Development, and the Assembly of U.S. AI Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
The United States is experiencing an unprecedented build-out of data center infrastructure to support artificial intelligence (AI) systems, assembled through two distinct pathways. The first is the pivot of Bitcoin mining sites to AI, allowing operators to reuse facilities, power purchase agreements, and grid interconnection positions. The second is speculative greenfield development led by real-estate, energy, and financial intermediaries new to the sector. 

Drawing on an original site-level dataset of 571 U.S. data center projects, cross-referenced against 319 Bitcoin-mining sites, this paper shows that these pathways occupy different stages of the development lifecycle: mining-linked sites dominate the built inventory, while intermediary-led greenfield projects dominate the proposed and approved pipeline, where public disclosure is weakest. Both pathways rely on common tactics such as land acquired through newly formed LLCs with no operating history, permits advanced under code names, and non-disclosure agreements that bar local officials from naming the operator during key approval stages. 

Case studies of Western Hospitality Partners, Project Louie in Indiana, the Arkansas Google sites, and Project Anthem in Tulsa show how this sequencing allows rezoning, tax abatements, and utility commitments to be secured before communities can evaluate the risks. The paper concludes that a continuously updated public registry of proposed data centers is necessary.

title: Military Engagement in Internal Security Operations in Nigeria: Restoring Security Governance in Jos North, Plateau State
affiliations: and Federal University Oye-Ekiti

detail.title: Military Engagement in Internal Security Operations in Nigeria: Restoring Security Governance in Jos North, Plateau State
detail.abstract: This study examines military engagement in internal security operations in Jos North Local Government Area, Plateau State, Nigeria, with a focus on security governance, civil-military relations, and democratic accountability. The region has been troubled by repeated ethno-religious disputes and violent attacks and military presence has been necessary because of the incompetence of civilians to police. A qualitative case study design and semi-structured interviews with twelve purposively selected participants including military personnel, police officers, community leaders and civilians were used to collect data. Primary data was complemented by documentary analysis. Thematic study showed that military deployment provides short term stabilization through curfews, patrols and fast response activities. Persistent issues, however, are excessive force, human rights violations, poor intelligence sharing, institutional overlap with civilian agencies and diminished democratic supervision. Even with the military there, there is still cyclical violence which indicates that the fundamental drivers of conflict have not been addressed, such as indigene-settler antagonism, land disputes, and political marginalization. The study concludes that military intervention provides short-term crisis management, but sustainable peace requires strong civilian policing institutions, improved interagency intelligence sharing, community-based conflict resolution mechanisms, and democratic oversight of security operations.

title: Interpreted Temporal Fields: Anticipation and the Composition of Generative Assessment

detail.title: Interpreted Temporal Fields: Anticipation and the Composition of Generative Assessment
detail.abstract: A previous paper proposed generative obstruction as a primitive explanatory object, defining it over the continuations available to a system in fact and restricting attributions of obstruction to parties within a relation. It deferred a class of cases its resources could not examine: conflict arising from foreclosure a party anticipates in place of foreclosure it undergoes. This paper takes up that case. It argues that the reference models the earlier paper established are temporally composite, assembled from an interpreted past, a present state, and an anticipated future, each entering through interpretation; and that a party's assessment of its own generative prospects is a function of all three. The extension reaches anticipatory conflict and offers a reading of grievance without introducing a further primitive, since both operate through models the earlier framework already required. Two limits are stated. The composition of the estimated space is tense-neutral while its evolution remains temporally ordered, which preserves the path-dependence of the earlier account and forecloses a stronger reading sometimes drawn from arguments of this kind. And the extension sharpens an evidential difficulty already present: where obstruction is assessed over an interpretive field, it becomes inaccessible to observation that lacks access to that field, so the framework grows in causal reach as it contracts in testability.

title: An Automated Framework for Discovering Subgroups and Explicit Functions under Unobserved Model Specification Heterogeneity
affiliations: and Dalian University of Technology

detail.title: An Automated Framework for Discovering Subgroups and Explicit Functions under Unobserved Model Specification Heterogeneity
detail.abstract: Unobserved heterogeneity is common in managerial data and may reflect latent subgroups characterized by different data-generating mechanism. Such heterogeneity is difficult to identify because subgroup assignment is unobserved and subgroup-specific mechanisms may involve not only coefficients but also model specification. To address this challenge, we propose Heterogeneityaware Symbolic Regression (HSR), an automated estimation framework that jointly identifies latent subgroups and subgroup-specific explicit functions. HSR embeds symbolic regression into a mixtureof-experts structure under generalized Expectation Maximization, forming an estimation core that integrates latent subgroup representation, subgroup-specific explicit function identification, and assignment-function joint updating. HSR accommodates heterogeneity ranging from coefficient variation within a common model family to subgroup-specific function forms identified adaptively from the data. Across synthetic settings, HSR provides accurate latent subgroup assignment, competitive predictive performance, and high accuracy in coefficient and function form identification. Across three empirical case studies spanning individual-level purchase behavior, organization-level workforce turnover, and facility-level environmental risk, HSR reveals model specification heterogeneity in how pre-purchase behaviors relate to purchase price, workforce conditions relate to turnover pressure, and facility and organizational conditions relate to environmental risk. These results show that HSR can identify interpretable subgroup-specific functions that provide a basis for interpretation and decisionrelevant analysis.

title: Lessons from Historical Transitions’ Stranded Assets
affiliations: University College London - UCL Energy Institute, University College London, University College London and University College London

detail.title: Lessons from Historical Transitions’ Stranded Assets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: We are grateful for funding support from the Oceankind, which has enabled this work.

detail.abstract: Low-carbon transitions in the electricity sector are widely expected to generate stranded assets among incumbent fossil fuel generators, yet empirical evidence of whether such stranding has materialised remains scarce. This paper addresses that gap through a retrospective analysis of two advanced transitions-in Germany and the United Kingdomdrawing on plant-level capacity data, utility financial statements, and credit rating reports to quantify stranded assets through early closures, under-utilisation, and financial impairments. Significant stranded assets materialised in both countries. Importantly, financial impacts began at the acceleration phase of the renewable energy transition, before the displacement of fossil fuel capacity was widely apparent. Long-term policy clarity enabled incumbent utilities to hedge their exposure through early renewable investment, but did not prevent stranding from occurring. These findings provide the first systematic retrospective empirical evidence on stranded assets in advanced low-carbon electricity transitions, with implications for how transition risk is measured, anticipated, and managed by investors and policymakers.

title: Common Credit Scoring, Cross-Market Competition, and Bank Adoption *

detail.title: Common Credit Scoring, Cross-Market Competition, and Bank Adoption *
detail.abstract: Why would a bank decline access to a credit score that improves screening? We study a bank that can connect to a nonexclusive score already used by a technology lender when the firms also compete for payment customers. Access sharpens the bank's screening but makes the score symmetric, intensifying lending competition and changing long-run payment relationships. The resulting customer-base loss makes adoption depend on the rival's cross-market incentives and data architecture. In sufficiently differentiated payment markets, the bank connects only if the technology payment provider internalizes enough downstream lending profit; the lender's access to payment-generated data lowers this threshold. A refinement that eliminates weakly dominated negative effective margins extends the access ordering to corner payment equilibria except when the bank is excluded under both access choices. Conditional on the organizational threshold, access occurs only at moderate project returns and, with costly matching, above a minimum score-coverage level. Comparing the decentralized and social adoption-cost thresholds classifies under-and over-adoption; in the * Zhao Li have benefited from the support from National Natural Science Foundation of China (Ref. title: Keeping the Gate: The European Commission Issues Its Specification Decision on Alphabet's Operating System Interoperability with AI Assistants

detail.title: Keeping the Gate: The European Commission Issues Its Specification Decision on Alphabet's Operating System Interoperability with AI Assistants
detail.abstract: This piece analyses the European Commission's Specification Decision on Alphabet's implementation of Article 6(7) DMA, which mandates vertical interoperability between Google's Android operating system and competing AI assistants. Comparing the final decision against the April Draft Implementation Measures, the article identifies a marked shift toward regulatory flexibility: while twelve of thirteen originally contemplated features remain in scope, five are now classified as restricted features subject to a gatekeeper-administered certification regime. This reintroduces discretionary control that the EC had previously foreclosed in its Apple specification decision, creating tension in the Commission's interpretation of the DMA's integrity defence. The analysis further traces procedural retrenchments, alongside a subtle but consequential drift away from API-based compliance toward outcome-oriented obligations. Collectively, these changes are argued to shift oversight from an automatable, verifiable fire alarm model toward resource-intensive, discretion-laden police patrol enforcement, raising questions about the EC's capacity to supervise Alphabet's compliance effectively.

title: Kimi K3 and FinTech: Open-Weight Scaling and the Democratization of Financial Services
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Kimi K3 and FinTech: Open-Weight Scaling and the Democratization of Financial Services
detail.abstract: DeepSeek, a Chinese AI company, demonstrated in early 2025 that high-performance language models could be developed at dramatically lower costs than previously thought. The July 2026 release of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion-parameter open-weight model, represents a different kind of disruption. Whereas DeepSeek showed that AI could be built more cheaply, Kimi K3 achieves performance parity with frontier proprietary systems such as OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 in key software engineering benchmarks. This paper examines the Kimi K3 phenomenon through the lens of financial technology democratization. I analyze how frontier-capable open-weight models lower barriers to entry for FinTech startups and established firms alike. The analysis addresses Kimi K3's benchmark performance, the infrastructure paradox created by unprecedented demand for compute capacity, and the implications for financial services innovation in lending, investment management, insurance, and payments. The findings suggest that open-weight scaling represents a new phase in AI democratization, with particular significance for emerging markets and underserved populations.

title: The Measurement of Geoeconomic Fragmentation: A Robustness Assessment
affiliations: University of Trento and University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: The Measurement of Geoeconomic Fragmentation: A Robustness Assessment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: Nothing to declare

detail.abstract: Fernández-Villaverde et al. (2024) propose a dynamic hierarchical factor model to measure geoeconomic fragmentation as a latent construct designed to capture its inherently multifaceted nature. This paper examines the robustness of that framework through four complementary exercises. First, we offer a reconstructive replication of the model and assess the sensitivity of the resulting estimates to alternative state-space representations and identification choices, with particular attention to issues of replicability and scalability. Second, we examine the framework's capacity to accommodate new sources of information by replacing an energy-related uncertainty indicator with a market-based measure constructed from the sensitivity of defense-sector equity returns to geopolitical news. Third, we investigate the role of taxonomy by reassigning selected indicators across the four domains underlying the fragmentation index. Fourth, we examine the behavior of the estimated factors across a set of historically grounded regimes spanning segmented integration, hyperglobalization, slowbalization, and strategic fragmentation. Across all exercises, the aggregate fragmentation factor displays a remarkably high degree of stability. By contrast, the interpretation of domain-specific factors proves considerably more sensitive to modeling choices, proxy selection, and the classification of indicators. The evidence suggests that aggregate measures of geoeconomic fragmentation are robust to a wide range of reasonable specifications, whereas their decomposition across channels remains closely tied to the informational structure through which the latent construct is identified.

title: Fair Value Gaps Work — Until You Try to Trade Them

detail.title: Fair Value Gaps Work — Until You Try to Trade Them
detail.abstract: We test the widely-taught belief that a Fair Value Gap (FVG) — a three-candle price imbalance — marks a level where price will reliably react, using seven years of data across four liquid futures markets, three timeframes, and roughly 40,000 detected occurrences. We measure not only whether price reacts at these levels, but whether it does so more than a random level at the same distance — the only test that separates a genuine signal from noise. We find the reaction is real as a measurement (approximately five percentage points above random) but carries no tradeable edge. Across five independent trade constructions — including the 5- and 15-minute versions most heavily marketed on social media — the effect is either a coin flip or, at its best, exactly consumed by realistic trading costs. The one construction that appears strongly profitable proves to be an artifact: it depends on resolving trade exits on coarse hourly bars, which smuggles in look-ahead bias; measured honestly on 1-minute data, the apparent edge collapses from a profit factor of ~2.4 to ~1.0. The result is consistent across all four instruments and every timeframe. We report the descriptive finding and the negative tradability result together, with full sample sizes and methodology, so that other researchers can verify, extend, or refute this work.

title: Trust but Verify: Benchmarking Gallup World Poll Employment Data Against the EU-Labour Force Survey
affiliations: and

detail.title: Trust but Verify: Benchmarking Gallup World Poll Employment Data Against the EU-Labour Force Survey
detail.abstract: The Gallup World Poll (GWP) links internationally comparable measures of well-being and attitudes to a short labour-market module. We benchmark its employment and hours variables against EU Labour Force Survey (EU LFS) microdata in available European countryyears from 2009 to 2023. Under a broad GWP definition that includes both part-time categories, the average country-level GWP-EU LFS employment-rate gap is approximately-1.0 percentage point. The pooled Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition yields a total gap of-0.85 points: observable composition accounts for-0.97 points and the unexplained component is +0.12 points, with a standard error of 1.99 points. This aggregate result masks country and demographic heterogeneity. A narrow definition that excludes part-time work understates employment by roughly 10-20 points. For hours, the GWP mean is 40.18 hours per week, compared with 37.41 in the EU LFS. Demographic reweighting reduces the aggregate difference from 2.77 to 1.99 hours, while group-specific reweighting raises each country-group difference by 0.11 to 0.58 hour. Hours reports generally require more recall and aggregation than binary employment status. The GWP limits this burden by anchoring employment to the preceding seven days and recording total weekly hours in five intervals. The resulting variable provides a common interval-based measure of work intensity; exact mean levels depend on the values assigned to those intervals.

title: Beauty and the Blades: The Local Economic Impact of Wind Turbines *
affiliations: , University of Amsterdam and Sapienza University Of Rome, Department of Social Sciences and Economics

detail.title: Beauty and the Blades: The Local Economic Impact of Wind Turbines *
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of wind turbine visibility on tourism outcomes. Using data from Italy from 1998-2019, we show that the visibility of wind turbines reduces tourist arrivals by 20%, with the effect peaking approximately seven years after installation. The effect is mainly driven by rural areas. Tourist spending follows a similar pattern, declining by about 19%. We further estimate that tourism-related losses offset up to 40% of the CO 2 emission savings resulting from wind turbine installations. These findings highlight the need for policies that mitigate local externalities while preserving broader environmental benefits.

title: The Power Structure of Knowledge in Co-creation: A Generative Relational Being Perspective

detail.title: The Power Structure of Knowledge in Co-creation: A Generative Relational Being Perspective
detail.abstract: Accounts of knowledge and power have taken two broad forms. On the first, knowledge is content, and power is a contamination that a well-ordered epistemic practice excludes. On the second, associated with Foucault and with the sociology of knowledge, power conditions what may count as knowledge, so that the two are historically inseparable. This paper proposes a third account. Knowledge is a relational structure through which interpretation is coordinated, and every such structure generates asymmetry among its participants. Upon that asymmetry the tendency of a position to maintain itself is itself generative: it produces the conditions of its own continuation. Power in knowledge is this self-maintaining generativity, which places it within generation rather than in opposition to it. Five channels through which an epistemic asymmetry maintains itself are distinguished, following the life of an interpretation (proposal, admission, validation, revision, attribution), together with the cost of exit that prices them. The paper argues that a configuration degrades when the generation issuing from a position turns to the production of its own conditions, and that the criterion of this turn is the closure of the revision loop: whether an exercise of revision alters the conditions under which the next interpretation is generated. Generative power is treated as power rather than as its benign alternative, marked by the erosion of the conditions on which the exercising position depends. The account is developed across education, intimacy, international relations, and academic knowledge production, which are taken as instances of one mechanism.

title:
Access Dilution in Contribution Economies 
Scarcity, Scale, and the Erosion of Contribution Purchasing Power

detail.title:
Access Dilution in Contribution Economies 
Scarcity, Scale, and the Erosion of Contribution Purchasing Power
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Contribution Purchasing Power (CPP) model to analyse how the value of participation changes as contribution-based systems scale. It defines Access Dilution as the decline in the effective value of benefits such as exclusivity, recognition, proximity, and meaningful interaction when participation grows without corresponding expansion in scarce resources. Building on the economics of positional goods and club goods, and drawing on platform theory, the model distinguishes Access Dilution from conventional inflation and deliberate platform degradation. The paper argues that Access Dilution is often a structural outcome of growth colliding with scarcity rather than extractive intent. It offers a contributor-centric framework for understanding contemporary membership, creator, and donor economies, supported by original figures and a real-world case study.

title: Innovation-Output Relationship: Does Location Matter?
affiliations: Delhi School of Economics and South Asian University

detail.title: Innovation-Output Relationship: Does Location Matter?
detail.abstract: This is an extensive review paper on the relationship pertaining to innovation and returns to investment. It begins by adhering to the view that innovation-output relationship differs across space as the spatial characteristics causally induce firms to innovate and the response to innovation in terms of total factor productivity growth or any other indicator also varies across space. Given this background each subsection considers a particular locational characteristic, and asks of it whether, first, the theory suggests that this should matter, and second, whether the evidence supports a genuine causal relation or it is a mere correlation which could have been produced for some other reason. It may be seen that the most prominent empirical claim made in this literature stands on shaky identification grounds. Location appears to be convincingly related to innovation in many settings and with many techniques, but the mechanisms behind the causal effect (density, spill-overs, diversity or quality of institutions) are still only partially identified. More in-depth research is required to decipher the firm level, industry level and the location-specific characteristics and the mechanisms through which they are related in certain situations.

title: Digital Assets: A Unified Global Framework of Property Law, Regulation, Accounting and Capital Treatment

detail.title: Digital Assets: A Unified Global Framework of Property Law, Regulation, Accounting and Capital Treatment
detail.abstract: A digital asset has to be classified twice over. Private law asks what the holder actually owns, a thing or only a claim, and that answer decides what happens when the intermediary holding the asset fails: the holder lifts the asset out of the estate, or proves in the insolvency as a creditor. Regulatory law asks which rulebook governs the asset, and so which supervisor, licence and disclosure rules apply. This book builds a single framework on those two questions and carries the private-law answer through to the two treatments that follow from it: the accounting under IFRS and United States GAAP, and the bank capital charge under the Basel cryptoasset standard (SCO60), in force since January 2026. On that scaffold it defines ten functional categories, grouped into five families, surveyed across nineteen jurisdictions, the world's leading frameworks, and against the principal international authorities: UNIDROIT, the Basel Committee, the Financial Stability Board, the FATF and the SEC's 2026 interpretive release. The categories track standards that already exist; the contribution is the layer those standards omit: the proprietary characterisation that the UNIDROIT and ELI Principles, by design, refer to other law, carried through to the accounting and capital treatment of every category. The book closes with practical protocols for the legal practitioner, the public accountant and the policymaker building a digital asset regime that interoperates globally.

title: Machine Learning, Return Predictability, and Implementable Alpha on the Ghana Stock Exchange
affiliations: , Ege University, Accra Technical University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Machine Learning, Return Predictability, and Implementable Alpha on the Ghana Stock Exchange

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We confirm that no authors of this manuscript have any competing financial or non-financial interests, currently or previously, including serving in an editorial capacity for the journal we are submitting to.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the return predictability and portfolio performance of machine learning models relative to conventional asset pricing models on the Ghana Stock Exchange using monthly equity, macroeconomic, and commodity price data from 2007:M12-2023:M4. Results show that Elastic Net delivers the strongest out-of-sample performance, achieving an R² of 28.23%, an annualised long-short portfolio return of 88.4%, and a gross Sharpe ratio of 3.28. This substantially outperforms CAPM (-0.08% return; Sharpe-0.003) and ARIMA (14.7% return; Sharpe 0.59). Although the market consists of a concentrated eight-stock liquid universe typical of frontier markets, the performance differential remains economically and statistically significant. After accounting for GSE-specific transaction costs of 1.5%-2.5% round-trip, net Sharpe ratios remain between 1.86 and 2.96. Subsample results further indicate improving predictive performance over time, implying that regularised nonlinear machine learning models can extract persistent alpha in emerging equity markets.

title: Executive Compensation and Conflicts of Interest in Analyst Research
affiliations: University of Oklahoma, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Oklahoma - Division of Finance

detail.title: Executive Compensation and Conflicts of Interest in Analyst Research
detail.abstract: The paper studies whether executive compensation incentives can affect how sell-side analysts produce and disseminate accounting information about other firms. We examine brokerage houses whose executives receive relative performance evaluation (RPE) awards based on total shareholder returns. By linking executive pay to named peers’ stock prices, these contracts create incentives for affiliated analysts to disclose unfavorable information about those peers when it is most relevant for the broker’s compensation outcome. We find that affiliated analysts devote more attention to RPE rivals, and their research becomes more negative during final performance-measurement windows: they revise earnings forecasts downward, write in a more pessimistic tone, and elicit more negative announcement returns. Forecast accuracy does not decline, consistent with strategic dissemination of credible negative information. The effects concentrate among peers whose stock price declines can improve the broker’s relative rank, and final rankings cluster on the payout-favorable side of rank cutoffs. Overall, the results show that executive incentives can create conflicts of interest in the production, timing, content, and tone of analyst research.

title: A Two-Stage Scheduling Heuristic for the Deadline-Constrained Traveling Salesman Problem with a Drone Station (TSP-DS)

detail.title: A Two-Stage Scheduling Heuristic for the Deadline-Constrained Traveling Salesman Problem with a Drone Station (TSP-DS)

keywords: Traveling Salesman Problem with Drone Stations

detail.abstract: This study investigates a deadline-constrained traveling salesman problem with drone stations in which a truck replenishes fixed drone pads and drones serve geographically eligible customers. The objective is to minimize total order tardiness under release times and soft delivery deadlines. A mixed-integer programming formulation jointly determines pad activation, truck routing, customer-to-pad assignment, drone sequencing, and delivery timing. Because the integrated model becomes computationally difficult at realistic demand scales, this study proposes LBIP-VND, an iterative two-stage heuristic combining load-balanced assignment, tardiness-based best insertion, variable-neighborhood descent, and truck routing guided by pad-level tardiness penalties. The method is evaluated on semi-synthetic Manhattan instances containing 48 candidate pads and approximately 1,500 orders with 60-minute delivery targets. Across all tested scales and departure settings, LBIP-VND produced feasible schedules within a few seconds. For full-size instances, average runtime was 2.88 seconds and average total tardiness was 9.53 hours across approximately 1,500 orders. Under a relaxed midnight-departure benchmark, all instances achieved zero tardiness. In contrast, the exact formulation exhibited rapidly increasing runtime and did not reliably produce competitive full-scale solutions within a two-hour limit. The results demonstrate that scheduling-based decomposition can provide scalable, service-level-oriented solutions for large fixed-pad truck--drone delivery systems.

title: Multifield Forecasting Model

detail.title: Multifield Forecasting Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Professor DoHwan Park of Stony Brook University suggested the paper to be written in a way that general public can understand. She isn't listed as author because Prof. Park did not write any of the parts in this MFM paper, nor had direct influence.

detail.abstract: This paper on Multifield Forecasting Model is the result of more than 660 statistical election projections for 73 nations all around the world reflecting 24,854,939 samples of 7,823 polling data, with the development in progress more than 5 years till early last year. Originally known as Universal Election Projection Model, it was completed to not include any other factor apart from scientific opinion polls directly asking the voters’ intention. Therefore, even though at first built to accurately predict election outcomes only, the model was generalized in a way that can be utilized for infinitely many fields by simply inputting the base data significant to the specific topic.

title: Data-and-structure-Driven Transshipment Policy in Heterogeneous Multi-Retailer System
affiliations: Shenzhen University - College of Economics, The University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen University, The University of Hong Kong, The University of Hong Kong - Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Systems Engineering, Jiutian Artificial Intelligence Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd., and Department of Data and Systems Engineering, The University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Data-and-structure-Driven Transshipment Policy in Heterogeneous Multi-Retailer System
detail.abstract: Retail networks may incur costly local stockouts even when inventory remains available elsewhere. Addressing this imbalance requires coordinated replenishment and shortage fulfillment across heterogeneous retailers. This study formulates the problem as an event driven Markov decision process under independent non-homogeneous Poisson demands. The analysis establishes a fixed target replenishment structure. It also derives two marginal value bounds and shows that a monotone inventory effect yields a transshipment threshold in single supplier states For larger systems, a structure-parameterized proximal policy optimization method named SP-PPO combines demand-informed action selection with structure-informed value learning. Its actor uses balanced policy scores to compare emergency orders with feasible transfers. Its critic applies soft penalties based on the marginal value bounds and the marginal monotonicity underlying the threshold. Across 90 synthetic observations, PPO-BP has the lowest pooled mean cost among implementable policies. SP-PPO performs best in selected network-size and transshipment-cost regimes. In the real-data-calibrated study SP-PPO reduces mean cost by 3.78% relative to the greedy algorithm and outperforms it in 17 of 20 emergency-cost and capacity settings. These findings provide a practical route from analytical structure to scalable inventory control in heterogeneous retail networks.

title: Verification by Design: The PROVEN Model for Strengthening Research Integrity in AI-Assisted Scholarship
affiliations: Coastline Community College

detail.title: Verification by Design: The PROVEN Model for Strengthening Research Integrity in AI-Assisted Scholarship

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There was no financial or personal relationships.
declarations.ethicsApproval: There were no participants involved
declarations.funderStatement: The research was not funded

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence now assists nearly every stage of the research lifecycle, yet integrity enforcement remains anchored in after-the-fact detection of AI involvement, an approach that is empirically unreliable, biased against nonnative English writers, adversarially evadable, and already outpaced by industrialized fraud. This article argues that the failure is structural rather than technical and advances an alternative paradigm: verification by design, in which integrity is engineered into research workflows as a property of process rather than adjudicated forensically from finished text. The article introduces the PROVEN model, which organizes six pillars (Provenance, Responsibility, Oversight, Verification, Education, and Norms) across five actor levels spanning the individual researcher, the team or laboratory, the institution, the publication venue, and the wider scholarly ecosystem. Three named constructs give the model operational force: integrity gates, human-accountable checkpoints where AI-influenced content is validated before propagating downstream; verification debt, the compounding risk of unverified hand-offs across artifact boundaries; and structural impossibility, the design goal of making entire classes of fabrication impossible rather than merely detectable. Applications include a stage-bystage lifecycle map of safeguards, an institutional adoption maturity rubric, and a reference implementation demonstrating that structural impossibility is achievable in working research tooling. Twelve testable propositions convert the framework into a research agenda. The model addresses researchers, institutions, publication venues, and policy bodies seeking to sustain trustworthy scholarship in higher education and scholarly publishing.

title: Single-Network Finite-sample Inference in Strategic Network Formation Models
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Single-Network Finite-sample Inference in Strategic Network Formation Models
detail.abstract: We develop a finite-sample valid inference procedure for strategic network formation models in which linking decisions depend on endogenous network statistics (say, the number of common friends). Only a single network is required to be observed, and we restrict neither its density, nor the dependence structure induced by strategic interaction, nor the equilibrium selection mechanism. We exploit a bounding-by-c technique to construct a set of sandwich inequalities that are valid realization by realization, with the middle term involving only the i.i.d. pairwise error. We then average the sandwich inequalities over cells of exogenous covariates, and obtain identifying restrictions under a nonstandard pathwise limit formulation. For inference, we construct test statistics whose finite-sample uncertainty can be controlled by statistics of the exogenous covariates and errors alone, whose conditional distributions are exactly simulable in both semiparametric and parametric settings. Our proposed inference procedure is also computationally tractable, with no need to solve, simulate, or enumerate equilibrium network structures. In simulations, our procedure easily scales to networks of size 10, 000, and yields confidence sets that certifies the sign of the strategic coefficient. In two empirical applications (with network size about 300∼9500), we find statistical evidence for positive link interdependence at 95% confidence level.

title: Governing the Computed Boundary: A Dynamic Transaction-Cost Theory of the Multi-Agent Firm

detail.title: Governing the Computed Boundary: A Dynamic Transaction-Cost Theory of the Multi-Agent Firm

declarations.declarationOfInterest: in full disclosure: author has a commercial interest in multiagent architecture and development
declarations.funderStatement: personal

detail.abstract: Transaction-cost economics explains the firm as a discriminating-alignment response to exchange hazards, assigning each transaction to a discrete governance mode so as to economize on the costs of exchange. This logic is comparative-static: it predicts where a boundary should sit, not how it moves. Multi-agent artificial-intelligence systems alter the object the theory must explain. When transactions are mediated by agents that adapt, learn, and are co-produced with foundationmodel vendors, the first-order economizing Williamson assigned to internal governance-effective adaptation and the elimination of waste-migrates to the agent and market layer and is performed continuously and at machine speed. The firm's constitutive act is correspondingly displaced from choosing a governance mode per transaction to governing the conditions under which agent-mediated transactions economize on its behalf. This paper develops that argument in three movements. First, it retrieves and formalizes the virtual-institution model of Olsen (1997)-a transaction-statedependent portfolio of governance structures, classified by a transfer/complementary/supplementary typology and assigned by an expected-net-present-value heuristic indexed to a transaction's proximity to the firm's nexus of intellectual assets-and shows that its governance constructs translate to agentic systems with a fidelity that exceeds analogy, because computational transactions instantiate by construction the discreteness the framework assumed. Second, it specifies the dynamic theory the 1997 program called for: the firm is a governance policy, a Markov-perfect equilibrium over a transaction state-space with an endogenously learning core, in which the boundary of the firm is computed each period as a Pareto-efficient frontier of permissible capability drift against appropriation risk. Third, it develops three extensions that exploit the higher fidelity of the computational domain-a five-dimensional typology of computational asset specificity that refines the typology into vector-valued proximity, a reframing of governance drift as continuous alignment governance, and an account of session-bounded protocols as the engineering instantiation of cyclebased governance. Appendix A states the model formally; a companion computational paper specifies estimation and evaluation.

title: How To Cite the Alien Terrorist Removal Court: A Citation Note On The ATRC's First Case
affiliations: Mitchell Hamline School of Law

detail.title: How To Cite the Alien Terrorist Removal Court: A Citation Note On The ATRC's First Case
detail.abstract:
The Alien Terrorist Removal Court, created in 1996 and modeled on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, sat dormant for thirty years. On July 15, 2026, the Government filed the Court's first-ever application, prompting an order from Chief Judge Joan N. Ericksen and raising a question the Bluebook has never had to answer: how does one cite this court?

This essay briefly surveys the sparse existing scholarship mentioning the Court, which had settled on "ATRC" as its working abbreviation. Drawing on the Court's own docket practice and on parallel approaches in related courts (FISA Courts), the essay proposes a citation form and notes some practical points, pending further guidance from the Court.

title: Strategic Communication and Organisational Well-Being in Startups with Female Leadership
affiliations: ,  and
