detail.abstract: Startups led by women often build their public identity through narratives centered on purpose, social impact and commitment to the local community, creating communication that is emotionally meaningful and focused on collective well-being. This paper presents an exploratory study on the communication styles and patterns of Andalusian women-led startups, to identify how well-being is reflected in their digital communication. Through a quantitative and qualitative analysis of their websites and social media, the results suggest women-led startups tend to integrate well-being into their digital communication. The findings suggest that communication can reinforce well-beingoriented entrepreneurial narratives.

title: Financially Constrained Procurement
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST), National University of Singapore (NUS), National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Finance and National University of Singapore

detail.title: Financially Constrained Procurement
detail.abstract: We investigate how the financial constraints of local governments interact with those of their corporate suppliers to affect outcomes in public procurement. Using auction-level data on Brazilian municipal procurement and population-based discontinuities in federal transfers, we show that higher transfers relieve local municipalities' constraints, allowing larger tenders and faster payments to suppliers. This draws new suppliers into competition, especially small, young, and distant firms that face participation and delivery costs and are themselves constrained. Higher supplier competition is associated with lower procurement prices especially for essential public goods and services, suggesting pass-through effects to local populations.

title: Lighting The Fire: A Pentagonal Pedagogy for Skill Consolidation in High-Ace Contexts: Facilitator Training, Individual Education, And the Path from Working Memory to Durable Practice

detail.title: Lighting The Fire: A Pentagonal Pedagogy for Skill Consolidation in High-Ace Contexts: Facilitator Training, Individual Education, And the Path from Working Memory to Durable Practice

The author was trained in the Lean tradition described herein and the work draws on the author's prior published corpus. The author has served in leadership of Alaska Native early-childhood, health, and Head Start organizations relevant to the paper's examples. detail.abstract: Conventional practitioner training programs in behavioral health, Indigenous community restoration, organizational wellness, and individual education face a persistent failure mode: skills taught in training do not consolidate into durable, automatized practice. This paper identifies the neurobiological substrate of that failure-body budget depletion, working memory suppression, and the absence of relational safety conditions that consolidation requires-and proposes a fivecomponent integrated pedagogical architecture that addresses it. The Pentagonal Walker Pedagogy integrates: (1) the Chugach School District's competency-based circular time pacing principle; (2) Training Within Industry's Learning Breakdown and four-step instruction sequence with the naming step explicit; (3) Oakley's chunking and spaced retrieval architecture; (4) the Disney sensory environment protocol as a body budget preparation sequence; and (5) the I.C.A.R.E. facilitation framework as the relational substrate maintenance protocol. The paper advances three arguments beyond its initial framing. First, the Pentagonal Pedagogy is a general theory of consolidation applicable across facilitator training, individual education, and self-directed learning-not only Walker curriculum delivery. Second, Sealaska Heritage Institute's Baby Raven Reads program is identified as the zero-to-five proof of concept for all five components operating simultaneously in an Indigenous early literacy context, providing the empirical anchor the theory requires. Third, the working memory to durable memory pathway is specified as a three-stage neurobiological sequence-encoding, hippocampal consolidation, and neocortical integrationwith each of the five pedagogical components mapped to its precise intervention point in that sequence. A three-phase metacognitive development model describes how individual learners progress from receiving the architecture passively to constructing and applying it independently. Fourteen falsifiable propositions are generated. The Pentagonal Walker Pedagogy is an Andersonoriginated construct; a search of the literature confirms that no prior use of this specific integrated five-component framework has been reported under this name.

title: Business Diversification and Informational Efficiency -causal Evidence from a Mandatory Non-diversification Reform
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Business, Department of Accounting, School of Management, Fudan University and Renmin University of China, School of Business

detail.title: Business Diversification and Informational Efficiency -causal Evidence from a Mandatory Non-diversification Reform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or other interests.

detail.abstract: By exploiting a mandatory non-diversification reform, we examine the causal effect of business diversification on informational efficiency. In an effort to urge state-owned enterprises to refocus, the Chinese government rolled out a staggering mandate which requires local SOEs to reduce the scope and heterogeneity of their business segments. We construct a pseudo conglomerate which consists of a portfolio of stand-alone firms mimicking each real conglomerate. Consistent with Cohen and Lou (2012), we find that pseudo conglomerates' stock returns positively predict real conglomerates' one-month-ahead stock returns, i.e., informational inefficiency associated with business diversification. Importantly, this return predictability significantly weakens for SOEs relative to non-SOEs after the nondiversification reform. The reform's effect on informational efficiency becomes more pronounced for firms with lower investor sophistication or poorer information environment before the reform, i.e., sources of return predictability. Mechanism analyses suggest that, through non-diversifications, SOEs experience improvements in the quality of both internal control and financial reporting. Collectively, empirical findings provide causal evidence regarding whether and how business diversification shapes informational efficiency.

title: Identification in Many-to-Many Matching Games
affiliations: The University of Sydney

detail.title: Identification in Many-to-Many Matching Games
detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural model of many-to-many matching with endogenous link formation under max-min preferences. Agents on both sides of the market form subsets of partners subject to capacity constraints, choosing links to maximize the minimum utility received across all connections. We characterize the limiting behavior of stable matchings as market size grows and establish convergence of conditional choice probabilities to closed-form expressions governed by inclusive value functions. We use degree distributions as a novel source of identification, and show that the degree of each agent follows a binomial distribution with parameters determined by inclusive values, which are in turn pinned down by equilibrium behavior. Our results extend existing one-to-one matching frameworks to more complex many-to-many environments.

title: Irreversible Investment in Alternative Projects under Regime Switching
affiliations: , The University of Osaka and The University of Osaka

detail.title: Irreversible Investment in Alternative Projects under Regime Switching
detail.abstract: We study how a firm should choose investment timing and project scale when profitability shifts between regimes. The firm can irreversibly undertake either a smaller, lower-cost project or a larger, higher-capacity project with higher sunk cost. Profitability follows a two-state Markov regime-switching process whose growth and volatility vary by regime. Combining regime switching with scale choice means that a regime shift affects both whether the firm invests and which project it selects. An upward transition from the bad to the good regime may trigger either project, depending on the earnings fundamental. A distinctive result is that, when both projects remain relevant, a downward transition from the good to the bad regime can trigger investment in the small project. The deterioration does not raise project profitability; instead, it can reduce the option value of waiting for the large project relative to immediate small-scale investment. Numerical analysis illustrates representative trigger patterns and how they vary with project characteristics and regime dynamics. The results show that regime shifts shape irreversible investment through the interaction of timing flexibility and endogenous scale choice.

title: Recursive Copula Aggregation for Market and Credit Portfolios
affiliations: University of Turin - Department of Management, Core Dynamics GmbH and

detail.title: Recursive Copula Aggregation for Market and Credit Portfolios
detail.abstract:
Risk aggregation is a central problem in financial risk management and regulatory capital assessment. While copula-based approaches are widely used due to their tractability and interpretability, standard implementations rely on flat dependence structures that may fail to capture hierarchical interactions across risk components. 

    This paper introduces a hierarchical copula framework for risk aggregation on trees, in which dependence is specified locally at each aggregation node and propagated through recursive rankbased reordering. The approach preserves marginal distributions while enabling flexible and economically interpretable modeling of dependence across multiple aggregation levels. 

     Copula parameters are calibrated from empirical data using Kendalls tau, and the methodology is illustrated using market and credit risk proxies. Robustness is assessed across alternative credit segments, including investment-grade and high-yield indices. Numerical results show that dependence strength increases under stress and varies systematically across credit quality, with important implications for risk measurement. 

     The proposed framework combines the transparency of copula-based aggregation with the structural richness of hierarchical models, providing a practical and scalable tool for enterprise risk management. This contributes to bridging bottom-up and top-down approaches to risk aggregation.

title: Change Course, Stay the Course: How People Respond to Persistent and Transitory Shocks
affiliations: and UNSW Australia Business School, School of Banking and Finance

detail.title: Change Course, Stay the Course: How People Respond to Persistent and Transitory Shocks
detail.abstract: Knowing when to change course or stay the course is only half the problem: rewardtriggered persistence and loss-triggered flight may obstruct execution. We test this idea in a high-stakes laboratory experiment with diagnostics separating expected-value misclassification from execution failures. Nearly one-third failed to classify a frequentwinner strategy as unprofitable. Among those with verified understanding, rewards delayed departure from a dying trend, interim losses induced abandonment of an optimal strategy, and temporary shocks triggered exit from positions known to recover. These patterns' timing and direction accord with a preregistered Pavlovian approach-avoidance account and challenge leading alternatives on their strongest margins.

title: Contagion through Opacity: Design and Survival in the November 2025 Stablecoin Cascade
affiliations: and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Contagion through Opacity: Design and Survival in the November 2025 Stablecoin Cascade
detail.abstract: In early November 2025 the yield-bearing stablecoin sector experienced its first systemic run: over roughly seventy-two hours, three synthetic dollar tokens lost between 94 and 99 percent of their value, set off by the disclosure of an external-manager loss at Stream Finance. Using hourly on-chain data we reconstruct the cascade and show that survival was not determined by on-chain exposure or scale-the largest instrument, sUSDe, held its peg while absorbing several hundred million dollars of redemptions-but by the quality of the backing and whether redemptions were honored under stress. We further show that the contagion did not travel through observable decentralized-finance composability: public lending exposure to the failed collateral was negligible. Transmission ran instead through off-chain reserve relationships and, in the single material public exposure, through a price oracle that remained frozen at the pre-crash value, implying a roughly 119-fold overvaluation weeks into the collapse, so that no liquidation fired and approximately $7.5 million of bad debt accrued without a single onchain bad-debt event. We read the episode as evidence that opacity in valuation, rather than composability, was the systemic channel, and draw implications for the disclosure, redemption, and oracle requirements that govern tokenized dollars. The paper is a descriptive and structural anatomy of one systemic episode; we make no causal-identification claim.

title: Consumer Value of Privacy: Evidence from an Online Retailer
affiliations: University College London,  and Mitchell E. Daniels, Jr School of Business, Purdue University

detail.title: Consumer Value of Privacy: Evidence from an Online Retailer
detail.abstract: We study how much consumers value personal information using data from an online retailer's tiered loyalty program. Consumers receive points for disclosing personal information. While points awarded are fixed, their effective value varies quasi-experimentally with distance to the tier-upgrade threshold. Exploiting this variation, we estimate how incentives affect disclosure, and recover bounds on the value of personal information. Disclosure increases with incentives, and valuations differ across data types. Consumers value mobile number ($0.99) and payment card details ($1.02) more than date of birth ($0.20). More engaged consumers value their information more, suggesting privacy valuations depend on consumer experience with firms.

title: The Thinnest Place: A Designation Architecture without an Offense, and the Reasonableness of Fear

detail.title: The Thinnest Place: A Designation Architecture without an Offense, and the Reasonableness of Fear
detail.abstract: Federal law defines domestic terrorism but creates no offense of domestic terrorism. What the definition supports is a sentencing enhancement and a set of investigative authorities, which means the label attaches without ever being submitted to a jury and therefore without ever being subject to acquittal. Federal law likewise provides no mechanism for designating a domestic organization a terrorist organization, though an executive directive has instructed the Attorney General to propose such designations. This article traces where an architecture built on an unchargeable label operates first, and argues that the answer follows from Fourth Amendment geography: it operates at the border, because that is the point at which a citizen's protection against search is thinnest and the Eleventh Circuit requires no suspicion of any kind. A prosecution arising from an Atlanta airport encounter supplies the worked example. The article then identifies a second problem the same architecture creates. Whether a person was seized, whether an encounter was custodial, and whether consent was voluntary are each measured by what a reasonable person would believe, and each test assumes a background in which fear of federal officers is unreasonable absent particularized threat. Where a government has generated a documented record of lethal force against citizens and has publicly characterized political opposition as terrorism, that assumption fails, and a doctrine that continues to apply it transfers the cost of the government's own posture onto the individual who felt its effect.

title: Long-Run Dynamics of US Profitability: Counteracting Tendencies and the Falling Rate of Profit
affiliations: and Aristotle University of Thessaloniki

detail.title: Long-Run Dynamics of US Profitability: Counteracting Tendencies and the Falling Rate of Profit

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author(s) declared no potential conflicts of interest with respect to the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval is not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author(s) received no financial support for the research, authorship, and/or publication of this article.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the tendency of the rate of profit to fall in Classical, Marxian, and Keynesian political economy, emphasizing Marx's counteracting tendencies. Using annual US data for 1950-2024, we estimate an autoregressive distributed lag model in which the profit rate depends on the organic composition of capital and various proxies of the principal counteracting tendencies to the aforementioned falling rate of profit. A higher organic composition of capital is associated with a lower profit rate. The cheapening of capital goods is the most robust counteracting factor, while the equity/GDP ratio also has a positive long-run association. These influences moderate but do not offset the long-run decline in US profitability.

title: Emergent Strategic Behaviour in a Macroeconomic Agent-Based Model with Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: Catholic University of Milan, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Università di Milano Cattolica and Catholic University of Milan

detail.title: Emergent Strategic Behaviour in a Macroeconomic Agent-Based Model with Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: In canonical macroeconomic agent-based model (ABM), firms pursue behavioural (non-optimal) price and quantity strategies, that take the form of heuristics. In this paper we incorporate reinforcement learning (RL) into an otherwise standard ABM by replacing a fraction of heuristic-using firms with RL agents that learn profitmaximizing strategies through repeated interaction with the economic environment. When RL agents adopt a shared Q-function, they endogenously converge to one of three distinct strategic regimes – market power, predatory pricing, or quasi-perfect competition – with the prevailing equilibrium depending on the degree of market competition and the share of RL agents. Under independent Q-functions, agents spontaneously segregate into heterogeneous strategies, yielding higher aggregate market power and producer surplus without explicit coordination. The prevalence of RL agents shapes aggregate output and volatility in a non-monotonic way. To rationalize these findings, we develop a stylized theoretical framework that links the competition intensity between RL and non-RL agents with the prevailing optimal pricing strategies.

title: Smartphones and Children's Mental Health

detail.title: Smartphones and Children's Mental Health
detail.abstract: Children's mental health has deteriorated across high-income countries since the early 2010s, coinciding with the mass adoption of smartphones among young people. I provide the first quasi-experimental evidence on delaying children's smartphone ownership through a community-led policy. Since 2024 the Smartphone Free Childhood movement has coordinated families across the United Kingdom through a "Parent Pact" to delay giving children a smartphone until age 14. Using a matched difference-in-differences design, I compare changes in children's mental-health needs in English schools where a large share of parents signed with changes in similar schools where very few did. Where at least one fifth of families signed, school-recorded social, emotional and mental health need falls by around 8 percent of the counterfactual. At the same time, child psychiatric disability claims, determined independently by the Department for Work and Pensions, also fall by about 6 percent in the same communities. The effects are larger among younger children who are less likely to already have a phone and in neighborhoods where more parents sign the pledge. The findings support coordinated ownership delay as a near-zero-cost complement to school phone bans and statutory age limits, and they give parents causal evidence for delaying a child's first smartphone through the primary-school years.

title: Changing Gender Norms Across Generations: Evidence from a Paternity Leave Reform
affiliations: , University of St. Gallen, Universitat Pompeu Fabra and

detail.title: Changing Gender Norms Across Generations: Evidence from a Paternity Leave Reform
detail.abstract: Social norms are an important barrier to gender convergence in economic outcomes. We study whether a public policy designed to promote gender equality at home can pave the way towards gender convergence by shaping gender norms in the next generation. We exploit the introduction of paid paternity leave in Spain in 2007, which granted fathers 13 days of non-transferable paid leave after childbirth. Eligibility depended sharply on the child’s date of birth. We combine this policy variation with original survey data collected from adolescents and implement a within-school difference-in-differences design comparing children born just before and after the reform cutoff within the same school cohort, using adjacent cohorts as controls. Children exposed to paternity leave eligibility display more egalitarian gender attitudes and beliefs in early adolescence. They are also more likely to engage in counter-stereotypical household chores, and hold less gender-stereotypical expectations regarding future work and family roles. The effects largely disappear in late adolescence.

title: How Does the Cost of Capital Affect Oil Production?
affiliations: Technical University of Denmark,  and Technical University of Denmark

detail.title: How Does the Cost of Capital Affect Oil Production?
detail.abstract: In the spirit of green finance taxonomies, restricting fossil-fuel producers' access to funds is hoped to help address the climate problem. We develop a project-level model of oil production, calibrate it to the universe of U.S. and Canadian oil projects producible over 2000-2024, and simulate the effects of the cost of capital. Modest increases in this cost are counterproductive, increasing oil production through industry short-termism while reducing project value. Effective costs of capital are unrealistically large, at odds with projects' internal rates of return. At the industry level, a higher cost of capital generates equilibrium adjustments that boost oil profitability.

title: Determinants of Rates of Return on Leveraged ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds)

detail.title: Determinants of Rates of Return on Leveraged ETFs (Exchange Traded Funds)
detail.abstract:
LETF (leveraged exchange traded fund) is a special case of ETF (exchange traded fund) which aims to obtain L-times the rate of return on the underlying instrument during the contractual period. Although the LETF market was created relatively recently, in 2006, assets under management of these funds have already exceeded USD 50 billion worldwide. At the same time there is a misunderstanding among investors and other market participants, as well as in academic circles, what LETF is and what long-term return rates is promised. The LETF's obligation to realize L-times rates of return on the underlying instrument in the short term (contractual period) is, counterintuitively, not the same as the promise of achieving the L-times return on the underlying instrument in the long term.
This dissertation shows that LETFs achieve their contractual objectives in the short term, which means that short-term rates of return from LETF are indeed L-times the rates of return on the underlying instrument. What is most controversial in the literature and practice are long-term returns, which, apart from costs, include also a complicated leverage effect. It is the existence of a complex leverage effect, defined and described in the dissertation, that makes the LETF's commitment to achieve L-times the rate of return on the underlying instrument during the contractual period not equivalent to achieve L-times the rate of return over the long term.
As shown in the dissertation, for a single path, either the LETF > L × ETF or LETF < L × ETF relationships can occur. Equality is practically impossible - even theoretically and without considering costs. The simulation showed that the relation LETF = L × ETF ± 0.1 p.p. is observed only in a few percent of possible paths. The LETF results depend on the characteristics of the rates of return on the underlying instrument, hence the percentage share of the paths LETF > L × ETF, LETF < L × ETF and LETF = L × ETF ± 0.1 p.p. differs for various distributions.
Conducted simulations have shown that the dominant share of paths meet the LETF < L × ETF condition, making it the rule, not the exception. Depending on the characteristics of the distribution of returns on the underlying instrument, the share of LETF > L × ETF paths is usually only about 30-40% for symmetrical distributions of returns and the long-term distribution of returns from S&P 500 TR.
Paths that meet the condition LETF > L × ETF are observed for extreme rates of return on the underlying instrument. Inversely, LETF < L × ETF paths occur for central rates of return from the underlying instrument. This is another rule observed for all the distributions analyzed in the dissertation.
In the dissertation, a theoretical model was introduced and the complex leverage effect was decomposed into a positive effect of leverage capitalization and a negative effect of sign volatility. It was pointed out that in paths LETF > L × ETF, the positive effect of leverage capitalization is stronger than the negative effect of sign volatility, whereas in paths LETF < L × ETF, the positive effect of leverage capitalization is weaker than the negative effect of sign volatility.
The dissertation showed that the Cheng-Madhavan (C-M) formula is not accurate in the case of outliers, and the differences between C-M and LETF can be up to several dozen percentage points. This observation is important from a practical point of view, because atypical rates of return occur in practice more often than it would appear from the theoretical normal distribution. Market events from March / April 2020 confirm the relatively frequent occurrence of outliers..
The determinants of rates of return from LETFs can be classified into: (1) factors related to the underlying instrument, such as expected rate of return, volatility, skewness, or kurtosis; and (2) LETF-specific factors, such as leverage ratio L or capitalization frequency. All of these factors affect the complex leverage effect that fully describes the relationship between LETF and L x ETF.

title: MICHELE: The Computation of Healthy Life Expectancy from Mortality Schedules
affiliations: and University of Göttingen - School of Law, Economics, Social Sciences

detail.title: MICHELE: The Computation of Healthy Life Expectancy from Mortality Schedules
detail.abstract: Healthy life expectancy is conventionally computed by combining life-table mortality with independently observed health information. This paper proposes an alternative approach that computes healthy life expectancy from mortality schedules alone. Building on the empirical regularities that adult mortality follows Gompertz's law and that mortality is related to the frailty index by a power law, we introduce Mortality-Implied Continuous Health-Equivalent Life Expectancy (MICHELE). The framework is validated using the Health and Retirement Study, where MICHELE closely reproduces directly observed Continuous Health-Equivalent Life Expectancy, and using Healthy Life Expectancy from the Global Burden of Disease Study, where mortality-implied health weights explain almost all age-related variation in disability-based health weights. The results suggest that mortality schedules contain substantially more information about the biological aging process underlying healthy longevity than has generally been recognized and provide a simple approach for estimating healthy life expectancy when comparable health data are unavailable.

title: Healthy Life Expectancy for Individuals
affiliations: and University of Göttingen - School of Law, Economics, Social Sciences

detail.title: Healthy Life Expectancy for Individuals
detail.abstract: Healthy life expectancy is traditionally measured as a population statistic that assigns the same expected healthy remaining lifetime to all individuals of the same age. We develop healthy life expectancy as an individual concept by combining projected health trajectories with survival probabilities conditional on an individual's observed frailty. Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study, we show that the logarithm of the frailty index increases approximately linearly with age after controlling for permanent individual heterogeneity, implying an exponential law of deficit accumulation. Together with a sex-specific Gompertz mortality model, this regularity provides a simple framework for computing individual healthy life expectancy. The resulting measure reveals substantial heterogeneity in healthy remaining lifetime among individuals of the same age. Although sex, education, geography, and race and ethnicity are associated with systematic differences, most variation occurs within rather than between these groups.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Non-performing Assets, and Financial Inclusion: The Economics of AI Adoption in Indian Banking an International Comparative Review with Evidence from China, the European Union, and the United States
affiliations: Awadhesh Pratap Singh University, and  Government Thakur Ranmat Singh Autonomous College

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Non-performing Assets, and Financial Inclusion: The Economics of AI Adoption in Indian Banking an International Comparative Review with Evidence from China, the European Union, and the United States
detail.abstract: Between 2018 and 2026, India's banking sector moved from the depths of a non-performing asset (NPA) crisis — a gross NPA ratio of 11.6 percent, a paralysed corporate credit market, and a fragmented insolvency regime — to a gross NPA ratio of 1.8 percent, a multi-decade low. Over the same period, artificial intelligence (AI) moved from a peripheral pilot activity to a central plank of both credit risk management and financial-inclusion policy, formalised most recently in the Reserve Bank of India's Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of AI (FREE-AI, 2025). This review examines what AI has actually contributed to this turnaround and to the parallel expansion of formal credit access, reading the evidence through the economics of information: Stiglitz and Weiss's (1981) foundational model of credit rationing under asymmetric information, the more recent literature on alternative-data credit scoring, and an emerging empirical literature on algorithmic bias in lending. Drawing on RBI Financial Stability Reports, the FREE-AI Committee's own findings, data on India's Account Aggregator and Unified Lending Interface frameworks, and a comparative reading of China's Sesame Credit system, the European Union's AI Act, and the United States' fair-lending jurisprudence, the review finds that AI-enabled early-warning systems and supervisory technology (SupTech) have plausibly shortened the lag between financial distress and detection, but that India's NPA recovery owes at least as much to the 2015 Asset Quality Review, the 2016 Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, and roughly ₹3.10 lakh crore in public-sector-bank recapitalisation as to any AI-specific intervention — a causal ambiguity this review treats as a first-order finding rather than a caveat. On financial inclusion, India's Account Aggregator framework, linking over 252.9 million users by December 2025, represents a genuinely novel, consent-based solution to the information-asymmetry problem Stiglitz and Weiss first modelled, enabling cash-flow-based lending to borrowers with no conventional credit history. Yet the review also documents AI's new and distinct risks — algorithmic bias, opacity, and AI-enabled cyber-fraud, which the RBI's own Financial Stability Report now flags as a leading near-term threat — and situates India's principles-based regulatory response against the European Union's more prescriptive, high-risk classification of AI credit scoring and China's experience of reining in platform-based social-credit lending after 2020. The review closes with policy lessons for the design of AI governance in credit-market institutions more broadly.

title: Not What It Seems: Collaboration and Digital Format, Not Topic, Drive Citations in the 15-Minute City Literature
affiliations: Central Bank of Armenia

detail.title: Not What It Seems: Collaboration and Digital Format, Not Topic, Drive Citations in the 15-Minute City Literature
detail.abstract: The 15-minute city is frequently portrayed as a unifying paradigm in contemporary urban discourse. This study challenges that narrative. Through an analysis of 396 bibliographic records-203 of which explicitly reference "15-minute", "15-min", "x-minute", or "minute-city"-substantive fragmentation across measurement, planning, mobility, and proximity domains is documented. Employing sentiment analysis, source modality classification, team size metrics, and topic clustering, negative binomial and zero-inflated negative binomial citation models are estimated. Results reveal a highly skewed citation distribution, a pronounced age effect, and robust differentials attributable to team size and title sentiment. PDF-tagged records underperform relative to HTML - tagged ones, and modality interacts significantly with age: HTML accessible papers exhibit accelerated citation accumulation over time. No book-tagged titles appear, underscoring the journal-and web-centric visibility of the field. It is concluded that the 15-minute city does not constitute a unified research programme but rather a contested arena in which scholarly visibility is shaped more by collaboration, dissemination format, and linguistic framing than by substantive focus.

detail.abstract: Cropping decisions are not always autonomous, but the result of structural factors that govern markets and policies. This article explores the vulnerabilities resulting from cropping pattern changes in the water stressed Marathwada region in India. We draw upon field research conducted during 2022-23 involving a survey of 184 households from two villages in the region. The area under soybean has seen phenomenal increase in two decades, which along with sugarcane cultivation, has led to unsustainable groundwater use. The changes have resulted in inequities largely disfavouring the small farmers. We conclude that the farmers are able to exercise little agency and are primarily responding to external signals in making cropping decisions, resulting in unsustainable resource use and unviable livelihoods.

detail.abstract: We analyze whether explaining the benefits of the information generated from experimentation can encourage individuals to experiment with an unknown option. In an experiment, subjects repeatedly face a two-decision one-armed bandit problem. At the start of the first bandit, subjects receive one of four possible messages regarding the bandit's two options. Two messages encourage initially experimenting with the unknown option and two messages encourage initially selecting the known option. After the first bandit, subjects repeatedly face this same bandit and receive this same message. We find that subjects who repeatedly receive the message explaining the informational benefits of experimentation consistently experiment at the highest rate across bandits. Importantly, this message leads to more experimentation than a control message that suggests experimentation without explaining its informational benefits. Our results suggest that it is possible to encourage experimentation when an individual faces a single bandit and that repeated messaging can lead to a durably higher experimentation rate across bandits. We also find that providing this explanation in one bandit environment can lead to more experimentation in a different bandit environment.

detail.abstract: We examine how exogenous latency shocks affect price discovery and transaction costs by analyzing the temporary relocation of two U.S. equity exchanges. We find that increased latency reduces the price discovery contribution of the affected venues and alters liquidity provision. Effective spreads and price impacts fall, while realized spreads rise, consistent with a separating equilibrium in which informed traders avoid slower venues. These findings suggest that latency differentials create measurable distortions in market quality, with implications for both trading behavior, market design, and regulatory policy.

title: Russia’s Wartime Economy: Measuring Regional Inequalities from Outer Space
affiliations: , University of Angers - Lille - Economics & Management (LEM) - Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (UMR CNRS 8179), Brunel University London - Economics and Finance and European Research University

detail.title: Russia’s Wartime Economy: Measuring Regional Inequalities from Outer Space
detail.abstract: We study Russia's February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine as a natural experiment to determine how sudden disruptions to international market access reshape sub-national economic inequalities. Using remotely-sensed nighttime lights as a proxy for economic activity, we estimate the economic effects of the war at the national and regional levels. We find that Russia experienced an overall economic slowdown after the start of the full-scale invasion. Regions in Western and North-Western Russia experienced significantly larger economic contractions, while Southern and Southeastern regions exhibit relative improvements in performance. These findings suggest that sanctions, a shift toward non-Western markets, and increased military production, have driven significant regional changes in Russia’s economy and urban structure.

detail.abstract: Saffron, as the world's most valuable spice, holds strategic importance in non-oil trade and sustainable agricultural development. This study evaluates Iran's alignment with global demand dynamics in saffron exports using the Constant Market Share model, which decomposes export changes into scale, competitiveness, and second-order effects. Based on ITC export data from 2013 to 2022, the analysis focuses on Iran's major markets-UAE, Spain, China, and Afghanistan. The findings reveal that fluctuations in export volume were largely driven by competitiveness, especially in the volatile Chinese market. Additionally, the negative second-order effect in most years and destinations highlights Iran's limited responsiveness to structural changes in global demand. These results emphasize the need to revise marketing strategies and enhance Iran's saffron competitiveness through improved branding, product quality, and packaging.

title: Medicaid Expansion and Employment among Adults with Disabilities in Vocational Rehabilitation
affiliations: Northwestern University

detail.title: Medicaid Expansion and Employment among Adults with Disabilities in Vocational Rehabilitation
detail.abstract: The Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion opened an income-based route to public insurance for low-income adults with disabilities, whose Medicaid access had often depended on disability-specific eligibility pathways. This paper links national administrative records for 1.84 million Vocational Rehabilitation cases involving applicants ages 19 to 64 to the timing of state Medicaid expansions from 2013 through 2018. A staggered-adoption difference-indifferences design shows that expansion increased Medicaid coverage at application by 9.9 percentage points, or 24 percent relative to the pre-expansion mean, and any insurance coverage by 7.8 percentage points. Employment at case closure remained unchanged despite this substantial coverage gain. The estimates also show no corresponding changes in competitive integrated employment, part-time work, or receipt of Supplemental Security Income or Social Security Disability Insurance. Medicaid expansion therefore increased insurance coverage among adults with disabilities already seeking employment assistance without producing a detectable average employment response or measurably changing participation in federal disability programs.

title: What Do We Mean by Societal Collapse?

detail.title: What Do We Mean by Societal Collapse?
detail.abstract: Claims of societal collapse, whether about the past or the future, have never been more common. The concept itself, however, remains fragmented. Disciplines work with incompatible definitions, which obstructs comparison across completed cases and leaves claims about future collapse without discipline. This paper argues that every collapse verdict rests on assumptions that existing definitions leave unstated, including the unit of analysis, the dimensions of social life that count, whose well-being is tracked, the baseline of comparison, and the horizon of evaluation. The paper develops a definition and an assessment protocol that make these assumptions explicit. Social stability rests on three foundational pillars, namely the productive system, the state, and the social fabric. Collapse is a structural failure of that pillar system, in which disruption within one or more pillars becomes severe enough that the remaining pillars cannot compensate, escalating through three transmission channels of resource flows, legitimacy relations, and coordination dependencies. The protocol is an ordered sequence of explicit choices through which the definition is applied to any case, completed or open. Because the channels activate before pillar-level deterioration completes, the definition applies while a trajectory is still in motion; because normative commitments are surfaced rather than smuggled, the same trajectory can be read across evaluative frames. The protocol is demonstrated backward, on the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the Soviet dissolution, and the recent Lebanese crisis, where long-standing disagreements dissolve into artifacts of unstated assumptions, and forward, on compound climate stress, where claims of inevitable breakdown become monitorable hypotheses.

title: How to Silence Researchers? Evidence from Illiberal Policies in Hungary
affiliations: and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: How to Silence Researchers? Evidence from Illiberal Policies in Hungary
detail.abstract: We explore how contemporary attacks against academic freedom have detrimental effects on innovation, focusing on academic research in Hungary after the election of Viktor Orbán in 2010. Using rich national research repositories and international bibliometric data, we show that academics' trajectories diverge sharply depending on their perceived political alignment towards the government. Academics perceived as politically non-aligned experience a large decrease in their productivity and quality of their work. We explain this loss through the shrinking networks and declining influence of these authors. Targeted academics respond strongly, including by leaving the country and expressing dissent against the government. We show that academics self-censor in their academic work. Finally, individual-level crosscountry comparisons allow us to estimate the broader effects of declining academic freedom: Hungarian researchers increasingly reallocate their publication efforts toward lower-ranked national-language journals and are more likely to leave the country altogether.

title: We Came Back to Rubble and Hunger: A Messy, Human-Centered Look at Forced Return to Sudan
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title: We Came Back to Rubble and Hunger: A Messy, Human-Centered Look at Forced Return to Sudan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The paper discusses essential issues of peace in Sudan. I am a displaced victim and I want to go home
declarations.ethicsApproval: I am the author
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding

detail.abstract: Since Sudan's civil war started in April 2023, approximately 3.4 million people have returned to the country, with most ending up in Khartoum and Al Jazirah states. This paper addresses a critical puzzle: why would anyone return to a place with 170% inflation, half the population unemployed, and actual famine in some towns? Drawing on established migration theories, push-pull, demographic transition, the New Economics of Labor Migration, and cumulative causation, I argue that these frameworks require significant modification for the Sudanese context. The paper introduces two concepts: "reverse mobility transition" and "cyclical precarity." Returns are not occurring because Sudan is recovering but because life in host countries, particularly Egypt and Chad, has become impossible due to legal precarity, economic pressure, and deportation threats. Social networks transmit information suggesting that conditions in some home areas are "less bad" than in host countries. Using World Bank, IOM, UNHCR, and IPC data, this paper demonstrates that returns are a sign of running out of options rather than a sign of hope. The collapse of essential services, water, electricity, healthcare, and sanitation, creates conditions where returnees face displacement-like circumstances upon arrival. The paper concludes with policy recommendations emphasizing that returns should trigger increased, not decreased, humanitarian funding and protection measures. The theoretical contribution lies in reconceptualizing migration frameworks for contexts of state collapse rather than development, proposing a "Stage C" of mobility transition characterized by cyclical, reactive, and survival-driven movement patterns.

title:
Economic Determinism on a Five-Dimensional Manifold
A Deterministic Reformulation of Financial Risk Calculus for the Nine-Capital, Triple-Ledger Framework

detail.title:
Economic Determinism on a Five-Dimensional Manifold
A Deterministic Reformulation of Financial Risk Calculus for the Nine-Capital, Triple-Ledger Framework
detail.abstract: Background. Contemporary financial risk models — Value-at-Risk, Expected Shortfall, Black–Scholes– Merton, Merton default, CAPM, Vasicek/HJM term-structure models, Solvency II, Basel III/IV, IFRS 9/17 — are one-dimensional projections of an intrinsically higher-dimensional decision phenomenon. The projections perform within a narrow regime and generate the very tail instability they purport to measure outside that regime. Recurrent crises (1987, 1998, 2000, 2008, 2020, 2023) are not statistical anomalies but structural artefacts of dimensional reduction. Objective. This paper proposes and axiomatises Economic Determinism: a deterministic reformulation of the full financial risk calculus on a five-dimensional manifold, hereafter the Curzi Manifold M⁵, and demonstrates that the incumbent framework is recovered as a rigorous limiting case. Methods. We construct M⁵ over the axes (i) ordinal position ω (well-ordered sequence, not cardinal magnitude), (ii) rational magnitude r ∈ ℝ, (iii) logical validity ℓ ∈ [0,1] with an Aristotelian syllogistic kernel, (iv) imaginary phase iφ ∈ iℝ carrying non-commutative structure, and (v) choice χ, an agential– temporal coordinate exhibiting Heisenberg-type observation dependence. On M⁵ we impose (a) the Coverage Hyperbola invariant r · ℓ ≥ 1.8; (b) the Zero-Preserving Division (ZPD) axiom x/(0·y) = y, resolving denominator pathologies without singularities; (c) the Fibonacci-Signed Paradox-Resolution Algebra (FS-PRA), a graded signed calculus in which contradictions at level n are annihilated by Fibonacci-count balanced postulate pairs at level n+1; (d) a financial wave-function analog Ψ(χ, t) with Hamiltonian H generating deterministic evolution of choice-conditioned exposure; and (e) a quantumatom-theory analog quantising sovereign reserve shells with selection rules and a Pauli-analog exclusion on double-pledged collateral. Each incumbent risk operator is re-expressed as a deterministic map ρ: M⁵ → ℂ, red-teamed for logical consistency, operational feasibility, and regulatory compatibility, and shown to reduce continuously to its legacy form under a specified projection π: M⁵ → ℝ. Results. Thirty-one papers (EDP-000 through EDP-030) reformulate the canonical apparatus across credit, market, liquidity, counterparty, IRRBB, operational, portfolio, derivatives, fixed-income, equity, sovereign, FX, balance-of-payments, monetary transmission, structured products, systemic, contagion/network, insurance solvency, actuarial reserving, pension/LDI, commodity, energy, agricultural, fair-value/impairment, consolidation, hedge-accounting, digital-asset, climate, and algorithmic-risk domains, terminated by a master glossary. Principal formal results: (i) rehypothecation chains that violate the Coverage Hyperbola are provably paradoxical under FS-PRA and admit a unique deterministic annihilation; (ii) the Merton–Black–Scholes call price recovers as the ℓ → 1, iφ → 0, χ collapsed limit of the deterministic derivative operator; (iii) VaR-style tail metrics recover as the ordinal-flattened, choiceintegrated projection of an unfolded M⁵ exposure surface; (iv) sovereign default is a shell-transition event with a selection rule expressible in closed form; and (v) systemic risk becomes a coverage-hyperbola violation counted with Fibonacci multiplicity. Contribution. The paper (a) formalises the first deterministic risk calculus that is dimensionally complete with respect to observable market structure; (b) supplies backward-compatible reductions to every current regulatory metric (Basel, Solvency, IFRS); (c) proposes a three-tier adoption pathway (shadow reporting → parallel books → primary ledger) preserving legal and accounting continuity; and (d) unifies the NineCapital taxonomy and the Triple-Ledger (Nostro / Vostro / Lux) architecture within a single risk-theoretic object. Implications. If the framework is correct, the persistent excess volatility, correlation breakdowns, liquidity air-pockets, and cross-asset contagion that classical risk systems misclassify as fat tails are instead deterministic consequences of operating a five-dimensional system with two-dimensional instruments. Adoption is optional, gradual, and reversible until the terminal tier; the reduction property guarantees that no institution is worse off at any adoption depth. The framework is offered as a convergent, cooperative, and non-coercive completion of the existing risk canon.

title: A Survey of Cases of the Pay-For-Delay Agreement in the Post-Actavis Era
affiliations: National Sun Yat-Sen University

detail.title: A Survey of Cases of the Pay-For-Delay Agreement in the Post-Actavis Era
detail.abstract: What are the further developments on pay-for-delay agreements following Actavis, the case decided by the US Supreme Court regarding a pay-for-delay dispute in 2013? We surveyed 17 pay-to-delay deals involving brand-name drug owners and generic companies to see how their deals were structured in light of Actavis, as well as the results of follow-on court cases involving such contracts. As a result, we posit here that a no-Authorized Generic (AG) provision, the clause in a pay-for-delay agreement that asks the company making the brand-name drug not to launch its own generic drug in the market, occurred in almost half of the deals in our survey. More importantly, we found that the judges in cases following Actavis did not establish a framework to analyse whether pay-for-delay payments were large and unjustified. Therefore, the judges could not adequately explain why a given pay-for-delay agreement may have been anti-competitive under the rule-of-reason test under Actavis. Through these findings, we inferred that drug manufacturers should be able to avoid including no-AG provisions in their settlements. Finally, we predicted that antitrust agencies and courts would achieve a stronger interpretation of 'large and unjustified payments' if they unified the analytical framework for pay-for-delay agreements. Keywords: pay-for-delay agreements, large and unjustified payment, rule-of-reason test, antitrust law 1. The first reverse payment case can be traced back to 2000. It was In re Terazosin Hydrochloride Antitrust Litigation, decided in the US District Court of the Southern District of Florida. 2. In 2017, the FTC stated that 28 such deals had been made and 127 such arrangements had been struck between 2005 and 2011 at an annual cost to consumers of $3.5 billion in artificially higher prices.

title: Stablecoins and (Non)Crypto Shocks: A 2026 Update
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Isenberg School of Management and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: Stablecoins and (Non)Crypto Shocks: A 2026 Update

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Stablecoins are digital assets whose value is pegged to that of a fiat currency, typically the U.S. dollar at a peg of $1.00 per token.  In a previous blog post, we described the rapid growth of stablecoins through early 2025, highlighted changes in stablecoins’ reserve-asset composition, and examined their reactions to Bitcoin price shocks. In this post, we document the growth of stablecoins since our last post. Then, we examine how shocks from outside the crypto industry can impact the composition of stablecoins’ reserve assets. For our case study, we use the 2023 failure of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and its impact on USD Coin (USDC, issued by Circle), the second-largest stablecoin by market capitalization.

To view post: https://libertystreeteconomics.newyorkfed.org/2026/07/stablecoins-and-noncrypto-shocks-a-2026-update/

title: Income Paths and the Marginal Utility of Income

detail.title: Income Paths and the Marginal Utility of Income
detail.abstract: Income is one of the most robust predictors of subjective well-being, yet its marginal value is usually treated as independent of the path through which current income is reached. We argue that the same income level may matter differently depending on recent income history. Using the German SocioEconomic Panel (SOEP) for 2000-2020, we classify income paths by net income growth over dynamic three-, four-, and five-year windows and estimate individual fixed-effects models of life satisfaction. The results reveal a clear asymmetry: current income has a larger association with life satisfaction after downward income paths than after upward paths, while flat paths lie between these cases. The difference is sizeable: across path windows, the upward-path income gradient is roughly one-third lower than the downward-path gradient, and about 40 percent lower in the four-year baseline specification. This pattern is consistent with income serving a stronger protective or restorative role after deterioration, whereas sustained gains are partly absorbed by adaptation and rising aspirations. The result is robust to alternative income definitions, the treatment of income outliers, initial-income-decile fixed effects, alternative path cutoffs, and alternative model specifications. We interpret the evidence as showing that the marginal utility of income is path-dependent: income matters not only because of where individuals stand today, but also because of the route by which they arrived there.

title: The Economic Impacts of Hurricanes on Fisheries in the United States
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: The Economic Impacts of Hurricanes on Fisheries in the United States
detail.abstract: Hurricanes routinely traverse water and land along the Southeastern United States, bringing with them hazardous weather conditions at sea, which presumably hinder fishing operations. Yet, work examining the impact of hurricanes on fisheries has mostly focused on supply chain analyses and post-disaster recovery, without paying attention to the first link in a long chain of events: how hazardous weather affects fisheries production. Here, we quantify the economic toll of hurricanes on commercial fisheries in the Southeastern United States. We construct a novel, high-frequency county-level panel linking daily commercial landings and revenue to hurricane exposure from 2005 to 2022. Our results indicate that county-level wind exposure reduces daily commercial landings and revenue by up to 60 and 70% under major-hurricane-force winds. Monetizing responses indicate cumulative revenue losses of $162.4 million over 2005--2022 due to hurricanes. These findings underscore the persistent vulnerability of coastal fisheries to extreme weather and provide an empirical foundation for targeted disaster preparedness and climate adaptation policy.

title: Numerical Validation of AnalyVa's PLS-SEM Engine Against SmartPLS 4: Simple Moderation, Extended Moderation, and Multiple Interaction Models
affiliations: Department of English Studies Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, Fes, Morocco and Department of English Studies Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, Fes, Morocco

detail.title: Numerical Validation of AnalyVa's PLS-SEM Engine Against SmartPLS 4: Simple Moderation, Extended Moderation, and Multiple Interaction Models

declarations.declarationOfInterest: A.B. is the principal developer of AnalyVa, which is distributed commercially; this constitutes a competing interest and is disclosed here. The authors report no other competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) is a widely used method in behavioral and social science research, but its use is limited by software access and specialized desktop software. AnalyVa is a desktop statistical analysis platform (offline, locally installed) based on Electron that provides complete PLS-SEM capabilities, such as reflective model estimation, moderation analysis, and second-stage interaction modeling, without the need for internet connection or programming skills. This tutorial compares AnalyVa with the current reference standard, SmartPLS 4, for three model specifications: (1) a simple four-construct reflective model, (2) an extended moderation model with one multi-item moderator, and (3) a multiple interaction model with three single-item moderators and all higher-order interaction terms. We compare outer loadings, construct reliability and validity, discriminant validity (HTMT and Fornell-Larcker criterion), structural path coefficients, effect sizes (f²), and model fit indices (SRMR and NFI) using an existing data set (n = 344) from the corporate reputation literature. Results show good agreement, with the largest absolute differences being less than .010 for path coefficients and less than .006 for outer loadings for all three models. Systematic divergences in model fit reporting are identified and explained: AnalyVa separately reports saturated and estimated model fit indices-a distinction SmartPLS 4 collapses for simple models. AnalyVa's Smart Model Health diagnostics flagged an elevated outer VIF in the extended moderation model ANALYVA VALIDATION AGAINST SMARTPLS 2 not surfaced by SmartPLS 4. The results indicate that AnalyVa is a methodologically sound and diagnostically useful desktop alternative to PLS-SEM practitioners.

title: Validating AnalyVa Against SmartPLS 4: A Benchmark of CB-SEM Factor Analysis, Latent Growth Curve Modelling, and Gaussian Copula Analysis
affiliations: Department of English Studies Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, Fes, Morocco and Department of English Studies Sidi Mohamed Ben Abdellah University, Fes, Morocco

detail.title: Validating AnalyVa Against SmartPLS 4: A Benchmark of CB-SEM Factor Analysis, Latent Growth Curve Modelling, and Gaussian Copula Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: A.B. is the principal developer of AnalyVa, which is distributed commercially; this constitutes a competing interest and is disclosed here. The authors report no other competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this study.

detail.abstract: The adoption of new statistical software platforms in behavioural and social science research requires rigorous cross-platform validation before any recommendation to the scholarly community. This paper reports the numerical validation of AnalyVa, an Electron-based desktop platform, against SmartPLS 4 across five benchmark studies encompassing covariance-based structural equation modelling (CB-SEM), configural multi-group analysis (MGA), latent growth curve modelling (LGCM), and Gaussian copula endogeneity correction in both OLS regression and PLS-SEM contexts. Using the classic Holzinger-Swineford dataset for CB-SEM studies, a simulated four-wave longitudinal dataset (n = 400) for LGCM, a purpose-built endogenous simulation (n = 500) for OLS copula, and the Corporate Reputation dataset (N = 344) for PLS-SEM copula, concordance was assessed via mean absolute deviation (MAD) against established thresholds. Results revealed a consistent gradient of agreement: perfect concordance in LGCM (MAD = .0000) and OLS copula (MAD = .000), excellent concordance in CFA standardized loadings (MAD = .0003), excellent MGA concordance in both subgroups (MAD = .001; maximum |Δ| = .005), and excellent PLS-SEM copula concordance across outer loadings (MAD = .003), structural paths (MAD = .007), and R² values (|Δ| ≤ .001). Minor deviations were attributable to established statistical artefacts-AGFI sensitivity at small sample sizes, RMSEA computation conventions, and copula-induced multicollinearity-rather than platform-specific algorithmic differences. These findings validate AnalyVa's CB-SEM, LGCM, and Gaussian copula implementations as numerically equivalent to SmartPLS 4, providing applied researchers with an empirically supported basis for adopting AnalyVa in confirmatory factor analysis, longitudinal growth modelling, and endogeneity-corrected regression.

title: Patriotism Deficit and Nigeria's Growth-Development Paradox
affiliations: Federal University Gashua and Federal University Gashua

detail.title: Patriotism Deficit and Nigeria's Growth-Development Paradox
detail.abstract: Growth and development are two distinct concepts that are often used interchangeably. While Nigeria has witnessed growth over the years, it has lagged behind on major key development indicators. The size of its economy has neither improved the socioeconomic condition of most of its citizens nor improved the country's development ranking. The steady growth of Nigeria's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is an evidence that it has the potential for development. Yet, its paradoxical low Human Development Index (HDI) is a strong indication of underdevelopment. Existing literature attributes this growth-development paradox to corruption and weak institutions, but under theorizes the attitudinal dimension of those elected to manage Nigeria's economy. This paper addresses this gap. Adopting Civic Nationalism Theory as analytical lens, the study uses content analysis of secondary data from the 2023 supplementary budget, 2024 Appropriation Act, and HDI/GDP reports. Findings reveal two key obstacles to national development: budget padding/misallocation and lavish spending by elected officials. Evidence shows that Nigerian rulers prioritize personal/constituency benefits over constitutional responsibility for collective welfare, violating civic nationalism's principle of shared responsibility. The paper concludes that attitudinal change, patriotism, and self-sacrifice, which must be exemplified by the ruling class, are the catalysts for national development. This paper strongly recommends that only patriotic and selfless Nigerians with verifiable track records of public/community services and absence of corruption should be elected to manage the country's economy in order to harness its resources for sustainable development. To enable this, citizens' enlightenment and education geared towards qualitative political participation are essential keys.

title: Advice as an Algorithm: Evaluating Intergenerational Knowledge Transfer in a Dynamic Social Learning Experiment
affiliations: Purdue University - Krannert School of Management, Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics and

detail.title: Advice as an Algorithm: Evaluating Intergenerational Knowledge Transfer in a Dynamic Social Learning Experiment
detail.abstract: We study intergenerational knowledge transfer in a social learning experiment in which subjects complete a 20-period consumption-and-saving task and then write free-form advice for the next generation who face a similar but distinct task. To measure the decision value of advice, we use a large language model to translate the text of advice into an executable consumption policy and evaluate that policy via simulations in the experimental environment. We refer to this simulated decision value as advice quality. We find that better-performing subjects write higher-quality advice, that mentor incentives raise advice quality, and that performance converts into advice quality more strongly when the task is more demonstrable. Importantly, we show that advice quality matters. It predicts successor performance and adds value beyond what the successor can infer from observation alone. However, we do not find that advice quality improves across generations. Instead, it reproduces only indirectly via the performance channel. Taken together, our results show that natural-language advice contains measurable behavioral content beyond word count and the observation of predecessor behavior.

title: Geographic Dispersion and the Cost of Debt

detail.title: Geographic Dispersion and the Cost of Debt
detail.abstract: Does operating across many states raise a firm's cost of debt? We measure geographic dispersion from the text of 294,290 annual reports filed between 1994 and 2025 and relate it to the pricing of syndicated loans, corporate bonds, and firm fundamentals. Dispersed firms pay more to borrow from banks, while the same firms' bonds do not price their footprint at all. Holding industry, year, size, and default risk fixed, a one-standard-deviation increase in the number of states a firm names raises its loan spread by about 1.7 percent, between three and four basis points at the median facility, and its accounting cost of debt rises with it. The gap between the two markets holds among borrowers who use both in the same year. Since a change in default risk would reach a bank and a bondholder alike, the premium reflects what a bank spends to evaluate and monitor a geographically complex borrower rather than a shift in credit quality. A change in the law sets the most concrete alternative aside. When the 2001 revision of secured-transactions law removed the state-by-state cost of taking collateral, the premium on dispersed borrowers did not fall, even as those borrowers pledged collateral more readily once it became cheaper to take. The reform moved the quantity of collateral, not the price of credit.

title: Pricing Clean Hydrogen and Its Derivatives: Evidence from a 2025 Practitioner Survey

detail.title: Pricing Clean Hydrogen and Its Derivatives: Evidence from a 2025 Practitioner Survey

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this article.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how pricing models for clean hydrogen and its derivatives are evolving, and what those models must deliver to support project-financed transactions in a market that still lacks a liquid spot price or settled benchmark. The analysis draws on a 2025 IPFA-facilitated survey of 19 senior practitioners, covering pricing models in use and stakeholder preferences on market price risk allocation. More than 80% of respondents were pursuing limited-or non-recourse financing: the structures that make pricing a bankability question. The paper reframes pricing as a two-task problem: first allocating a structural cost gap between public support, offtaker willingness to pay and producer returns; then allocating market price risk over a long-dated offtake. Survey evidence indicates that pricing approaches are diversifying rather than converging on a single model: fixed-price structures remain the anchor but are likely losing dominance to benchmark-linked pricing, with respondents expecting a mix of fossil-linked, regional and project-specific pricing models. The findings are reassessed against the 2026 Strait of Hormuz oil shock and the broader shift in sector investment and expectations since the survey. No firm offtake at scale or durable narrowing of the cost gap is on the horizon, yet these trends recast clean hydrogen from a climate choice into an energy security tool and strengthen the case for regional, not global, price references. For lenders, three implications follow: cost competitiveness as the first credit question, minimum-price protection as central to debt sizing, and case-by-case market and regulatory due diligence as a precondition for committing capital.

title: The Factor Structure of 0DTE Option Returns
affiliations: HEC Montreal, HEC Montréal and

detail.title: The Factor Structure of 0DTE Option Returns

declarations.funderStatement: Canadian Derivatives Institute and Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council funded this research

detail.abstract: Zero-days-to-expiration (0DTE) options have become half of SPX trading volume. We ask which systematic risks their returns compensate and whether their prices are efficient. Six factors: three realized return moments and three variance-dynamics components, span 30-minute SPX option returns at maturities from 45 minutes up to 15 days and price 0DTEs jointly with longer-dated contracts. Warehousing gamma and absorbing jump-skewness exposure earn premiums; the variance-component premiums differ but sum to zero intraday. Remaining alpha concentrates in 0DTEs, yet a factorneutral strategy becomes infeasible under minimal transaction costs. Option alphas fall as inventories build and, secondarily, intermediary balance sheet conditions tighten.

title: Beyond Risk-Based Rhetoric: What Basel III Reveals About AI Governance Challenges

detail.title: Beyond Risk-Based Rhetoric: What Basel III Reveals About AI Governance Challenges

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The research was conducted while the author was a student at UCL. The author is currently employed at a UK government-backed investment fund; the views expressed are the author's own and the research was completed prior to that employment.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study involved analysis of publicly available regulatory documents only; no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no funding for this research.

detail.abstract:
The regulation of general-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) poses fundamental challenges for regulatory theory, stemming from rapid technological change, cross-sectoral applications, and uncertain risk profiles. While risk-based regulation (RBR) is frequently proposed as a leading approach to balance innovation and safety, much existing literature relies on idealised frameworks or superficial domain comparisons.

This study employs structured-focused comparison with a functional decomposition of regulatory tasks to examine analogous mechanisms across banking and AI governance, comparing Basel III's three pillars with three nascent AI arrangements: the EU AI Act's GPAI provisions, the UK AI Safety Institute, and Singapore's AI Verify Framework. Through directed content analysis of primary regulatory texts, the study uncovers three key findings. First, compute thresholds may be insufficient proxies for underlying risks in AI governance, challenging core RBR functions. Second, voluntary arrangements may prove structurally incompatible with RBR's proportionate resource allocation logic due to adverse selection dynamics. Third, the emphasis on adaptation in AI approaches reflects epistemic uncertainty rather than deliberate design. These findings contribute to regulatory theory by specifying conditions for effective RBR implementation and highlighting that RBR's applicability may be bounded by a domain's methodological maturity and institutional prerequisites. The analysis suggests that effective AI governance may necessitate either a theoretical adaptation of RBR principles or the development of alternative regulatory paradigms.

title: Crude Oil Price Shocks and State Tax Implications
