The opinions expressed in this study are exclusively those of the authors, and do not reflect or represent the views of Visa USA, Charles River Associates, or any other institutions with which the authors are, or have been, affilicated
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Visa USA

detail.abstract: The evidence suggests that labor productivity in the U.S. retail sector has increased substantially since 1995. A few studies also show that investments in information technology by retailers have contributed to raising labor productivity. To our knowledge, however, the link between digital-payment use and retail productivity remains unexamined. We explore the issue by combining publicly available panels from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and the U.S. Census Bureau's County Business Patterns with a dataset on payment-card use by county and retail subsector. We estimate a variety of econometric specifications, including instrumental-variable models that address the potential endogeneity of digital-payment use. We find that a 10-percent increase in the share of digital payments in total sales is associated with an increase in retail labor productivity of between half of a percent and one and a half percent.

title: Activity Moves, Volatility does not: Falsification Evidence from a Regulator-mandated Expiry-day Reassignment
affiliations: Vijayanagara Sri Krishnadevaraya University and Vijayanagara Sri Krishnadevaraya University

detail.title: Activity Moves, Volatility does not: Falsification Evidence from a Regulator-mandated Expiry-day Reassignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses publicly available aggregate market and bibliographic data and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of this article.

detail.abstract:
Purpose. This study asks whether a regulator can relocate expiry-day trading activity by administrative decision, and whether such a relocation carries measurable consequences for volatility. It exploits a reassignment of weekly derivatives expiry days that moved two competing Indian exchanges to opposite weekdays on the same date.

Design. Following Securities and Exchange Board of India circular SEBI/HO/MRD/MRD-TPD-1/P/CIR/2025/76, the National Stock Exchange moved Nifty 50 weekly expiry from Thursday to Tuesday on 1 September 2025 while BSE Limited moved Sensex weekly expiry from Tuesday to Thursday. Difference-in-differences and triple-difference models are estimated on 387 trading days spanning 1 January 2025 to 28 July 2026. Because the design rests on only two exchanges, every headline estimate is subjected to a four-part falsification battery: randomisation inference over 200 placebo event dates excluding a ninety-day window around the true one, specifications with weekday-specific linear time trends, quarterly event studies, and placebo weekdays.

Findings. Trading activity relocated sharply and the result survives every test. At the BSE the Tuesday turnover premium fell from 46.8 to −9.7 per cent and the Thursday premium rose from −4.7 to 61.8 per cent, both interactions significant beyond the 0.1 per cent level. The actual estimates lie outside the 95 per cent placebo interval, giving randomisation p-values below 0.001; the coefficients strengthen rather than weaken when weekday time trends are added; the event study shows a flat pre-period and a discontinuity at the migration; and among the five weekdays only Tuesday and Thursday move. Volatility tells the opposite story. The triple-difference coefficient of 0.000365 is significant under clustered standard errors (p = 0.006) but fails every falsification test: the randomisation p-value is 0.233, the coefficient collapses by 99 per cent to 0.000004 once an index-specific Tuesday trend is included, and the event study reveals a steady slope rather than a break. What appeared to be a volatility effect is a pre-existing trend in the relative volatility of the two indices. Expiry days also carry no abnormal returns in either regime.

Originality. This is the first study of a regulator-mandated, bidirectional expiry-day reassignment. Its methodological contribution is to show that in a two-venue difference-in-differences design, conventional clustered standard errors can indicate significance where randomisation inference and trend controls do not, and that reporting both is necessary rather than optional.

Practical implications. Settlement-day assignment is an effective instrument for redistributing trading activity across the week. The evidence does not, however, support the inference that redistributing activity alters volatility, which bears directly on the regulator’s stated objective of de-concentrating expiry-day risk.

title: Diagnosing How College Basketball Teams Defend: An Opponent-Adjusted Public-Data Decision-Support Framework
affiliations: University of Waterloo - Department of Management Sciences

detail.title: Diagnosing How College Basketball Teams Defend: An Opponent-Adjusted Public-Data Decision-Support Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available team-level and game-level basketball data and does not involve human participants, intervention, private personal information, or biological material. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: The author received no specific funding for this work.

detail.abstract: Defensive rankings make college basketball look cleaner than scouting rooms usually feel. Teams with similar adjusted efficiency often create different preparation problems: one defense ends possessions through pressure, another protects shot quality, and another taxes fouls or rebounds. This paper develops an opponent-adjusted public-data performanceanalysis framework that turns standard NCAA team-game records into defensive scouting channels. The framework treats prediction as a pregame scouting task, asking whether those channels identify future matchups where scoring risk deserves attention. The adjusted defensive dimensions carry most of the framework's value. Risk-oriented validation translates those dimensions into matchup triage, while the lagged spatial scouting supplement adds a secondary source of court-location evidence. The paper contributes a validated scouting language between public rankings and film-based preparation.

title: Refugee Absorption and Electoral Change: Evidence from the Indian Partition
affiliations: and University of Luxembourg

detail.title: Refugee Absorption and Electoral Change: Evidence from the Indian Partition
detail.abstract: The 1947 Partition of British India triggered the largest forced migration of the twentieth century, redistributing millions of refugees across newly independent India. We study whether this demographic shock left a lasting imprint on democratic politics. Combining district-level refugee shares from the 1951 Census with constituency-level electoral data covering Indian state assembly elections between 1960 and 2007, we estimate the long-run effects of refugee settlement on electoral competition. We find that constituencies exposed to larger refugee inflows exhibit higher voter turnout, narrower victory margins, and a lower likelihood of electing candidates from national parties. Instead, refugee settlement shifted electoral support toward regional parties and contributed to the long-run denationalization of political competition. Our findings show that large demographic shocks can leave enduring political legacies, reshaping patterns of political representation and party competition long after displacement itself has ended.

title: Confidence and Algorithmic Advice
affiliations: Humboldt University of Berlin - Faculty of Economics,  and Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin) - Faculty of Economics and Management

detail.title: Confidence and Algorithmic Advice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest: none.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval by the Technical University Berlin Faculty of Economics and Management (VII) Ethics Committee (project number 20251016).
declarations.funderStatement: German Research Foundation (DFG)

detail.abstract: Human decision-makers are increasingly interacting with algorithms, which often serve as advisors. The literature on advice-taking suggests that people discount other's advice, especially when they feel competent. We propose an experiment to study how self-confidence influences the reliance on algorithmic advice in terms of advise utilization and confidence in the final decision. In our online experiment, participants make age predictions and estimates about the accuracy of their predictions before and after receiving algorithmic advice. We exogenously vary subjects' confidence by implementing different (perceived) task difficulties and the (observed) quality of the algorithmic advisor. While we find that participants generally put more weight on high quality advice, we observe, contrary to the extant literature on advice-seeking, that participants are less influenced by advice when they perceive the task as difficult. By contrasting age and accuracy predictions, we show that people who feel proficient at a task appreciate the advice of a high-quality algorithmic advisor but barely follow it. Rather, this is expressed as an increase of the confidence in the accuracy of their prediction. When people feel less proficient at a task, they are more reluctant to adjust their predictions toward the advice of a low-quality algorithmic advisor.

title: Youth-Type Blackhole Economy: Behavioral Rerouting and Future Effective Stock in Japan

detail.title: Youth-Type Blackhole Economy: Behavioral Rerouting and Future Effective Stock in Japan
detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Youth-Type Blackhole Economy as a theory of temporal disconnection in which present resources exist but fail to reinforce an efficient, credible, and recursively shared path to future livelihood security. Its central claim is that trust-induced behavioral rerouting constitutes a causal channel distinct from income, taxation, or liquidity constraints. The resulting welfare loss arises not necessarily from a reduction in objective resources, but from the weakening of shared risk pooling, intertemporal continuity, and allocative efficiency.

The concept is not a synonym for poverty, low saving, or physical resource disappearance. Younger generations generate labor income, pay compulsory social insurance contributions, accumulate employment and contribution histories, and form human capital. The analytical problem arises when these resources are routed through channels whose conversion performance, portability, risk-sharing capacity, or perceived credibility is weak, causing resources to leave or fail to strengthen the shared risk-pooling circuit.

The paper introduces a channel-based dynamic model. Objective Stock formation occurs through public, occupational, and private transfer routes, each with its own allocation share, conversion efficiency, and rate of return. Transtemporal trust is represented operationally by route-specific perceived credibility γ. It does not directly reduce objective Stock. Instead, it influences route choice, voluntary allocation, and reliance on liquid self-insurance. A decline in perceived credibility may therefore increase private saving for some individuals, increase liquidity preference for others, or increase current consumption for others. The principal falsifiable prediction is not a uniform change in total Stock, but systematic behavioral rerouting across institutional channels following exogenous changes in perceived credibility under conditions where liquidity constraints do not bind.

The model also includes a later-life release circuit in which accumulated Stock must be converted into current livelihood Flow. Objective barriers and subjective defensive preferences are separated. Public social insurance is treated as imperfectly substitutable with private accumulation because longevity pooling, disability and survivor protection, and broadly accessible inflation-adjusted lifetime claims cannot generally be replicated on equivalent terms through individual saving alone. This produces a temporal symmetry between forward disconnection in youth and release disconnection in later life.

A Cabinet Office survey item on old-age planning is presented only as an illustrative behavioral proxy. The paper explicitly identifies the age-period-cohort problem and does not infer cohort-specific trust from one cross-section. The contribution is a falsifiable conceptual framework for studying when institutionally transferred resources remain formally present yet generate welfare losses because participants reroute, duplicate, or immobilize resources in response to channels they do not regard as credible.

title: The Broken Promise of Social Mobility? Education Policy, Employability, and Inequality in Morocco: A Scoping Review

detail.title: The Broken Promise of Social Mobility? Education Policy, Employability, and Inequality in Morocco: A Scoping Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this scoping review used published literature and did not involve human participants, identifiable personal data, or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Morocco has invested heavily in education reform, vocational training, higher education expansion, digital transformation, and youth employability initiatives. Yet persistent inequalities, graduate unemployment, skills mismatch, and uneven social mobility continue to raise questions about whether education still functions as a reliable pathway to opportunity. This scoping review maps the academic literature on education policy, skills mismatch, employability, and youth opportunity in Morocco. Following a PRISMA-ScR-informed approach, records were identified through Scopus and HAL, deduplicated in Zotero, and screened. After title and abstract screening, 95 full texts/files were assessed. The final synthesis included 81 core studies and 14 background/context sources. The evidence was organized into seven themes: inequality, social mobility, and territorial/gender disparities; digital transformation, ICT, and AI skills; higher education employability and graduate transitions; vocational training, mismatch, and continuing training; dropout, youth risk, and remedial reintegration; education policy, governance, and system quality; and language, internationalization, and cultural capital, together with a cross-cutting strand on trust, legitimacy, and the politics of credentialed unemployment. The review finds that Morocco has expanded access to education, but this expansion has not consistently translated into equal opportunity, secure employment, or upward social mobility. Instead, the literature points to a broken chain between schooling, skills, credentials, labour-market insertion, and social mobility. The paper argues that Morocco's education challenge is not simply one of access or reform design, but of implementation, coordination, and equity across the full education-to-work transition. The review's contribution is threefold: it consolidates a fragmented, multilingual literature; it reframes Morocco's challenge as one of conversion rather than access, grounded in the capability approach; and it identifies the education-trust link as one of the most consequential evidence gaps identified by this review.

title: Why Baby Raven Reads Endures

detail.title: Why Baby Raven Reads Endures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial conflict of interest. The author previously held leadership roles in Alaska Native early-childhood and Head Start programming and at Chugachmiut, Inc., and the framework advanced here draws on the author's prior published corpus; these professional relationships are disclosed in the interest of transparency. The author holds no financial interest in the Sealaska Heritage Institute, Baby Raven Reads, or the Chugach School District.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this work. The paper is a conceptual and secondary analysis drawing exclusively on previously published program evaluations and publicly available aggregate data; it involved no primary data collection, no human participants, and no personally identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Conventional pre-kindergarten interventions, Head Start chief among them, reliably produce measurable cognitive gains that fade within one to three years of school entrythe well-documented "fade-out" effect (Puma et al., 2010, 2012). Baby Raven Reads (BRR), the Sealaska Heritage Institute's culturally grounded early-literacy program, produces early gains that the field's standard explanations do not readily account for, and whose durability the standard models cannot predict. The contrast between the two programs, I contend, is not a difference of quality but of architecture. Drawing on the Shaman's Trail / Haa Latseení framework-integrating Barrett's body-budget account of predictive regulation, Oakley's consolidation-and-chunking model of durable learning, the Adverse Childhood Experiences corpus, Dunbar's social-brain architecture, and Ortiz's epistemology of circular and relational time-I argue that literacy endures only when it consolidates within a regulated, belonging-anchored child, and that it consolidates there only when the learning is inseparable from relationship, identity, and family. Head Start, as commonly delivered, transmits decontextualized skills to children whose relational floor is unbuilt; the gains do not consolidate and thus fade. Baby Raven Reads does not teach literacy and then add culture-the literacy happens through belonging, and so it holds. Two further design features of conventional programs sharpen the contrast: an early effect that resource injection and a temporarily constructed adult relationship will produce regardless of pedagogy (the Hawthorne problem), which evaluation cannot separate from durable learning; and the absence of breakthrough-initiative thinking, in which a fixed proficiency target is taught to as one teaches to a minimum-competency exit exam, making the bar a ceiling and guaranteeing the population's catch-up. Reframing the evaluation question "from a Head Start perspective"-asking what actually constitutes a durable head startreveals BRR not as a regional curiosity but as a proof of architecture. The same architecture, scaled to a whole district, appears in Alaska's Chugach School District, which abandoned seat-time schooling for mastery-and-relationship and then surpassed the state average on the very exit exam it had stopped teaching toward. I close by confronting the decisive methodological objection-that the programs draw from differently selected populations-and argue it does not dissolve the thesis but dictates its test: a longitudinal

title: The Accounting System for Natural Persons (SCPP)

detail.title: The Accounting System for Natural Persons (SCPP)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the originator and rights holder of the SCPP framework and heads L'N EXPERTISE (Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso). No other competing interests are declared.

detail.abstract: In Africa, and more particularly within the OHADA legal space, the existing accounting regulatory framework governs legal entities exclusively. Natural persons-who broadly dominate the economic fabric in Burkina Faso and neighbouring countries-operate in an absolute methodological void, deprived of accountability tools adapted to their realities. This void produces seven documented structural consequences: financial exclusion of informal households, fiscal under-mobilization, heightened vulnerability to corruption and moneylaundering risks, statistical underestimation of real GDP, a structural accountability gap, the absence of dedicated accounting informatization, and a structural deficit in financial literacy. Existing responses-group microfinance, simplified standards for very small enterprises, presumptive tax regimes, and personal-finance applications-each address only part of the problem. This paper proposes the doctrinal and functional framework for a Personal Accounting System (SCPP), grounded in the principles of double-entry bookkeeping adapted to African socioeconomic realities. The framework integrates three accountability systems according to the user's economic profile (Normal, Simplified, Subsistence), a nine-class chart of accounts incorporating African specificities (tontines-rotating community savings-and-credit associations-, biological assets, community solidarity, personal cost accounting), and three original analytical indicators: the Social Pressure Index (IPS), the Residual Living Capacity (RAV), and the SCPP Confidence Score (SCS). The practical implications of the SCPP for financial inclusion through the financial system (commercial banks and MFIs) and for the fiscal transition of the informal sector are analysed. We also submit, in three coordinated annexes, a draft OHADA Uniform Act (AUSCPP), its companion doctrinal application Guide, and the Adaptable Chart of Accounts for Natural Persons (PASCO) intended for international interoperability.

title: The Last Signal Wins: How Recent Performance Information Shapes Subsequent Performance Under Contradictory Signals
affiliations: University of Navarra - Business, Universidad de Navarra and University of Navarra - IESE Business School

detail.title: The Last Signal Wins: How Recent Performance Information Shapes Subsequent Performance Under Contradictory Signals
detail.abstract: We extend research on relative performance information (RPI) by examining how individuals respond to recent performance signals when they receive contradictory RPI in highstakes settings. Drawing on recency theory, we predict that the latest signal carries greater weight in shaping motivation and behaviour. We test this prediction using professional bestof-three-set tennis matches that reach a deciding third set. We find that a recent positive signal is associated with better subsequent performance than a recent negative signal, even when both occur close in time. We further document substantial heterogeneity in this relationship, with RPI informativeness moderating the recency effect. Responses also differ by gender. The recency effect is attenuated among male players classified as Top Players-our proxy for higher self-efficacy-but persists among other male players and among female players. Responses also differ depending on whether recent RPI is positive or negative: women tend to underperform following unexpected positive signals, consistent with choking under pressure, whereas men respond more negatively to recent setbacks, consistent with the Golem effect. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of recency as a motivational dimension of performance information and show how individual characteristics and signal properties shape responses to and interpretations of recent performance signals.

title: Party Lines or Voter Preferences? Explaining Political Realignment

detail.title: Party Lines or Voter Preferences? Explaining Political Realignment
detail.abstract: This paper estimates a political equilibrium model to disentangle demand factors (voters) from supply factors (politicians) in shaping political outcomes, focusing on the recent realignment of blue-collar voters away from left-wing parties. I jointly evaluate the impact of changes in voter preferences and voter demographics (demand side) and party positions and party discipline (supply side) on voters' partisan realignment as observed in U.S. House elections between 2000 and 2020. To measure candidate ideological positioning, I estimate a multimodal text-and-survey model using campaign websites. To estimate voter preferences, I build a new panel of precinct-level election results (N=1.6 million), which allows me to exploit congressional district border discontinuities for identification. The paper ultimately identifies parties' stronger polarization on cultural issues compared to economic issues as the main driver of voters' partisan realignment. In contrast, shifts in voter preferences-particularly the increasing support among blue-collar voters for progressive economic policies-have mitigated their defection from the Democratic Party. Absent these demand-side changes, partisan realignment would have been even more pronounced.

title: Fishing for the Biodiversity Risk Factors in Corporate Bonds: An Empty Pond
affiliations: University of Turin and University of Turin

detail.title: Fishing for the Biodiversity Risk Factors in Corporate Bonds: An Empty Pond
detail.abstract: Do biodiversity risks command a premium in corporate bonds? We examine 4,023 United States bonds issued by 329 non-financial firms between 2018 and 2023, adopting a double-materiality perspective that captures both firms' impacts on biodiversity (transition risks) and their dependence on ecosystem services (physical risks). By sorting bonds and firms into long-short portfolios, we evaluate both raw and riskadjusted returns and find no robust evidence of a biodiversity premium, at either the bond or issuer level, for both physical and transition biodiversity risks. This result holds across alternative weighting schemes and credit-rating groups, as well as in the post-Kunming Declaration in October 2021. Our findings carry an important implication for investors and the asset management industry. Biodiversity risk remains unpriced in corporate bond markets, leaving investors unrewarded for bearing exposures that may become material in future.

title: PyXtabond2 Methodological Note : GMM Theory, the IFE-GMM Extension, and Validation Against Stata’s xtabond2
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: PyXtabond2 Methodological Note : GMM Theory, the IFE-GMM Extension, and Validation Against Stata’s xtabond2
detail.abstract: This note provides the full econometric derivation underlying pyxtabond2, together with a complete, primary-source-grounded account of its validation. Section 2 derives the standard dynamic panel GMM estimator (Difference and System GMM), its one-and two-step weighting matrices, the Windmeijer [2005] finite-sample variance correction, and the smallsample degrees-of-freedom corrections, each tied explicitly to the corresponding construction in Stata's xtabond2.mata [Roodman, 2009a]. Section 3 derives the Sargan/Hansen, Difference-in-Sargan/Hansen, and Arellano-Bond AR() test statistics. Section 4 derives IFE-GMM, an original extension not present in xtabond2: an iterative, PCA-based estimator for dynamic panels contaminated by interactive fixed effects [Bai, 2009], combining automatic factor-count selection [Bai and Ng, 2002, Ahn and Horenstein, 2013], a profile-GMM defactoring loop [Hong et al., 2022], and a split-panel jackknife bias correction [Dhaene and Jochmans, 2015]. Section 5 reports, in full, the findings of two validation passes conducted against xtabond2.mata and a real Stata run, alongside every confirmed-correct result and every documented, unresolved limitation.

title: Exporting Gas, Exporting Emissions: The Externalization of Climate Costs through the Southern Gas Corridor
affiliations: Economic Research Center (ERC)

detail.title: Exporting Gas, Exporting Emissions: The Externalization of Climate Costs through the Southern Gas Corridor
detail.abstract:
This article examines the structural tension between Azerbaijan's international climate commitments and its expanding role as a major natural gas exporter to Europe. Since hosting COP29 in 2024, Azerbaijan has positioned itself as an active participant in global environmental governance while simultaneously accelerating hydrocarbon production, developing new gas fields (including Absheron Phase II, Babek, and non-associated gas at ACG), and deepening its strategic energy partnership with the EU through the Southern Gas Corridor (SGC) and Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP). Drawing on the concept of "exported emissions," the article argues that while European states may reduce territorial emissions by substituting Azerbaijani gas for more carbon-intensive fuels, a substantial share of the associated methane emissions-generated during extraction, processing, compression, and transmission-remains externalized to Azerbaijan and other points along the supply chain. 
The analysis assesses whether existing environmental, health and safety, and human rights safeguards imposed by EU legislation, EBRD, EIB, IFC, OECD, and Equator Principles standards, as well as the new EU Methane Regulation (2024/1787), are adequate to address this challenge. It finds that although TAP operates under one of the most extensive formal governance frameworks applied to energy infrastructure, effective implementation depends heavily on independent monitoring, transparency, and civic space-all of which are significantly constrained in Azerbaijan and, to varying degrees, in Georgia and Türkiye. Restrictions on civil society, journalists, and human rights defenders limit the ability of independent actors to verify compliance, creating a gap between formal regulatory commitments and actual environmental and social outcomes. 
The article concludes that Azerbaijan's declining performance in the World Economic Forum's 2026 Energy Transition Index-driven by weaknesses in institutional and regulatory "Transition Readiness" rather than technical system performance-illustrates a broader dilemma facing hydrocarbon-exporting states: the credibility of climate commitments ultimately hinges not only on renewable energy targets, but on methane governance, transparency, and protection of the civic space needed to hold gas export infrastructure accountable throughout its operational lifecycle.

title: Who Decides Washington State? Who Returns the Ballot? Age Composition in Washington's Odd-Year Electorate, 2021-2025

detail.title: Who Decides Washington State? Who Returns the Ballot? Age Composition in Washington's Odd-Year Electorate, 2021-2025

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the principal of Tikor Consulting and of Kirby Law Office, PLLC. This paper was produced with a voter-file and election-data codebase that the author also develops for commercial political-analytics and campaign-services applications, including partisan campaign work. This descriptive study was not commissioned, funded, or reviewed prior to release by any political party, campaign, political action committee, or client; it makes no partisan or policy recommendation; and the author has no financial interest in the outcome of any election-timing policy. AI assistance is disclosed separately.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a secondary analysis of public-record data — Washington's statewide voter-registration database, obtained under RCW 29A.08.710, and certified aggregate election results from the Secretary of State. It involved no intervention with or contact with human subjects, and it released no individual-level records; all published outputs are aggregate counts. Conducted by an independent (non-institutional) researcher, it was not subject to Institutional Review Board review. The design corresponds to the categories U.S. federal regulations treat as exempt or not-human-subjects research (secondary use of publicly available information; 45 CFR 46.104). Use of the voter file was confined to the political and scholarly purposes permitted by RCW 29A.08.720, and no data are redistributed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author; no grant, institution, political party, campaign, political action committee, or client provided financial support or commissioned the work.

detail.abstract: Many of Washington's local officesare filled in odd-year Novemberelections, when turnout runs far below presidential years.This paper asks who returns those ballots. Using Washington's statewide voter-registration database,a 5.51-millionvoter roll linked to 27.1 million individual vote-history records with the voter's year of birth, it measures the age make-up of every November general electorate from 2021 through 2025.The central finding is descriptive: Washington's odd-year electorate is markedly older than its presidential one. Voters 65 and older were 36.7%, 40.2%,and 40.3% of the 2021, 2023, and 2025 odd-yearelectorates,against 28.5% in 2024; voters 18–29 fell from 14.2% in 2024 to about 7.6% off-cycle.The result survives voter-file coverage validation against certified ballot counts, formal bounds for current-roll survivorship,a closer-in-time roll cross-check,alternative birth-year assumptions, county-level checks,and exclusion of any single off-year. The off-yearelectorate isalso older than the registered roll and the citizen voting-age population. Individual records show it is largely the presidential electorate's habitual core (92–97% of off-year votersalso vote in presidential years), while the peripheral voters who drop off off-cycle skew young.The paper measures ballot return, not votes cast in specific downballot contests,and does not estimate partisan or policy consequences. Its contribution isa validated, individual-record measurement of age composition across the presidential–midterm–off-year salience gradient, in a universal vote-by-mail state where the formal administrative cost of voting is comparatively low.

title: Fragile Hands: Bondholders' Portfolios and the Transmission of Monetary Policy to Credit Markets
affiliations: Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences,  and Universite de Toulouse 1 Capitole

detail.title: Fragile Hands: Bondholders' Portfolios and the Transmission of Monetary Policy to Credit Markets
detail.abstract: How does the composition of a firm's creditor base affect the transmission of monetary policy to credit markets? Using bond-level institutional holdings matched to CDS data over 2001-2019, we show that CDS spreads respond more to high-frequency monetary policy surprises when bonds are held by investors whose portfolios are concentrated in low-rated or long-duration securities, consistent with binding portfolio constraints that force rebalancing. Mutual fund ownership no longer amplifies shocks once bondholders' portfolio exposures and trading intensity are controlled for. Ownership concentration dampens transmission only when large holders are constrained. Bondholders' balance sheets, not institutional labels, shape monetary transmission.

title: Optimizers as Scale Mixtures, from Adam to Muon
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Optimizers as Scale Mixtures, from Adam to Muon
detail.abstract: We give a unifying account of geometry-aware optimizers, including Muon, Shampoo, and Ada-factor, through the lens of scale mixtures of Gaussians and matrix-variate priors. The organizing principle is a duality: a training step is steepest descent under a chosen norm, and that norm is dual to a prior under which the step is a maximum a posteriori move. The Euclidean norm returns stochastic gradient descent, the coordinate max-norm returns sign descent and the sign geometry of Adam, and the spectral operator norm returns Muon, whose Newton-Schulz orthogonalization computes the polar factor  of the momentum matrix. Adaptive second-moment methods form a hierarchy of scale mixtures: Adam is a per-coordinate local scale, Adafactor is a separable rank-one scale that factors the second moment into row and column statistics, and Shampoo is a Kronecker matrix-normal scale. Muon sits at the spectral end of this hierarchy, where the update is whitened so that every singular direction moves at a common rate, the matrix analogue of the common global scale in a horseshoe prior. We make the norm-to-prior correspondence precise, show that Ada-factor is the maximum-likelihood separable scale mixture, and connect fast compute, Newton-Schulz iteration and factored moments, to our generative Bayesian computation program. Illustrative numerical studies on anisotropic objectives display the invariance the geometry predicts: the spectral and Kronecker methods are unchanged under an orthogonal change of frame, while coordinate methods lose several orders of magnitude of accuracy when the same anisotropy is rotated off-axis.

title: Retail Attention, Odd-Lot Trading, and Daily Stock Volatility
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University - Graduate School of Business Administration and Bar Ilan University

detail.title: Retail Attention, Odd-Lot Trading, and Daily Stock Volatility
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether online investor attention and small-trade activity contain distinct information about daily stock volatility. Using a panel of ten large-cap U.S. stocks from 2012 to 2022, we combine Google Trends Relative Search Volume with the share of trading volume executed in odd lots and relate both measures to a daily range-based volatility proxy. Because odd-lot transactions may originate from retail, institutional, or algorithmic traders, we interpret the odd-lot measure as an indicator of small-trade intensity rather than a pure proxy for retail trading. Across specifications in levels, logarithmic levels, and daily logarithmic changes, higher search intensity and greater oddlot activity are associated with wider daily price movements. Odd-lot activity is the more stable correlate across specifications, whereas search activity retains explanatory content after conditioning on small-trade intensity. The design is descriptive and does not identify the direction of causality. The findings indicate that online information demand and small-trade order flow capture related but distinct dimensions of investor engagement that coincide with short-run volatility states, even in highly liquid, institutionally dominated stocks.

title: Energy, Security and the State: A Hobbesian Critique of the Social Contract in the Climate Era
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Energy, Security and the State: A Hobbesian Critique of the Social Contract in the Climate Era
detail.abstract: The deepening climate crisis has revived fundamental questions about the purpose of the state, the reach of political authority, and the conditions under which citizens owe obedience to public power. This article revisits Thomas Hobbes' social contract theory as an analytical framework for evaluating contemporary state obligations in the governance of energy and climate security. It argues that the Hobbesian security covenant, premised on the exchange of natural liberty for sovereign protection, generates a normative standard by which states may be assessed when they fail to address existential environmental threats. Applying Hobbes' foundational concepts of natural insecurity, the state of nature, sovereign authorisation, and the protection-obligation nexus, the article examines how the climate emergency reconfigures the terrain of political legitimacy. Three core claims are advanced: first, that unchecked climate change reproduces the structural logic of the Hobbesian state of nature at both domestic and global levels; second, that the sovereign's foundational duty of protection extends to foreseeable environmental threats, making inadequate climate governance a failure at the level of constitutive political authority; and third, that while the Hobbesian framework provides a compelling diagnosis of the global governance deficit, its weak account of rights against the sovereign and its domestic orientation require supplementation by stronger accountability mechanisms. The article concludes that a reconstructed Hobbesian approach, one that preserves the security imperative while insisting on minimum rights constraints and multilateral institutional accountability, offers a productive lens for evaluating the obligations of states in the age of energy transition.

title: The Corporate Affairs Commission’s Enforcement of Statutory Particulars on Business Letters: A Compliance Imperative for Companies
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Corporate Affairs Commission’s Enforcement of Statutory Particulars on Business Letters: A Compliance Imperative for Companies
detail.abstract:
On 8 July 2026, the Corporate Affairs Commission (the “Commission” or “CAC”) issued a public notice titled, ‘Particulars on Company Business Letters’ (the “Notice”). The Notice confirms that, with effect from 1 August 2026, the CAC will commence active enforcement of the requirements under sections 304(1) and (2) of the Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2020 (the “Act” or “CAMA”) relating to the particulars that companies must display on their trade circulars, show cards and business letters with sanctions for non-compliance.

The Notice is commercially significant as it signals the commencement of active enforcement of a long-standing statutory obligation that applies to some of the most frequently used corporate documents. With only a short compliance window remaining, it is advisable for companies to take immediate steps to ensure their Business Letters comply with CAMA requirements.

title:
A Bargaining Model of Regional Secession, Cross-Border Ethnic Externalities, Economic Retaliation, The Architecture of Managed Chaos, And Popular Mobilization as a Strategic Force Multiplier 

Definitive Edition -Revised Following Peer Review
affiliations: Al-Neelain University - Department of Economics

detail.title:
A Bargaining Model of Regional Secession, Cross-Border Ethnic Externalities, Economic Retaliation, The Architecture of Managed Chaos, And Popular Mobilization as a Strategic Force Multiplier 

Definitive Edition -Revised Following Peer Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Strategic planning for the recovery of Sudan
declarations.ethicsApproval: There is no conflict of interest; I am the only author
declarations.funderStatement: No finding

detail.abstract: This paper presents the definitive formal and empirical analysis of Sudan's fragmentation risk, integrating five analytical layers. First, a Fearon-Alesina-Spolaore bargaining model calibrated against 2024-2025 primary data reduces the probability of viable Eastern Sudanese secession from 60-70% (Mohamed and Alfarouk, 2025) to a credible interval of 5-18%, replacing the original point estimate following peerreview challenge. Second, a systematic mapping of cross-border tribal dynamics across all seven neighbours establishes a 5:1 opposition coalition, with the UAE identified as preferring controlled instability over a new state. Third, a formal retaliation game (Proposition 4) calibrates Sudan's economic coercive capacity against South Sudan (≈4.7:1), Egypt (≈4.8-11.5:1), and the UAE (≈5-20:1), reframed as threshold instruments targeting specific payoff differentials rather than war-of-attrition tools. Fourth, managed chaos is formalised as a Nash equilibrium (Proposition 5: Dissolution Theorem) with three dissolution instruments and three falsification conditions; Russia is distinguished from Africa Corps as a gold mercenary enterprise structurally incompatible with resolution. Fifth, popular will P is introduced as an economic variable with two channels: cost-imposer on external actors (equation 22) and force multiplier for the SAF (equation 25, Proposition 7). At P = 0.7 with β ≈ 0.55 ± 50%, the SAF's effective military capacity exceeds its baseline by 19-57% (central estimate 38%). Proposition 6 (Calcification Theorem) specifies T* through four observable indicators and an empirical range of 2027-2031. The modal outcome is managed chaos (55-65%). Sudan will not disintegrateit will calcify. Whether it resolves or calcifies depends on whether the dissolution instruments are activated before T* is reached, and whether the SAF earns the popular mobilisation that no external actor can provide or deny.

title: Predator-Prey Dynamics of Market Liquidity: Deterministic Stability and a Stochastic Extension
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Predator-Prey Dynamics of Market Liquidity: Deterministic Stability and a Stochastic Extension
detail.abstract: I develop a phenomenological dynamical-systems model of aggregate market liquid ity by adapting the Lotka–Volterra predator–prey framework, treating aggregate resting liquidity (“supply”, 𝑃) as prey and aggregate marketable order flow (“demand”, 𝐿) as predator. I analyze a hierarchy of three deterministic models — the classical system, a logistic variant with finite market carrying capacity, and a prey-dependent system with a Holling Type II saturating interaction — and for each I derive the interior equilibrium, linearize, and classify local stability from the Jacobian spectrum. The classical model is a structurally unstable center; the logistic model is a stable focus (damped oscillations toward equilibrium); and the Holling Type II model exhibits a threshold, at 𝛿 = 𝛾ℎ, separating a demand-extinction regime from stable coexistence. Because real liquidity is stochastic rather than periodic, I then introduce a stochastic Lotka–Volterra model — the same drift with multiplicative Brownian noise — and simulate it via Euler–Maruyama, showing that noise sustains irregular, non-periodic fluctuations and occasional sharp liquidity droughts that the deterministic models cannot produce. I am explicit that the model is a stylized aggregate anal ogy, not a micro-founded order-book model, and that the parameters are illustrative rather than empirically calibrated; I position it against the microstructure and market-ecology literatures and outline the calibration and jump-diffusion extensions needed to make it empirical.

title: Cheering for the Laundry
affiliations: University of Mississippi School of Law

detail.title: Cheering for the Laundry
detail.abstract:
The NCAA is disappearing. Its rules have long violated antitrust law, and there may be no pro-competitive antitrust justification for keeping any of its rules. The pro-competitive benefit in the entertainment market that would justify the NCAA's use of its rules relates only to the athlete wearing the logo and uniform of the university. Fans will keep watching irrespective of whether athletes are paid, or are even students, because they cheer for the laundry.

So, what might that world of intercollegiate athletics--one without NCAA rules--look like? This article stares into the crystal ball and examines a likely path forward for college sports in light of the economic interests of the universities, the athletes, the NCAA, the conferences, the coaches, the fans & boosters, and the networks & corporate sponsors. Specifically, it argues that without the adoption of a conference-employee model or some other path to an antitrust exemption, colleges and universities will soon be in the business, if they are not already, of running professional athletic programs.

Part I provides a short overview of the move from an amateur to a commercial model of intercollegiate athletics. Part II of the Article frames the conversation by providing a brief overview of the respective compatible and competing interests in intercollegiate athletics. Part III outlines the legal landscape that provides parameters that limit, shape, and, in some senses, drive this uncertain future. And Part IV offers a model of what a post-NCAA college sports landscape might look like.

title: Prediction Markets as Weather Hedges: Geographic Basis Risk, Settlement Constraints, and Contract Replication

detail.title: Prediction Markets as Weather Hedges: Geographic Basis Risk, Settlement Constraints, and Contract Replication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study used only public available market and weather data, and involves no human participants or personally identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: The research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Kalshi's CFTC-regulated weather markets settle daily on official NWS station observations, making them the first retail-accessible, continuously priced instrument written directly on local U.S. weather. We ask whether these contracts can transfer weather risk rather than predict it. First, on 287,909 price observations from 15,994 resolved contracts, simple univariate post-hoc recalibration (isotonic, Platt) does not improve the probabilistic accuracy of raw prices out of sample. This null motivates a shift from price correction toward hedging effectiveness. Second, we map the binding constraint on that tradability: the residual basis risk between each contract's fixed settlement-station degree-day index and a customer-proxy local exposure index, across 30 station pairs and two trigger types over 24 years. Residual basis risk is large on average (mean 0.386) but predictable: it rises with station distance and is systematically lower for heating-than cooling-degree-day triggers. It is not reliably reduced by the static hedge constructions we consider: multi-station portfolios beat the best single station out of sample in only 43% of cases, and ridge shrinkage does not change that verdict. Third, the contract layer adds little measured friction: the implied-temperature bias (market-implied minus realized settlement value) is ≈0, and although the realized temperature escapes Kalshi's 8°F bin ladder on 17% of days, the binarization (replication) cost of synthesizing a degree-day claim from binary bins is ~1% of exposure variance, an order of magnitude below geographic basis risk, a gap that survives a joint daily-level decomposition (replacing the ideal index with the strip raises residual basis risk by a median of +0.007, with near-zero geography-replication correlation). A prospectively specified winter test with locked quantitative predictions extends the analysis to winter, where the two error sources are predicted to trade off. In our warmseason sample, the measured frictions of a prediction-market weather hedge are dominated by geography, so the basis-risk map, rather than the price of the contracts, is the first-order pricing object for parametric risk transfer.
