title: Arbitrage Exists, but Not at Retail: Measuring the Retail Accessibility of Cryptocurrency Arbitrage

detail.title: Arbitrage Exists, but Not at Retail: Measuring the Retail Accessibility of Cryptocurrency Arbitrage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests. The author operates the open-source measurement system described in this paper for personal research purposes, including an ongoing paper-trading (simulated, non-monetary) forward validation; the author holds no positions in, and received no compensation from, any cryptocurrency exchange or related entity.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We measure whether cryptocurrency arbitrage is accessible to a retail participant using commodity infrastructure, and report primarily negative results. Streaming Binance best-bid/offer data for 2.74 days (66,476,148 ticks) across five connected spot markets, an event-driven negative-cycle detector found zero executable triangular-arbitrage cycles once an execution-realistic simultaneity constraint (0.2-second maximum quote-age spread) was imposed. A detector without this constraint over-reports phantom opportunities—here up to +51.6 basis points—assembled from non-simultaneous quotes, reconciling prior work that finds arbitrage captured by co-located bots with prior work that finds it unexploitable at retail. On the funding-carry track, a two-year backtest over 151 perpetual-futures symbols reproduces a pitfall: a "no opportunity" conclusion under a curated major-coin universe reverses to positive validation-window profit under a volume-ranked broad universe, so the conclusion is driven by universe selection. A post-hoc placebo test (N = 1000, seed = 42) then finds the funding entry rule's profit not distinguishable from random entry timing (37.8th percentile; one-sided p = 0.622): in attribution terms, the return is beta to a carry factor, not alpha from timing skill. In our sample, arbitrage-like returns exist but are not accessible to retail as a skill-based edge.

title: Deleting Information: Evidence from the Digital Service Act
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and

detail.title: Deleting Information: Evidence from the Digital Service Act
detail.abstract: We study how the European Union's Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires platforms to act expeditiously on notices flagging content as allegedly illegal, affects the deletion of employee reviews on Glassdoor. Exploiting variation in firms' EU exposure in a difference-indifferences design, we find that deletions increase significantly post-DSA for EU-exposed firms relative to non-exposed firms. Using large language model classification to evaluate each review against Glassdoor's content guidelines, we find that the majority of deleted reviews contain no policy violation identifiable from the review text, and the flagged-review increase is concentrated in highdiscretion categories where enforcement is subjective. The deletion increase is concentrated in negative and critical reviews, with no statistically significant change for positive reviews, and is larger for firms with stronger strategic incentives. Displayed average ratings increase significantly post-DSA and become stronger predictors of both worker inflows and outflows, consistent with selectively curated ratings attracting workers who subsequently discover conditions that diverge from displayed scores.

title: Carbon Crediting When Better Measurement Is Not Enough
affiliations: and

detail.title: Carbon Crediting When Better Measurement Is Not Enough
detail.abstract: Carbon-crediting methodologies determine how imperfect monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) evidence is translated into issued credits. When project developers can influence measured outcomes, greater reliance on project-specific data improves targeting but also strengthens incentives to manipulate the signal. We develop a model in which a crediting authority commits to a crediting rule while anticipating the project developer's response. The framework distinguishes statistical accuracy from gaming robustness. The optimal rule generally attenuates the MRV signal: greater accuracy and robustness justify stronger reliance on project-specific evidence, whereas higher credit prices and greater heterogeneity in gaming ability call for a flatter rule. Even when manipulation becomes prohibitively difficult, measurement noise alone implies attenuation. We also characterize how market and project conditions affect the relative value of improving accuracy versus robustness. An illustration using project-level data on cookstove carbon credits shows how independent reassessments can inform the framework and highlights the data requirements for empirical implementation.

title: Level Breaks and Finite-Sample GLS Detrending: The Point-Optimal Unit Root Test and the Purchasing Power Parity Puzzle

detail.title: Level Breaks and Finite-Sample GLS Detrending: The Point-Optimal Unit Root Test and the Purchasing Power Parity Puzzle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research received no external funding, and the author declares no competing interests. This document is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed; any remaining errors are the author's own.

detail.abstract: Carrion-i-Silvestre et al. (2009) calibrate the GLS detrending parameter c for break specications that retain a linear trend, leaving unworked the no-trend case agged in their Remark 1. We develop it: Model LB, a constant with level-shift dummies. The point-optimal test is asymptotically invariant to the number and location of the breaks, so up to a regularity condition conrmed by simulation the optimal c keeps the Elliott et al. (1996) demeaned limit-7 for every conguration. In nite samples the optimum departs from that value by a remainder of order (m + 1)/T , which we calibrate. The result is a tabulated surface c(m, T) with critical values for ve M-class statistics statistic and critical value as the coupled output of one calibration. We apply the pair to the purchasing power parity puzzle on post-Bretton Woods annual data for eight admissible OECD currencies against the US dollar, a short sample. Seven currencies do not reject the unit root at nominal size, and the Canadian dollar falls exactly at the boundary (p = 0.049). At the feasible power of 0.450.48 that the calibration quanties, a joint non-rejection would be rare under independence but retains probability near one tenth under the measured cross-sectional dependence of the eight-currency set thin information in either direction and is not read as evidence for PPP. Modeling the exogenous level breaks nonetheless sharpens the measurement of persistence: it lowers the median half-life of PPP deviations from 7.0 to 3.0 years and bounds three of the four half-life condence intervals that the constant-only specication leaves unbounded. Part of the glacial half-life is an unmodeled level break, and part genuinely remains a correction to measurement, not a resolution of the puzzle.

title: Web4: A Seven-Layer Sovereign-Ownership Architecture for the Next Generation of the Internet

detail.title: Web4: A Seven-Layer Sovereign-Ownership Architecture for the Next Generation of the Internet
detail.abstract: The evolution of the World Wide Web is conventionally described in three eras-Web1 (read), Web2 (read-write), and Web3 (read-write-own)-each of which relocated a distinct form of power along the value chain: from publishers, to platforms, to ledger-anchored token holders. This paper introduces and defends a fourth: Web4 (read-write-own-act), in which sovereign ownership is not confined to tokens or ledger records but is co-specified across every operational plane of the network-identity, physical connectivity, compute, naming, developer tooling, application delivery, and consumer hardware-and in which autonomous agents act on behalf of that ownership under cryptographic, time-boxed capability grants. The central original contribution is the Ownership Thesis: the axiom that every layer of the stack must be reducible to a claim controlled by a decentralized identifier the subject holds directly, not one that is issued or held by an operator on the subject's behalf. From this axiom we derive a seven-layer reference architecture and formalize the Synthetic Web as the class of network activity structurally defined by agent-executed action under such capability grants. We position each layer against the relevant standards (W3C DID Core v1.1, W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model v2.0, Model Context Protocol, Agent-to-Agent v1.0.0, NIST CAISI AI Agent Standards Initiative) and provide a security analysis covering key management, alias unlinkability via BBS+ selective disclosure, Sybil resistance, delegated-authority scope creep, and data-sovereignty enforcement, with explicit identification of open problems that require further verification.

title: From Invention to Education: Impact of Technological Innovation on Human Capital Formation in China
affiliations: , The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Economics

detail.title: From Invention to Education: Impact of Technological Innovation on Human Capital Formation in China
detail.abstract: This paper examines the causal effect of China's surge in technological innovation on educational attainment between 2000 and 2015. Exploiting heterogeneous prefecturelevel exposure to global innovation shocks and an instrumental-variables design based on patent-citation networks, we find that faster local patent growth significantly raises both high school and college attainment rates, with effects concentrated among rural youth. We show that this pattern is driven less by rising wage premia for educated urban workers and more by innovation-induced expansion of non-agricultural employment opportunities. Because rural youth increasingly transition into non-agricultural jobs-either locally or through migration to urban labor markets-these expanding opportunities raise the returns to schooling for rural households, motivating greater educational investment. Overall, these results highlight technological innovation as an important driver of educational upgrading and human capital accumulation. Our findings also indicate that technological change can narrow, rather than widen, educational disparities between urban and rural areas in developing economies.

title: Bank Stability under Private Credit Stress
affiliations: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, California State Polytechnic University, San Luis Obispo - Finance Area, Eastern Connecticut State University and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics (SUFE) - Dishui Lake Advanced Finance Institute (DAFI)

detail.title: Bank Stability under Private Credit Stress
detail.abstract: We use the unique setting of the 2026 redemption-cap events among Business Development Companies (BDCs) to examine whether private credit stress affects bank stability. Leveraging detailed regulatory filings on BDC financing arrangements and credit agreements, we identify banks linked to affected BDCs. We find that exposed banks experience significantly larger increases in systemic risk and lose approximately 12 percent of their equity value during the stress episode. The effects are strongest among banks directly linked to affected BDCs, consistent with credit agreements serving as an important transmission channel. Our findings provide new evidence that private credit stress can spill over to the banking sector through existing bank–BDC linkages.

title: Partial Retirement and Labor Supply: Quasi-experimental Evidence from Sweden

detail.title: Partial Retirement and Labor Supply: Quasi-experimental Evidence from Sweden

contentType.other: Accepted for publication in the Canadian Journal of Economics. This is the author-accepted manuscript; the final published version is not yet available.

detail.abstract: The declining share of the working-age population (20-64) has led many countries to introduce social security reforms to extend the working lives of older employees. While reforms such as raising the early retirement age can effectively achieve this goal, they are often perceived as forced. Partial retirement schemes, which allow individuals to work part-time while receiving a significant portion of their previous wages, offer a more flexible alternative. However, the impact of these schemes on the overall labor supply remains ambiguous. On one hand, partial retirement may increase labor supply by encouraging part-time work over early retirement; on the other hand, it may reduce labor supply if full-time workers choose to shift to part-time work. This paper investigates these effects by studying the introduction of a partial retirement scheme for central government employees aged 61-65 in Sweden. The findings show a 6.35% drop in average earnings, suggesting that generous partial retirement terms, which replace a substantial share of prior income, incentivize a shift from full-time to part-time work, thereby reducing the overall labor supply.

title: Retirement Mismatch Among Older Adults: Expectations, Preparedness, and Retirement Security
affiliations: Texas Tech University and Texas Tech University

detail.title: Retirement Mismatch Among Older Adults: Expectations, Preparedness, and Retirement Security
detail.abstract: Can older individuals accurately anticipate when they will retire and whether they are financially prepared for retirement? Conventional retirement models largely evaluate retirement security through the accumulation of financial resources, implicitly assuming that older individuals form reasonably accurate expectations regarding both retirement timing and retirement preparedness. This paper introduces the Great Retirement Mismatch Framework, a unified behavioral framework that distinguishes between two complementary dimensions of retirement mismatch: Retirement Timing Surprise, which captures deviations between expected and realized retirement timing, and Retirement Calibration Status, which captures the alignment between perceived and objectively measured retirement preparedness. Using longitudinal data from the RAND Health and Retirement Study (1992-2022), the analysis examines the demographic, financial, health, and functional characteristics associated with these two forms of retirement mismatch among older Americans. The findings reveal that retirement mismatch is widespread and systematically associated with observable individual characteristics rather than arising randomly. More broadly, the evidence suggests that retirement insecurity reflects not only the adequacy of financial resources but also older individuals' ability to accurately anticipate retirement transitions and correctly assess their preparedness for retirement. The study extends the retirement and aging literature by demonstrating that understanding retirement security requires considering both financial adequacy and expectation accuracy. The findings offer new insights for retirement economics and have important implications for aging policy, retirement planning, and the design of personalized decision-support tools that promote financial security in later life.

title: Age-Dependent Taxation: The Role of r-g
affiliations: National Taiwan Normal University and HKUST(GZ)

detail.title: Age-Dependent Taxation: The Role of r-g
detail.abstract: This paper shows that the relationship between the real interest rate on household savings (r) and the real GDP growth rate (g) is a key determinant of the optimal labor income tax depending on age. When the economy satisfies r > g, the default case in the literature, the optimal labor tax increases with age. However, when r < g, the empirically more relevant case, the pattern reverses and the optimal labor tax decreases with age. In a counterfactual where r = g and other mechanisms favoring agedependent taxation remain present, the optimal labor tax exhibits almost no explicit age-dependence. By decomposing the source of welfare gains from age-dependent labor taxation, we find that the channel governed by rg contributes most of welfare improvements rather than those typically emphasized, such as reduced distortions in life-cycle labor supply or enhanced risk-sharing among households.

title: Digital Maps : IP Paradigms and New Technology

detail.title: Digital Maps : IP Paradigms and New Technology
detail.abstract: This monograph undertakes a comprehensive legal examination of digital maps through the lens of copyright law, addressing a significant gap in both Polish and international legal literature. Against the backdrop of rapid advancements in geolocation technologies and the emergence of the geoinformation society, the study critically analyses whether existing intellectual property frameworks—developed largely in the analogue era—can adequately accommodate the unique characteristics of contemporary digital cartographic products.

title: Contracting for Equity
affiliations: Notre Dame Law School

detail.title: Contracting for Equity
detail.abstract: Modern contract theory often treats equity as a defect of contract doctrine because it supposedly undermines party intent. Discretionary, ex post scrutiny of contracts is said to frustrate ex-ante planning and reduce contractual value. Theorists point to the hyperformalist contracting practices of particular groups as models to which general contract law should conform. Inaccurate histories-claiming that equity once served a narrow function in contract that is now obsolete-support excising equity from contract law. This Article corrects the contemporary empirics and the history. It shows that equity has long functioned, and continues to function, as a core mechanism for giving effect to party intent under conditions of incomplete contracting, bounded rationality, informational asymmetry, and opportunism. Today, in a range of contexts, sophisticated parties choose equitable adjudication, authorizing decisionmakers to depart from strict legal rules in favor of commercial purpose and fairness. Historically, equity was not a marginal factor but the very root of modern contract law. Rather than undermining autonomy, equity operates as a cost-effective device for aligning legal enforcement with contractual purpose where rigid rules predictably fail. When properly calibrated and competently administered, equity supports rather than threatens party intent and contract value.

title: Reading the Bylaws: Event-Anchored Governance Amendments from 8-K Item 5.03 as a Cross-Sectional Signal

detail.title: Reading the Bylaws: Event-Anchored Governance Amendments from 8-K Item 5.03 as a Cross-Sectional Signal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose. The research was conducted independently, without funding or affiliation with any entity that has a financial interest in the subject matter of the paper. No consulting, advisory, or employment relationship exists with any firm or investor whose interests are related to the empirical findings.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available archival data --- Securities and Exchange Commission 8-K filings via EDGAR, Definitive 14A proxy statements via EDGAR, Center for Research in Security Prices daily stock file returns, and Ken French Data Library factor returns. No human subjects, patient data, or personally identifiable information are involved. No institutional review board approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. All computational and data costs were borne by the author. Data sources are publicly available (SEC EDGAR) or licensed via institutional academic subscription (Center for Research in Security Prices daily stock file version 2 via Wharton Research Data Services).

detail.abstract: I introduce a zero-shot large language model classification of U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) 8-K Item 5.03 body narratives — the mandated disclosure of amendments to articles of incorporation or bylaws — and show that the resulting governance-improvement class, combined with a recurring-amender cluster indicator, predicts a persistent multi-horizon post-event cumulative abnor- mal return. On an eight-year 2017–2024 sample of 8,442 firm-events from the SEC EDGAR public filing index joined to the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) daily stock file, the governance-improvement cohort’s mean cumulative ab- normal return, after controlling for market exposure, Fama-French twelve-industry × calendar-quarter fixed effects, and the same firm’s language-model-extracted Bebchuk-Cohen-Ferrell entrenchment index, is +3.7% at the 126 trading-day hori- zon with a 𝑡-statistic of +4.42 (𝑝 = 1.15 × 10−4 under a Newey-West cross-horizon Wald joint test). Three of four horizons in the same cohort (twenty, sixty-three, and one hundred twenty-six trading days) survive a family-wise Bonferroni correction at the 5% level over twelve classification-by-horizon cells. Because the specifi- cation controls for the same firm’s static entrenchment-index level, the residual signal reflects event-level directional shifts in bylaw provisions that the annual- snapshot index does not capture. A five-ablation robustness battery (sub-industry demean, recurring-window sensitivity from one year through seven years, intraday- timing anchor, one-year holding horizon, and a Yahoo Finance versus CRSP daily stock file vendor cross-check with a Pearson correlation of 0.954 at the sixty-three trading-day horizon) confirms the finding across every alternative specification. On an ex-ante mid-capitalization recurring-amender subcohort (𝑛 = 300; five hun- dred million to three billion U.S. dollars), the sixty-three trading-day mean cumu- lative abnormal return is +7.7% (𝑡 = +4.21). The full pipeline, including the classification prompts, the two-vendor agreement audit, and the reproducibility scripts, is publicly documented.

title: How Synthetic Risk Transfer Is Building the Next Systemic Credit Crisis

detail.title: How Synthetic Risk Transfer Is Building the Next Systemic Credit Crisis
detail.abstract: Since Basel III took effect, banks have made extensive use of synthetic risk transfer instruments, Significant Risk Transfer (SRT) and Credit-Linked Notes (CLN), to release regulatory capital and manage credit exposure. In parallel, the private credit market has expanded rapidly, financing borrowers through covenant-lite loan structures and, in a growing share of cases, payment-in-kind (PIK) interest. This paper argues that this architecture has not dispersed credit risk so much as relocated and concentrated it in entities that are frequently opaque, interconnected, and thinly capitalized relative to the risk they carry. In a recovery-rate shock, protection sellers would likely be the first to come under strain, and the credit risk banks believed they had transferred could return to bank balance sheets, with the potential, if it occurs broadly enough, to trigger a systemic event. The events of June 2026 (Apollo's gating of a flagship fund, the sharp decline in Banca Ifis's share price, and Lee Robinson's short position on insurers with private credit exposure) are consistent with the mechanism described here, though they should be read as early data points rather than as complete confirmation of the thesis.

title: The Effects of Loan-to-Value Limits on Mortgage Lending and Housing Purchase: Evidence from Taiwan
affiliations: National Taiwan University - Department of Economics and Academia Sinica - Institute of Economics

detail.title: The Effects of Loan-to-Value Limits on Mortgage Lending and Housing Purchase: Evidence from Taiwan
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effect of loan-to-value ratio ceilings on mortgage lending and housing purchase decisions. We exploit a sudden tightening of LTV restrictions in Taiwan in December 2020, which imposed a maximum LTV ratio of 60 percent on borrowers whose newly originated mortgage was their third or subsequent loan. Using loan-borrower-matched administrative data, we implement a difference-in-differences design that compares third-mortgage borrowers with second-mortgage borrowers before and after the policy change. We find that the policy significantly reduced LTV ratios by 10.5% relative to the pre-reform baseline. Housing purchase prices fell by 5.8%, implying an elasticity of purchase prices with respect to LTV ratios of approximately 0.55. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the effects of the LTV limits on housing purchase prices were concentrated among borrowers with lower educational attainment, a group more likely to face liquidity constraints.

title: Legal Threats and Online Dissent: Evidence from Social Media Regulation in Turkey
affiliations: University of Calgary, Wilfrid Laurier University and

detail.title: Legal Threats and Online Dissent: Evidence from Social Media Regulation in Turkey
detail.abstract: We study how legal threats to social media platforms shape online political communication. We exploit the sharp implementation of a 2020 Turkish law that required social media companies to establish local offices and provide user data to the government on request. Assembling a panel of over 700 Twitter users and 7 million posts, we use a differences-in-differences design to compare dissenters, individuals publicly critical of the reform when announced, to other groups unlikely to be affected, such as celebrities. We find that dissenters and political exiles post 15-20 percent fewer tweets following implementation, and engagement with their content falls sharply. These short-run chilling effects emerge despite limited platform compliance, indicating that anticipated enforcement risk, rather than actual enforcement, drives the effect. In the long run, the chilling effects dissipate. Our findings suggest that states can govern online speech indirectly, by regulating platforms rather than users, but that such effects may be self-limiting in the absence of visible enforcement.

title: Can Sport Events Reduce Tourism Seasonality? Evidence from an Emerging Coastal Destination
affiliations: Aleksandër Moisiu University of Durrës

detail.title: Can Sport Events Reduce Tourism Seasonality? Evidence from an Emerging Coastal Destination

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used publicly available aggregated secondary data from INSTAT (Institute of Statistics, Albania) and did not involve human or animal participants. No individual-level or sensitive data were used; therefore, institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Sport events are increasingly considered strategic tools for destination marketing and tourism diversification. Tourism seasonality remains a persistent structural challenge for coastal destinations, where visitor arrivals are concentrated within a limited number of peak months. This study examines tourism seasonality patterns in Albania and explores whether sports events can help reduce seasonal concentration in tourism demand. The analysis is based on monthly tourism data for the period 2018-2025, comprising 96 observations of visitor arrivals and overnight stays in accommodation establishments. Descriptive statistics were used to identify seasonal patterns, while a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) tested whether tourism demand differs across months. Additionally, an independent-samples t-test examined differences between months that hosted major sports events and nonevent months. The findings reveal a pronounced seasonal pattern, with international visitor arrivals peaking in July and August and significantly lower during the winter months. ANOVA results indicate statistically significant variation across months (Welch ANOVA: F(11, 32.7) = 3.85, p = 0.001), confirming strong tourism seasonality. However, no statistically significant difference was found between event and non-event months (t(94) =-0.064, p = 0.949). The findings indicate that sport events held in shoulder seasons are not associated with statistically significant changes in international tourism demand. This suggests that participation-based sport events, at their current scale, have limited capacity to influence mobility patterns. From a sport science perspective, the results highlight the importance of event scale and integration within broader sport systems in shaping seasonal tourism dynamics.

title: Assessing the Effects of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Higher Education Outcomes: Evidence from Ethiopian Public Universities

detail.title: Assessing the Effects of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Higher Education Outcomes: Evidence from Ethiopian Public Universities
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education by enhancing teaching, learning, research, and administrative processes. Technologies such as machine learning, learning analytics, intelligent tutoring systems, and generative AI provide significant opportunities to improve educational quality, relevance, and accessibility while addressing the demands of the digital era. Despite these advancements, empirical evidence on the impact of AI adoption in higher education remains limited in developing countries, particularly Ethiopia. This study examined the effect of AI adoption on higher education outcomes in Ethiopian public universities, focusing on relevance, quality, and accessibility. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected from academic and administrative staff using a structured questionnaire. Descriptive statistics and multiple regression analysis were used to analyze the data. The findings reveal that AI adoption is widely perceived as enhancing curriculum modernization, student engagement, personalized learning, research productivity, and educational inclusiveness. Regression results indicate that AI adoption has a positive and statistically significant effect on the relevance of higher education (β = 0.220, p < 0.001) and accessibility (β = 0.151, p = 0.016). Although AI also demonstrated a positive effect on educational quality (β = 0.113), the relationship was only marginally significant (p = 0.074). Overall, the findings suggest that AI adoption has considerable potential to strengthen higher education outcomes, particularly by improving relevance and accessibility. The study recommends increased investment in digital infrastructure, institutional capacity building, faculty development, and supportive policy frameworks to accelerate the effective integration of AI across Ethiopian public universities.

title: Does Military Spending Fuel Inflation in Developing Countries? Evidence from Nigeria
affiliations: Centre for the Study of the Economies of Africa, Department of Economics, Faculty of Economics and Management Sciences, University of Ibadan, Ibadan, Oyo State, Nigeria and Centre for the Study of the Economies of Africa (CSEA)

detail.title: Does Military Spending Fuel Inflation in Developing Countries? Evidence from Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no form of conflict among the authors.
declarations.funderStatement: Authors do not receive any financial support to conduct this study.

detail.abstract: This study analyses the nexus between military spending and inflation in Nigeria, comparing the results from the mean-based OLS, FMOLS, DOLS, and GMM estimators with those obtained from Instrumental Variable Quantile Regression (IVQR), as well as the Toda-Yamamoto (TY) and LA-VAR time-varying Granger causality tests. While the mean-based estimators indicated that military spending has no significant effect on inflation, the IVQR results revealed significant heterogeneous effects across different inflation quantiles. The TY causality test identified a unidirectional causal relationship running from military spending to inflation. In contrast, the forward, rolling, and recursive time-varying Granger causality tests consistently indicated a bidirectional causal relationship between the two variables. This suggests that military spending and inflation in Nigeria are mutually endogenous. Furthermore, the plots of the algorithmic test statistics against the corresponding 90th and 95th percentile critical values confirmed that the direction and intensity of causality varied over time. Overall, the findings underscore the need for flexible and adaptive macroeconomic policies capable of addressing the evolving dynamics between rising military expenditure and inflationary pressures.

title: Extracting Predictability: A Time-Varying Factor-Augmented Approach under Mixed Persistence
affiliations: Nankai University, Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Nankai University

detail.title: Extracting Predictability: A Time-Varying Factor-Augmented Approach under Mixed Persistence
detail.abstract: This paper develops a time-varying factor-augmented forecasting model designed to extract predictable variation in the target variable when predictors exhibit mixed persistence. The framework accommodates stationary, nonstationary, and a mixture of observable and latent predictors, and allows latent predictors to follow either static or dynamic factor structures, thereby nesting many classical and new models as special cases. We develop an easy-to-implement sieve estimation procedure for the time-varying coefficients, establish its large-sample properties, and construct prediction intervals for the forecasts. Simulation studies show that the proposed methods perform well in finite samples. In an empirical application to U.S. inflation forecasting, the proposed model performs favorably relative to several competitors. Further analyses indicate that latent factors remain informative even when inflation exhibits autoregressive dynamics, since they absorb predictable variation that would otherwise be left in the autoregressive model errors.

title: Cost of Capital, Investment Risk and De-risking Instruments for Low-carbon Technologies in Asia
affiliations: University of Oxford,  and University of Oxford - Smith School of Enterprise and the Environment

detail.title: Cost of Capital, Investment Risk and De-risking Instruments for Low-carbon Technologies in Asia
detail.abstract: This study examines how the terms of capital for low-carbon technologies in Asia vary with project-level and country-level risks, and what this implies for public de-risking policy. Using loan-level data from Asian project finance, the paper links loan spreads to a structured set of risk channels, including governance quality, permitting frictions, macroeconomic volatility, technology maturity, project pipeline strength, disaster resilience, and fossil-fuel lock-in. The evidence shows that low-carbon finance is priced through more than engineering cost alone: stricter rule of law, political stability, and regulatory quality are associated with lower spreads and longer maturities, while property frictions, slower contract enforcement, inflation, and coal rents raise the cost of capital. The India comparison sharpens the analysis by showing that governance credibility, permitting efficiency, disaster resilience, and the maturity of the domestic clean-energy ecosystem are especially important in India-specific low-carbon project finance. Overall, the findings suggest that the cost of capital is a risk-pricing outcome rather than a simple reflection of technology cost, and that effective de-risking must be targeted to the binding constraint in each market.

title: Bank Lending and Environmental Quality in Gulf Cooperation Council Countries

detail.title: Bank Lending and Environmental Quality in Gulf Cooperation Council Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: To achieve economies with net-zero carbon emissions, it is essential to develop a robust green financial intermediary channel. This study seeks empirical evidence on how domestic bank lending to sovereign and private sectors in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries impacts carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas emissions. We employ PMG-ARDL model to panel data comprising six countries in GCC over twenty years for carbon dioxide emissions and nineteen years for greenhouse gas emissions. Our findings reveal a long-term positive impact of both bank lending variables on carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas emissions. In addition, lending to the government shows a negative short-term effect on greenhouse gas emissions. The crosscountry results demonstrate the presence of a long-run effect of explanatory variables on both types of emissions, except for greenhouse gas in Saudi Arabia. The sort-term impact of the explanatory variables on carbon dioxide and greenhouse gas emissions is quite diverse. Not only do these effects differ across countries, but some variables have opposing effects on the two types of emissions within a single country. The findings of this study present a new perspective for GCC economies: neglecting total greenhouse gas emissions and concentrating solely on carbon dioxide emissions means missing critical information for devising effective strategies to combat threats of environmental degradation and achieve net-zero goals.

title: Pricing Efficiency and Liquidity Dynamics in Real-World Asset (RWA) Tokenization: A DeFi Market Microstructure Perspective

detail.title: Pricing Efficiency and Liquidity Dynamics in Real-World Asset (RWA) Tokenization: A DeFi Market Microstructure Perspective
detail.abstract: The tokenization of Real-World Assets (RWAs) via Decentralized Finance (DeFi) protocols promises fractional ownership and continuous liquidity for traditionally illiquid asset classes, yet the market microstructure governing on-chain RWA pricing efficiency and pool liquidity remains under-theorised and empirically unresolved. This paper develops a quantitative market-microstructure framework to evaluate pricing errors, slippage dynamics and liquidity-pool efficiency in RWA tokenization relative to traditional Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs). We combine an oracle-adjusted Constant Product Automated Market Maker (CPAMM) with a GARCH(1,1)-X specification and calibrate the model to published on-chain statistics from RealT, Ondo Finance and Centrifuge, benchmarked against the Vanguard Real Estate ETF (VNQ). Simulation-based evidence indicates that (i) RWA tokenization lowers the implied cost of capital by 115-140 basis points; (ii) asset-level idiosyncratic volatility induces nonlinear slippage in constant-product pools during stress regimes; and (iii) oracle latency dominates the persistence of pricing deviation (PEₜ). We propose an oracle-conditioned hybrid liquidity architecture that significantly mitigates pricing deviation and enhances market efficiency.

title: Shock-Responsive Climate Notes: Rethinking Sovereign Debt Architecture in a Climate-Constrained World. A Conceptual and Theoretical Perspective
affiliations: , Mohammed VI Polytechnic University and Mohammed VI Polytechnic University

detail.title: Shock-Responsive Climate Notes: Rethinking Sovereign Debt Architecture in a Climate-Constrained World. A Conceptual and Theoretical Perspective
detail.abstract: Two bodies of literature bear directly on the fiscal consequences of climate change but have rarely been brought into contact with each other. The first establishes that climate-related shocks-floods, droughts, cyclones, heat extremes-translate systematically into fiscal stress: rising public debt, contracting tax revenues, and elevated sovereign borrowing costs, even in economies that borrow on concessional terms. The second offers a contractual toolkit, in the form of state-contingent debt instruments, for reducing the procyclicality of sovereign borrowing. The gap between them points to a structural flaw in climate finance itself: existing instruments are built on contracts that do not know a climate shock has happened. Debt service obligations remain fixed precisely when fiscal capacity collapses. This paper proposes the Shock-Responsive Climate Note (SRCN): a sovereign debt instrument that embeds climate contingency directly into the contract. When a qualifying climate shock occurs, debt service adjusts automatically-interest rates fall, principal repayments are deferred, maturities extend-without negotiation or restructuring. Under stable conditions the instrument behaves like an ordinary long-maturity concessional loan. We develop the instrument formally in a state-contingent debt framework and establish three properties that no existing instrument currently combines: fiscal stability dominance over conventional concessional loans under any positive climate shock; vulnerability alignment, reversing the allocation bias that channels climate finance toward low-risk, high-income borrowers; and incentive compatibility, maintaining private capital engagement through transparent contractual risk-sharing rather than implicit public guarantees. The paper is conceptual and theoretical in intent. The contribution is architectural: it demonstrates that the design of financial contracts is as consequential as the scale of capital mobilized, and that re-engineering the debt contract itself, rather than layering relief on top of it, is a coherent and superior response to the growing fiscal risk that climate change poses for sovereign borrowers.

title: Accounting for Cliff Risk: A Dynamic Framework for Horizontal Merger Analysis
affiliations: , ,  and

detail.title: Accounting for Cliff Risk: A Dynamic Framework for Horizontal Merger Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel framework to incorporate dynamic incentives into the antitrust analysis of horizontal mergers, specifically for industries facing the risk of permanent demand disruption. We motivate our analysis through the proposed 2020 Arch/Peabody thermal coal joint venture, where the threat of coal-fired power plant retirement-driven by competition from natural gas-created a powerful incentive for coal producers to maintain low prices to preserve future demand. We derive a dynamic Lerner condition for oligopoly that endogenizes this risk of demand transition, demonstrating that post-merger upward pricing pressure is significantly attenuated when forward-looking firms internalize the link between current pricing and long-term demand. Finally, we propose a tractable approach to calibrate this risk and simulate post-merger price effects using limited data typically available to regulators. Our results demonstrate that traditional static models likely overestimate competitive harm in industries facing stochastic, irreversible demand transitions: what we refer to as "cliff risk."

title: Buy, Borrow, and Sell Anyway: Insider Share Pledging and the Limits of Buy-Borrow-Die
affiliations: University of Cincinnati - Department of Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Buy, Borrow, and Sell Anyway: Insider Share Pledging and the Limits of Buy-Borrow-Die
detail.abstract: In the "buy-borrow-die" account of top-end taxation, the wealthy borrow against appreciated stock instead of selling it, deferring tax until the basis step-up at death erases the gain. The borrowing itself has never been measured at the top. Since 2006, SEC proxy statements must disclose, by name, the shares their directors and named executives have pledged as loan collateral, and they also report blockholder pledges that could shift control; we extract every such disclosure from every proxy statement filed over 2007-2022 and link each pledger to their complete trading record. Pledged collateral peaks at $155 billion in 2021 and is hyper-concentrated: one holder accounts for seventeen percent of it and a hundred holders for more than two-thirds, a Gini of 0.93. Yet the behavior the account predicts does not appear. Pledgers realize gains at the same rate whether pledged or not, show no significant gradient in the tax incentive to defer, and do not defer when rates rise. Nor are pledgers the never-selling type the story describes: compared with non-pledging insiders at the same firms and of the same size, they are seven to eleven percentage points less likely never to sell. What tracks pledging is instead the cost of credit. These are facts about disclosed insiders, the one population whose pledging and trading are both observable, and the population the debate itself names. Among them, borrowing against stock looks like a credit instrument rather than the tax-deferral engine the debate assumes.

title: Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences
affiliations: University of Michigan, Ann Arbor and Yale University

detail.title: Order Auctions with Private Position Preferences
detail.abstract: We study auctions where two positions are sold to unit-demand bidders with private heterogeneous order preferences: some are specialists who value only the first position, while others are generalists indifferent between the two. First, we consider a first-price rule which allocates the first and second items to the highest and secondhighest bidders, respectively. We show that no strategy profile ex-post implements the efficient allocation at every type profile, irrespective of payments, and provide a distribution-free equilibrium welfare guarantee of 1/2. To augment this result, we prove that for deterministic one-round auctions and discrete bids, the efficient allocation requires each bidder to communicate at least one bit more than its bid's binary representation. We next ask what the same bit accomplishes in winner-pays-bid formats where bidders can also specify specific item preferences. In particular, we show that this strengthens our distribution-free equilibrium welfare guarantee to 1-1/e. Finally, we discuss the applicability to priority service and blockchain transaction ordering.

title: Conversion Injustice: A Generative Relational Account of Value Conversion

detail.title: Conversion Injustice: A Generative Relational Account of Value Conversion
detail.abstract: One party takes a value belonging to a category and returns a value belonging to another, holding that the second is equivalent to the first. Wages returned for labour, money returned for land, compensation returned for the dead: the transaction may balance and still be felt as a wrong, and the wrong is not located where distributive theory looks for it. This paper locates it in the proposition of equivalence itself. It argues, first, that the capacity to write such a proposition is not held in advance but generated by the act of crossing categories, so that the question of who owns the right of interpretation is the wrong question; and second, that alienation cannot serve as the criterion of injustice, since if every interpretation carries power then alienation distinguishes nothing. The criterion offered instead is closure: a conversion is unjust when the party who received the return can no longer put the equivalence itself back in question, but at most appeal within a rate already fixed. Two forms of closure are distinguished, procedural and structural, the latter arising where the conversion removes the very subject who would reopen it; incommensurability is recast as the limiting case of the second rather than as an independent prohibition. The account is stated with its cost: closed rates tend to be stable and open ones to fail, so revisability raises the frequency of conflict while lowering its intensity, and no inference from stability to legitimacy is available. The paper does not claim to settle value conversion but to identify it as a neglected structure, and closes by setting out the eight questions that follow if the structure is real, the last of which asks under what conditions a conversion rule can be kept open at all.

title: Modeling Volatility in the Indian Stock Market: A GARCH Analysis of the NIFTY 50 and Political Risk

detail.title: Modeling Volatility in the Indian Stock Market: A GARCH Analysis of the NIFTY 50 and Political Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available financial market data and does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or cell lines. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the conditional volatility of the Indian stock market, with particular focus on the NIFTY~50 index and the main sectoral indices of the National Stock Exchange (NSE). GARCH(1,1), GJR-GARCH(1,1) and EGARCH(1,1) models are estimated by maximum likelihood to characterize the dynamics of conditional variance, comparing the Indian market with the S\&P~500 as a benchmark for a developed market. Sectoral analysis reveals that energy and metals exhibit the highest levels of structural volatility. As a case study, we examine the extraordinary volatility spike following the electoral outcome of June 4, 2024, in which Prime Minister Narendra Modi lost his absolute majority. A formal event analysis shows that NIFTY~Energy displays the largest relative reaction of the entire sample (peak-to-pre-event ratio of 4.23), even larger than that of the general index, whereas NIFTY~Metal —despite starting from the highest baseline volatility level— reacts proportionally less than the aggregate NIFTY~50 itself. This result qualifies the hypothesis of a generic political risk and points instead to a channel specific to the energy sector, consistent with the index's high concentration in two conglomerates (Reliance Industries and Adani Group).

title: APCD: Adaptive Path-Contrastive Decoding for Reliable Large Language Model Generation
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: APCD: Adaptive Path-Contrastive Decoding for Reliable Large Language Model Generation
detail.abstract: Reliable text generation is critical for deploying large language models (LLMs) in real-world applications, particularly in high-stakes domains such as medicine. To improve factual reliability, various inference-time methods have been proposed, including logit-level methods that modify token probability distributions and representation-level methods that manipulate intermediate model representations. However, most existing approaches operate on a single decoding trajectory, limiting their ability to explore alternative reasoning paths and making them susceptible to error accumulation. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Path-Contrastive Decoding (APCD), an adaptive multi-path contrastive decoding framework that improves factual reliability without model retraining or fine-tuning. APCD comprises two key components: Entropy-Driven Path Expansion, which adaptively expands the decoding process only at high-uncertainty decision points, and Divergence-Aware Path Contrast, which dynamically regulates contrastive interactions among parallel decoding paths based on their distributional divergence to balance diversity and coherence. We evaluate APCD on four LLM backbones across eight benchmarks spanning both general-domain and medical question answering tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that APCD consistently outperforms strong inference-time baselines in factual accuracy while maintaining competitive inference efficiency. These results demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of APCD across diverse models and tasks, highlighting its effectiveness as a practical inference-time decoding framework for reliable LLM deployment, particularly in high-stakes domains such as medicine. Code is available at https://github.com/zty-king/APCD.

title: Identifying Fairness with No Envy: an Axiomatization
affiliations: University of Vienna - Department of Economics

detail.title: Identifying Fairness with No Envy: an Axiomatization
detail.abstract: Envy-freeness is arguably the most popular fairness principle for evaluating an allocation of goods to individuals. A given allocation is envy-free if no individual strictly prefers the bundle given to someone else. We present the first axiomatization of this principle. The desire for no envy emerges from our axioms even though none of them have the goal to avoid any kind of individual discontent with bundles being allocated to others. Through the lens of our axioms, a very basic behavioral trait (envy) emerges formally as being the obstacle to achieving fairness.

title: A Normalizing Flow Approach to Portfolio Optimization using the NTS Model with Volatility Clustering
affiliations: College of Business, Stony Brook University and Stony Brook University

detail.title: A Normalizing Flow Approach to Portfolio Optimization using the NTS Model with Volatility Clustering
detail.abstract: We propose a new multivariate model for portfolio optimization that combines an ARMA-GARCH model with normal tempered stable (NTS) innovations and a normalizing flow model, Real NVP, which is a Generative AI technique. Capturing both the fat tails and the dependence structure of asset returns is critical for portfolio optimization, but traditional covariance measures and standard parametric copulas cannot fully describe asymmetric tail dependence. The NTS distribution alone can capture fat tails in the marginal distribution of each asset, but it remains restrictive as a copula for describing dependence. Real NVP alone can flexibly learn the dependence structure, but it does not directly model fat tails in the marginal distributions. We combine the two models: each marginal residual follows an NTS distribution, while the dependence among the residuals is described by a copula built from Real NVP. We apply this combined model to market factors extracted from asset returns via principal component analysis (PCA). In an empirical study on the components of the DJIA index, the combined model gives a better riskadjusted portfolio than a model using only the NTS distribution or only Real NVP.

title: Does Natural Resource Dependence Restrict Green Development? An Investigation from The “Belt and Road” Countries
affiliations: Ningbo University, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School, University of Auckland Business School and University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Does Natural Resource Dependence Restrict Green Development? An Investigation from The “Belt and Road” Countries
detail.abstract: Addressing natural resource dependence is integral to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals by promoting economic diversification, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. This study explores the effect of natural resource dependence on green development by adopting the balanced panel dataset from the "Belt and Road" countries from 2005 to 2019. Notably, the novelty of our analysis lies in the empirical analysis using instrument-based techniques that consolidate the "green development curse hypothesis" in the Belt and Road countries. The mechanism analysis reveals that natural resource dependence curbs green development by weakening innovative capability, disturbing institutional quality, reducing population density, and crowding out human capital. Further, the dynamic panel threshold model handling endogeneity verifies the nonlinear relationship between natural resource dependence and green development. Interestingly, digital trade offers greater "resilience" than traditional trade, correcting the resource curse dilemma. Finally, heterogeneity analyses indicate that the green development curse hypothesis only exists in countries with high-level environmental regulations and resource-based countries. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envres.2024.119108

title: Greener on the Other Side: General Equilibrium Asset Pricing in a Technological Transition
affiliations: Monash University, Boston University - Questrom School of Business and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Greener on the Other Side: General Equilibrium Asset Pricing in a Technological Transition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: Not externally funded.

detail.abstract: We study the equilibrium asset-pricing implications of a technological transition. A firm endogenously reallocates capital from a mature brown technology to a more productive but initially nascent green technology. Investment in green determines the intensity of infrequent breakthroughs, which create green capital while destroying brown capital. The optimal transition path is non-monotonic and is shaped by two competing forces: diversification and growth. As the economy becomes greener, the dominant force shifts from diversification to growth. Early in the transition, breakthroughs reduce total capital and are therefore priced as disasters. Green capital hedges this creative-destruction risk and earns a lower risk premium than brown capital. As the economy greens, breakthroughs become expansionary and are priced as booms, causing the brown-minus-green risk-premium wedge to reverse sign.

title: A Scalable Array of Integrated LiDAR-Camera Units for Continuous Colourised 3D Monitoring of Underground Longwall Operations
affiliations: , University of New South Wales, University of Southern Queensland, Beijing Tianma Intelligent Control Technology Co., Ltd, Beijing Tianma Intelligent Control Technology Co., Ltd and University of New South Wales (UNSW)

detail.title: A Scalable Array of Integrated LiDAR-Camera Units for Continuous Colourised 3D Monitoring of Underground Longwall Operations
detail.abstract: Safe and efficient longwall mining depends on continuous awareness of the working face, where the shearer, roof supports, conveyor, and personnel interact in a confined and hazardous space. Current practice relies on fixed cameras that provide fragmented two-dimensional views, provide no distance measurement, and lose reliability in low light, dust, and occlusion. Three-dimensional sensing provides geometry but is limited to periodic surveys; a single protected LiDAR-camera unit covers only part of the face. This paper scales the unit into an array for continuous colourised 3D monitoring. The system combines a device-level software pipeline, deployment-level coverage analysis, and constrained array reconstruction. Onboard processing performs low-light enhancement, enclosure-aware calibration, LiDAR-camera fusion, point-cloud reduction, orientation estimation, and data streaming, reducing the transmitted data rate from more than 2.4 Gb/s to below 25 Mb/s per unit. Coverage analysis showed that a 15°-20° downward mounting angle improves visibility beneath the roof-support canopy, with a 20° tilt increasing footprint by more than 66%, while 6.3 m spacing provides continuous neighbouring coverage with approximately 15% overlap. The reconstruction method uses known installation spacing, IMU prior, roof-plane pre-alignment, overlap-region registration, and pose-graph optimisation to merge device outputs into a common frame. In a 50-device simulated longwall evaluation, the method achieved 1.01° rotation error and translation errors of 0.01 m along the deployment axis and 0.09 m along the cross-axis. It achieved 100% success, while five standard registration baselines failed. These results establish a validated pathway from a single sensing unit to continuous panel-wide 3D monitoring.

title: ETF Tax Efficiency vs. Structural Risk: An ETF / Index Mutual Fund Framework Applied to Bond Markets

detail.title: ETF Tax Efficiency vs. Structural Risk: An ETF / Index Mutual Fund Framework Applied to Bond Markets
detail.abstract: ETFs are increasingly common investment vehicles, due in part to the common understanding that these vessels carry a tax-efficiency advantage, especially when compared to its open-ended mutual fund brethren. This is of course caused by the in-kind creation/redemption mechanism that allows ETFs to avoid forced sales, and the distributed capital gains that come with it. The mechanism of this efficiency depends on a network of authorized participants (AP’s) willing to step in and arbitrage the ETF market price towards its net asset value (NAV) Shim and Todorov (2023) document AP impact as far more fragile for less liquid asset classes, particularly corporate bonds. In comparison Equities which are much more liquid, experience less of an impact. Those less liquid asset classes end up with larger and more persistent premium/discount dislocations when markets experience stress. This paper treats Shim and Todorov findings as a baseline for risk-side of our model, which acts in conjunction with an original tax-side analysis to one end; answering whether in a matched set of ETF and index mutual fund pairs it is possible to determine how large the tax efficiency advantage is in practice. The central finding is that the size of the advantage shrinks as liquidity falls, while the AP-related risk Shim & Todorov describe grows in opposite. These two trends move in conjunction have a direct impact on how an investor, or institution managing a bond portfolio should weigh ETF vs. Mutual fund exposure in any given asset class.

title: Was Stalin Necessary? Counterfactual Evidence on Soviet Growth

detail.title: Was Stalin Necessary? Counterfactual Evidence on Soviet Growth
detail.abstract: This article evaluates whether the exceptionally rapid growth of the Russian and Soviet economy after 1928 requires a specifically Stalinist explanation. The empirical design treats the historical claim as a sequence of increasingly demanding counterfactual comparisons rather than as a binary contest between observed growth and one preferred alternative. Long-run output series from the Global Macro Database and the Maddison Project are combined with synthetic control, augmented synthetic control, synthetic difference-indifferences , interactive-factor models, low-rank matrix completion, robust prediction benchmarks, historical analogues, exact spatial placebos, fake treatment dates, recovery placebos, donor-pool perturbations, endpoint sensitivity, and independent Soviet national-account reconstructions. A central methodological change concerns the New Economic Policy alternative. Mechanical extrapolation of the 1922-1928 recovery rate is rejected because it confounds trend growth with the closure of a war and civil-war output gap. The revised NEP counterfactual is estimated as a bootstrap recovery-gap process whose trend is anchored in the pre-1914 record and whose persistence is estimated from the observed 1921-1928 closure of the Russian output gap. The Russian-core specifications exceed the median admissible frontier at every endpoint and exceed the primary 90th-percentile frontier from the mid-1930s onward. The broader Soviet territorial aggregate remains more conservative and does not exceed that frontier. Donor perturbations preserve a positive Russian-core premium, but the small effective placebo set, weak pre-treatment fit for several estimators, recovery-related false positives, source dependence, and hostile upper bounds prevent an inference of unique or absolute historical necessity. The evidence supports a conditional growth premium and a narrower proposition: the observed acceleration required an unusually strong resource-mobilisation mechanism, while the available data do not identify Stalin as the only institutionally possible route.

title:
Anchored to Prices Past: 
Managerial Beliefs about Stock Value
affiliations: Korea University Business School and

detail.title:
Anchored to Prices Past: 
Managerial Beliefs about Stock Value
detail.abstract: Using novel data on explicit undervaluation claims in earnings calls, we study how managers form beliefs about their firms' stock value. Appearing in only 4.7% of calls, these claims seem to capture genuine managerial beliefs: they elicit strong positive price reactions without reversal, predict opportunistic repurchases, and are more common when managers have greater long-term equity exposure. Yet these beliefs are anchored to salient past prices: undervaluation claims are more likely following sharp declines from prior peaks. Consistent with persistent anchoring, technology firms that experienced extreme dot-com valuations remain more likely than peers listed after the dot-com bubble to claim undervaluation and repurchase shares opportunistically, with both effects weakening as dot-comera managers leave. Our findings suggest that financial-market bubbles can leave a lasting imprint on managerial beliefs and thereby distort corporate financial policy long after bubble prices recede.

title: Median-anchored Adjustment of Joint VaR-ES Forecasts
affiliations: and University of California, Riverside (UCR)

detail.title: Median-anchored Adjustment of Joint VaR-ES Forecasts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Risk managers often work with a fitted forecasting model they cannot replace even when its tail forecasts need adjustment. We propose a median-anchored rule that multiplies the distances from the fitted median to Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) by a common positive multiplier. The rule preserves VaR-ES ordering, and minimizing VaR check loss gives a closed-form weighted-quantile estimator. We establish consistency, give an asymptotic distribution under high-level conditions accounting for baseline estimation, and derive a VaR coverage-error bound at the forecast origin. When the same multiplier correctly adjusts both VaR and ES, the adjusted pair has lower conditional zero-homogeneous Fissler-Ziegel (FZ0) risk at that origin. Monte Carlo experiments examine this condition and several forms of misspecification. In rolling S&P 500 forecasts the adjustment lowers FZ0 loss in all four GARCH cells, each pairwise significant, with the largest and most robust gain, 10.4%, for Gaussian GARCH at the 1% tail; the 5% gains do not survive the most conservative family-wise adjustments. A quantile-regression baseline marks the boundary: when the fitted tail is already flexible, one multiplier adds little. Filtered historical simulation quantifies what standardized residuals and conditional scales add when available.

title: Policy Priorities for the Global Labor Market Transition to the Capability Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Policy Priorities for the Global Labor Market Transition to the Capability Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All three authors are employed by Takamol Holding, the publisher of this paper. Takamol Holding runs digital labor market systems in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including several of the programs and platforms discussed in the paper, among them the Qiwa platform, the Waad National Training Campaign, and the National Skills Platform, and works in partnership with the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development. Takamol Holding also convenes the Global Labor Market Conference, whose proceedings form part of the evidence base. Readers should take this institutional relationship into account when assessing the treatment of Saudi Arabian labor market policy, which the paper presents alongside comparative material on Singapore, Germany, Finland, France, Estonia, India, and the United States. The authors have no personal or financial interests to declare beyond their employment.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a policy analysis based on published secondary data from international organizations, including the World Economic Forum, the International Labour Organization, the OECD, and the World Bank, together with proceedings from the Global Labor Market Conference. The research involved no human participants, no patient data, and no collection of personal information, so ethics approval was not required. The illustrative worker scenario in Box 5 is a composite constructed from published statistical patterns and describes no actual individual.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by Takamol Holding as part of its institutional policy research program. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
Labor market institutions in industrialized economies developed over the twentieth century as a single interlocking settlement, in which wage employment mediated access to social protection, payroll contributions financed social insurance, educational credentials served as the dominant signal of workplace capability, and periodic surveys supplied the statistical basis for policy. Each of those conditions has since weakened, and they have weakened in concert, which gives the resulting institutional mismatch a systemic character.

Drawing on proceedings from three editions of the Global Labor Market Conference, together with data from the World Economic Forum, the International Labour Organization, the OECD, the World Bank, and BCG, this paper documents five structural transformations, beginning with the movement from credentials toward verified skills and extending through intensifying competition for labor capacity, the reorganization of task composition by artificial intelligence, the fragmentation of employment into platform and multi-engagement arrangements, and the growing distance between labor market activity and the statistical systems designed to observe it.

The evidence assembled includes the 39 percent of core skills projected to change by 2030, the two billion workers who remain in informal employment, social security contributions that constitute a quarter of OECD tax revenue, and the 47.7 percent of workers globally whose qualifications correspond to the requirements of their jobs.

Six policy priorities follow from that analysis. They would establish skills as primary economic signals, treat workforce capacity as strategic infrastructure, govern artificial intelligence as a workforce multiplier, align fiscal systems with capability-based economies, design portable and adaptive protection systems, and build computational labor intelligence systems.

title: Freemium is all you need
affiliations: State University of New York (SUNY) - University at Buffalo and Yale University

detail.title: Freemium is all you need
detail.abstract: Free access to a generative AI (GenAI) service requires costly compute, yet can also produce data that improve future service quality. We study a service provider whose users differ in request value and privacy preference, under the constraint that paid requests are kept private, while free requests can be used to improve model quality which otherwise reverts toward a baseline. In particular, we characterize service demand and prove that quality converges to a unique steady state for every stationary service strategy. Next, we analyze optimal pricing and quality policies and show that these can be expressed using two endogenous user value thresholds. For uniform values, we provide a closed-form optimal service strategy and characterize the sufficient conditions for offering free services as dependent on inference cost.

title: Preference Robust Distortion Risk Measures
affiliations: Grenoble Ecole de Management and

detail.title: Preference Robust Distortion Risk Measures
detail.abstract: We introduce a framework for preference-robust decision making when preferences over risk are modelled through generalised distortion risk measures. Unlike distributional robustness, our approach addresses ambiguity in the risk functional itself. We construct ambiguity sets on distortion (weight) functions using the Wasserstein distance and Bregman divergences, and derive closed-form expressions for the worst-and best-case distortion risk measures. We further extend the framework to rank-dependent utility, yielding preference-robust behavioural models. In particular, rank-dependent utility appears as a robustification of the expected utility model, yielding a novel way to address the Allais paradox.

title: Insider Trading and the Non-Public Character of Information: Reflections on the CJEU’s Brännelius Judgment

detail.title: Insider Trading and the Non-Public Character of Information: Reflections on the CJEU’s Brännelius Judgment
detail.abstract: The Court of Justice of the European Union marked a significant development in EU insider trading law. In its April 2026 Brännelius judgment, it adopted a restrictive interpretation of the non-public character of inside information, holding that information ceases to qualify as inside information only once it has been publicly disclosed by the issuer in accordance with Article 17 of the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR). While this approach effectively prevents insiders and tippees from exploiting information that is merely accessible but not yet reflected in market prices, it also gives rise to significant conceptual and practical difficulties. This article identifies two major shortcomings of the judgment. First, it produces paradoxical consequences for inside information that concerns issuers only indirectly and for issuers’ failures to comply with their disclosure obligations. Second, if interpreted broadly, Brännelius risks extending the insider trading prohibition to informed outsiders who independently uncover material information, thereby undermining information-search incentives and market efficiency. The article advocates a narrow reading of the judgment and concludes by highlighting the structural limits of the current formulation of the EU insider trading prohibition.

title: The Reopened Window: Revisiting the Choice Between IPO and Private Sale for Venture-Backed Technology Companies in the 2024-2026 Liquidity Cycle

detail.title: The Reopened Window: Revisiting the Choice Between IPO and Private Sale for Venture-Backed Technology Companies in the 2024-2026 Liquidity Cycle
detail.abstract: The 2022-2024 collapse in exit activity for venture-backed technology companies produced the longest liquidity drought in modern private-market history, followed by an unusually rapid reopening of the IPO window in 2025-2026. This paper revisits the classic IPO-versus-acquisition exit decision in light of that cycle. Drawing on exit data from Renaissance Capital, PitchBook/NVCA, PwC, and investment-bank commentary, I document a pronounced bifurcation: while public listings have re-emerged as the value-maximizing route for the largest, later-stage companies-dominated by AI-adjacent issuers and sponsor-backed portfolio companies-acquisitions accounted for roughly 94 percent of US venture-backed exit events in 2025. I argue that the reopened window has not restored the pre-2022 exit hierarchy but has instead entrenched a two-tier market in which scale, sector narrative, and sponsor overhang, rather than company quality alone, determine route availability. I propose a simple decision framework for founders, boards, and early-stage investors, and discuss implications for private-market valuation practice and for the design of dual-track processes.

title: Capital markets in Italy - Mid-year update 2026
