detail.title: Capital markets in Italy - Mid-year update 2026
detail.abstract:
Capital Markets in Italy: Mid-Year Update 2026 is a Consob report structured into four chapters that provides a comparative overview of the main trends and risks affecting the Italian financial system during the first half of 2026. The chapters are devoted to:

1. Macroeconomic and financial landscape, that examines recent developments in the global economy and financial markets. It discusses the economic consequences of renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, their impact on energy prices, inflation and monetary policy, as well as cross-country differences in growth dynamics, public debt sustainability and financial conditions. The chapter also reviews developments in gold and crypto-asset markets.

2. Financial market performances, that illustrates the behaviour of global and domestic financial markets during the first half of 2026. It reviews the performance of major equity indices, sectoral drivers of stock market returns, valuation trends, volatility and liquidity conditions, as well as developments in corporate and sovereign bond markets following geopolitical shocks.

3. Capital markets development, that examines the evolution of capital markets across major economies. Attention is devoted to equity market capitalisation, market concentration, the growing importance of private equity and private credit, and the increasing role of private markets in financing business growth, especially in technology-intensive sectors.

4. Primary market trends, that provides a general overview of IPO and delisting activity in a global and European context. The chapter highlights the declining role of European public markets, recent developments in Euronext Milan and Euronext Growth Milan, and the impact of listing and delisting dynamics on the size and structure of the Italian equity market.

title: Multi-Layer Semantic Integrity Framework for Knowledge-Reliable and Consistent Responses in Large Language Models
affiliations: Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka, Central Queensland University and Central Queensland University

detail.title: Multi-Layer Semantic Integrity Framework for Knowledge-Reliable and Consistent Responses in Large Language Models
detail.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate responses that appear fluent yet may contain hallucinations, inconsistencies, or biased reasoning, that can pose significant integrity risks for knowledge-based applications. This paper proposes a Multi-Layer Semantic Integrity Framework (MLSIF) that automatically evaluates the integrity of LLM responses based on six complementary metrics: response consistency, semantic similarity, reasoning quality, adversarial robustness, bias estimation, and perplexity. These metrics are combined into a novel Semantic Integrity Index (SII) that provides a unified interpretable reliability score per model. The framework is evaluated on eight open-source LLMs including Gemma2 9B, DeepSeek-R1 7B, LLaMA2 7B, LLaMA3.1 8B, LLaMA3.2 3B, Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral 7B, and Vicuna 7B using 200 structured prompts that span five knowledge categories, namely factual, reasoning, contextual, adversarial, and sensitive. Experimental results reveal that LLaMA3.2 3B achieves the highest SII (0.688) despite being the smallest model, demonstrating that parameter count alone does not imply semantic reliability. DeepSeek-R1 7B leads in reasoning quality (mean = 0.600), while Mistral 7B achieves the highest adversarial robustness (mean = 0.809). ANOVA and Tukey HSD analysis confirm statistically significant differences between the tested models on response consistency, reasoning quality, adversarial robustness, and bias estimation. Noteworthy, the proposed framework is model-agnostic and extensible, providing a principled pre-deployment validation mechanism for LLM’s integration into knowledge-based systems.

title: Behavioural Real Options in Electric Vehicle Replacement: Carbon Externalities and Policy Instrument Choice
affiliations: Corvinus University of Budapest and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Behavioural Real Options in Electric Vehicle Replacement: Carbon Externalities and Policy Instrument Choice
detail.abstract: We develop a behavioural real-options model of vehicle-replacement timing, in which a household decides when to replace an internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle with an electric vehicle (EV) as EV prices decline over time and carbon emissions are costly. The model has two clocks: calendar time governs prices and the externality, while vehicle age governs the replacement hazard and a behavioural friction. Solving the associated free-boundary problem yields an age-dependent value of deferral that vanishes at forced replacement, and a dynamic wedge between private and social replacement timing. We calibrate the model to European Union (EU) and Hungarian registration data. The registration flow prices the switch with little deferral value: forced replacements carry none, and voluntary switches concentrate late in ownership spells, where the option premium has decayed; the calibrated friction (EU +EUR 2.0k, Hungary +EUR 4.4k) is stable across assumed fleet ages and deferral assumptions. The EU-Hungary adoption gap is attributed to friction, not fleet age: an older fleet changes the volume of replacements, not the EV share among them. In the policy comparison, instruments that reduce the friction (charging-access vouchers, residual-value guarantees) abate carbon emissions at EUR 120-140 per tonne, below the social cost of carbon, against EUR 377-732 for price subsidies at an equal budget, and reach a five percentage-point adoption target at a quarter to a third of the fiscal cost, under calibrated policy-cost assumptions.

title: Is Cost Sharing Valid Under Loper Bright?
affiliations: University of Michigan Law School

detail.title: Is Cost Sharing Valid Under Loper Bright?
detail.abstract: On July 15, 2026, Meta Platforms Inc. filed its motion for summary judgement in its Tax Court case challenging the validity of Treas. Reg. § §1.482-7(a)(4), (d)(1)(iii), and (d)(3)(ii)(2011) (the "SBC Rule"), requiring the inclusion of stock-based compensation ("SBC") in the pool of intangible development costs ("IDCs") to be shared under a qualifying cost sharing agreement (CSA). This issue is also before the courts in cases brought by Abbot Labs and McKesson, and all of these cases represent an attempt to overturn the IRS victory in Altera, in which the Ninth Circuit held that SBC must be included in IDCs. But unlike the other cases, the focus of Meta`s motion is not the conflict between the SBC Rule and the arm`s length standard (ALS), but rather the conflict with the language of the statute itself. This paper argues that Meta should lose and that Treasury should withdraw Treas. Reg. 1.482-7 in its entirety because it is inconsistent with the text of the statute, as required under the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright and by the Presidential Memorandum on Directing the Repeal of Unlawful Regulations (Apr. 10, 2025).

title: Beliefs and Norm Violations: Experimental Investigation of Perceptions of Human and AI Mistakes
affiliations: University of Zurich, University of Basel and University of Zurich

detail.title: Beliefs and Norm Violations: Experimental Investigation of Perceptions of Human and AI Mistakes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is funded by ERC Chanse/Hera Program as part of Norms of Assertion in Linguistic Human-AI Interaction (NIHAI) project.

detail.abstract: How do people evaluate mistakes made by human versus AI agents in information-seeking interactions? We study this question in an inquiry-response setting in which an agent provides flight-gate information that is epistemically justied at the time of response but false ex post. Building on work on algorithm aversion/appreciation, we distinguish two channels behind humanAI evaluation gaps: a frequency-belief channel (dierent inferred error rates) and a normative-threshold channel (different tolerated error rates, conditional on beliefs). Across two pre-registered experiments with human versus AI framing and description versus experience formats, we measure perceived error frequency, acceptability of the false assertion, and personally tolerated error frequency. We also manipulate true error rates (1% in Experiment 1; 20% in Experiment 2) to test whether equalizing beliefs attenuates the acceptability gap. Results show a robust and substantively large humanAI acceptability gap in both experiments. Beliefs about error frequency are negatively associated with acceptability, but belief dierences are comparatively small and do not fully account for the gap. After frequency information is provided, belief gaps attenuate, whereas acceptability gaps largely persist (with partial attenuation in the high-error environment). Additional analyses show that norm-violation states (perceived errors exceeding personal tolerance) are strongly associated with lower acceptability and mediate a non-trivial share of the humanAI gap. The findings suggest that stricter normative standards for AI, rather than beliefs alone, play a central role in how people evaluate AI mistakes.

title: The Effect of Exchange Rate and Financial Sanctions on the Return of the Tehran Stock Exchange Index
affiliations: University of Birjand, Institute for Humanities and Cultural Studies and University of Birjand

detail.title: The Effect of Exchange Rate and Financial Sanctions on the Return of the Tehran Stock Exchange Index
detail.abstract: This study examines the dynamic effects of exchange rate fluctuations and financial sanctions on the returns of the Tehran Stock Exchange (TSE) Index over the period March 2011 to March 2023. Employing a Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregression (TVP-VAR) model, the model captures the evolving and asymmetric interactions between exchange rate growth, sanction intensity-proxied by changes in Iran's oil revenues-and stock market performance. The findings reveal that exchange rate shocks generally stimulate short-term increases in TSE returns but may reverse under heightened uncertainty, while intensified sanctions exert predominantly negative impacts, particularly during the EU oil sanctions period (2012-2015) sanctions and the post-2018 U.S. withdrawal from the JCPOA. Impulse response analysis shows that neither exchange rate nor sanctions shocks converge to long-term equilibrium, indicating structural vulnerabilities and limited market depth within the Iranian financial system. These results contribute to the literature on financial markets in sanction-prone, oil-dependent economies and provide evidence-based insights for policymakers and investors aiming to enhance market stability and resilience.

title: Seminal Human Behavior Insights

detail.title: Seminal Human Behavior Insights
detail.abstract: This is a condensed version of a monograph I wrote in 2021. The objective is to explain Perceptual Control Theory (PCT) in sufficient detail so that you can make an informed choice about a theory to serve as your foundational understanding of human behavior. Over many years, I have accumulated myriad PCT books and journal articles. As questions concerned me, I have been fortunate to get answers from the leading researchers, including Bill Powers who developed PCT. This paper distills the work of Bill Powers and his colleagues in developing PCT and highlights the potential wide application of PCT.  A widespread belief is that human behavior is about responses to stimuli (e.g., carrots and sticks management approach often seen in business) and/or that our brain plans in detail with incredible speed our every action to deal with disturbances in the environment. In this paper, a strong case is made that these approaches are decidedly inferior to the PCT approach focused on controlled perceptual input. We human beings live purposeful lives which can easily be ignored with a stimulus-response approach to understanding human behavior. Due to a continual stream of environmental disturbances, actions are varied in order to cancel the effects of these disturbances on our perceptions of controlled (important to our goals) variables. Behavior is control of perception. Two sections at the end of this paper, PCT for Business Firms and Concluding Thoughts, may provide new ideas for improving culture and performance measurement at all levels of the firm leading to a higher level of sustained value creation.

title: Float Scarcity and Price Formation in Ultra-Low-Float Mega-IPOs

detail.title: Float Scarcity and Price Formation in Ultra-Low-Float Mega-IPOs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study. The research uses only publicly available documents and market information and does not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Ultra-low-float mega-IPOs concentrate, within a single security, several forces that the asset-pricing literature has typically examined in isolation and in retrospective settings: downward-sloping demand for shares, divergence of opinion under short-sale constraints, index-driven demand, scheduled lock-updriven supply expansion, and the difference between headline market capitalization and economic value. This paper establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for a research program on this class of listings. It advances a framework rather than a result, makes no causal, predictive, or valuation claims, and does not assess whether any security is mispriced. The paper makes two contributions. First, it provides a unified decomposition that defines free float, effective tradable supply, lendable supply, float scarcity, index demand, lock-up supply expansion, headline market capitalization, and an economic value benchmark as separately specified constructs, each associated with a distinct observable proxy and a distinct identifying event. Second, it sets out an identification strategy that specifies, on the partly disclosed event calendar of such a listing, how each channel would be isolated as contractual supply restrictions lapse, as index-inclusion demand arrives, and as borrow and options markets form; fixing these constructs, proxies, and tests prospectively is one of several methodological safeguards-alongside the explicit construct definitions and a documented evidentiary basis-that discipline the empirical work to follow. We treat channel separability as a design objective to be tested rather than as a maintained assumption, and we identify where the relevant event windows overlap and thereby threaten identification. The June 2026 public listing of SpaceX-the largest initial public offering on record, with a base-offering free float of approximately four percent of total common stock-serves as the first worked instance of the class and as an informative empirical setting for the empirical papers that follow; it is a repeatable template rather than evidence, and the empirical execution is carried out in the sequel.

title: Digital Technology and Models of Demand for and Supply of Religion: Empirical Evidence from World Values Surveys

detail.title: Digital Technology and Models of Demand for and Supply of Religion: Empirical Evidence from World Values Surveys
detail.abstract: Existing studies on secularisation-religious market doctrines largely presume-often implicitly-that forms of religious communication, organisation, and authority are fundamentally territorially bounded and mediated by stable organisational structures. Thus, we develop a framework that simultaneously reexamines the secularisation thesis and the religious market hypothesis with digital connectivity as a structural mediator at the nexus of development, the state and religiosity. Using a panel of 78 countries and data from the World Values Survey, International Religious Freedom, and the Religion and State Project between 2001 and 2022, we estimate a Structural Equation Model (SEM) with Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML). The results show that development through digital connectivity is negatively associated with religious beliefs and not religious participation, partially confirming the secularisation thesis. At the same time, we find robust support for the religious market model: state intervention consistently suppresses both participation and belief, and digital connectivity does not fully offset these constraints. These findings make three contributions. First, they demonstrate that new media modifies the mechanisms underlying both secularisation and religious market dynamics. Second, they reconcile competing theories by showing that development produces dual effects: weakening doctrinal belief while sustaining participation through digitally mediated supply. Third, they advance a revised framework in which religiosity persists not despite modernisation, but through its technological transformation.

title: Rationalizing the Overhead Myth: Donor Aversion as a Selection Mechanism
affiliations: Rutgers Business School -- Newark and New Brunswick and Mississippi State University

detail.title: Rationalizing the Overhead Myth: Donor Aversion as a Selection Mechanism
detail.abstract: The overhead myth-the belief that a charity's fundraising ratio measures how well it serves its mission-has been debunked repeatedly since 2009, yet donors, raters, and regulators keep using the ratio. We argue the myth persists because it works, not as a way to rank charities but as a way to select them. Modeling fundraising as investment in a durable, depreciating stock of donor relationships, we show three things. First, the ratio is a poor ranking device: it confounds fundraising productivity with life cycle, volatility, and revenue mix, so a more effective charity can report a higher ratio than a less effective one. Second, donor aversion to the ratio in effect taxes fundraising, and the tax is survivable only for charities whose fundraising is productive and whose donor relationships are durable. Below a quality threshold, fundraising policy cannot offset depreciation and the charity is starved out. Third, this starvation is not merely a cost; it is a selection mechanism. Donor overhead aversion culls low-quality fundraisers and raises the quality floor of the surviving sector. If fundraising is competitive across entities, culling the least effective fundraisers can raise the output the sector delivers per donated dollar. The same filter, however, is biased against young, growing, and donation-reliant charities, which it culls along with the genuinely ineffective. Whether the overhead myth is on balance beneficial or detrimental, thus, is an empirical question about the distribution of fundraising quality, not a settled case of donor myopia.

title: The Legal Determination of Currency Value: Contradictions of Economic Theories and Econometric Projections 2026-2045
affiliations: and Universidad de los Andes, Venezuela

detail.title: The Legal Determination of Currency Value: Contradictions of Economic Theories and Econometric Projections 2026-2045
detail.abstract: This article critically examines the five most widespread explanations of how the value of one currency against another is determined: international reserves, portfolio theory linked to the size of economies, the law of supply and demand, the trust of countries, and mathematical patterns. Drawing on literature indexed in Scopus and Web of Science, it shows that these theories incur mutual logical contradictions and that none of them consistently outperforms the random walk in exchange rate forecasting. Through an econometric exercise using eurodollar exchange rate data from 2000 to 2025 and twenty-year projections (2026-2045), the indeterminacy of economic predictions is quantified: the 95% confidence interval reaches a width of 136% of the projected central level. By contrast, International Monetary Fund evidence shows that more than two thirds of States fix the value of their currency through legal decisions-anchors, bands and managed arrangements-and the projected trend raises that proportion toward 2045. The article concludes that contemporary currency value is predominantly a legal-institutional fact rather than the outcome of an economic rule.

title: Multilevel Analysis of the Perceived Greenwashing Across Age Cohorts
affiliations: Tehran University, , Presidency University and Tehran University

detail.title: Multilevel Analysis of the Perceived Greenwashing Across Age Cohorts
detail.abstract: Amid growing consumer demand for sustainability, corporate greenwashing-deceptive environmental marketing-has emerged as a significant threat to consumer trust. This study aims to develop a multilevel model to identify the key predictors of Perceived Greenwashing (PGW), with a specific focus on the role of generational cohorts in a cross-national context. A survey was conducted with 280 consumers from India and Iran. Multilevel Modelling (MLM) or Hierarchical Linear Modelling (HLM) was employed to analyse the data, with individuals (Level 1) nested within countries (Level 2), and predictors including generational cohort, awareness of greenwashing (AG), and exposure to greenwashing (EG). The analysis revealed that consumer awareness (β = 0.510) and exposure (β = 0.301) are the most powerful positive predictors of PGW. Critically, the widely assumed effect of generational cohort becomes non-significant after controlling for these experiential factors. Perceptions of industry type and regulations also emerged as significant, albeit smaller, predictors. The findings suggest that the perception of greenwashing is driven more by cognitive and experiential factors than by demographic identity. This study contributes to the literature by reframing the 'generational effect' as a function of information exposure and awareness. For practitioners, it underscores the importance of targeting consumer knowledge levels.

title: Analytical Redundancy for False Alarm Suppression in Edge-based Semiconductor Process Control

detail.title: Analytical Redundancy for False Alarm Suppression in Edge-based Semiconductor Process Control

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Funding recieved, it's my personal interest.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: With the scaling of semiconductor manufacturing technology towards sub-7nm nodes, the need for real-time Statistical Process Control (SPC) has led to the use of Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) on the edge. However, applying univariate anomaly detection algorithms on resource-limited microcontrollers poses an inherent risk, namely that of distinguishing whether the observed anomaly is due to real yield-affecting process excursion or simply isolated sensor failure. This paper presents a novel, localized causal verification method which offers an analytical solution to the problem without the necessity of any additional hardware infrastructure or cloud connection. Using hierarchical agglomerative clustering to map mutual information of anonymized fab sensors into "Virtual Modules," the presented method is able to interrupt traditional Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) signals and assess spatial-temporal stability of neighboring sensors. Testing the proposed solution on the SECOM semiconductor manufacturing dataset resulted in a ternary diagnosis, separating sensor fault from real process change with nearly 100% false alarm reduction while maintaining 100% anomaly sensitivity. Additionally, micro-architectural profiling proves the algorithm requires less memory space and runs within a microsecond latency range, ensuring viability of the approach for cloud-less, ultra-low power edge deployment.

title: Community Knowledge Preservation and Activation Program (CKPAP™): A Framework for Preserving, Activating, and Transmitting the Knowledge Communities Have Always Carried

detail.title: Community Knowledge Preservation and Activation Program (CKPAP™): A Framework for Preserving, Activating, and Transmitting the Knowledge Communities Have Always Carried

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is a conceptual and theoretical work. It does not report research involving human participants, identifiable personal data, or animal subjects. Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external grant funding. The research, framework development, and manuscript preparation were independently conducted by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Community Knowledge Preservation and Activation Program (CKPAP) as a comprehensive community-centered framework for identifying, preserving, translating, and transmitting experiential knowledge developed within grassroots, faith-based, artistic, cultural, culinary, and community environments. CKPAP is the fourth paper in the Brown Theory of Experiential Intelligence ecosystem and represents its most community-grounded contribution.

The paper argues that community knowledge — the accumulated wisdom of cooks who out-cook credentialed chefs, musicians who transmit cultural memory across generations, faith leaders who counsel without clinical titles, grassroots organizers who stabilize neighborhoods without institutional authority, and artists whose work embodies centuries of community identity — represents one of humanity's most significant and most systematically underpreserved intellectual resources. This knowledge disappears not gradually but suddenly, through displacement, death, gentrification, political disruption, and institutional neglect. CKPAP was developed to address that disappearance before it becomes irreversible.

Grounded in Paulo Freire's philosophy of naming as liberation, Dorothy Smith's institutional ethnography, Etienne Wenger's communities of practice theory, and the Brown Theory of Experiential Intelligence, the paper presents CKPAP's six governing principles, four-phase methodology, and a comprehensive implementation toolkit of nine tools designed for use across diverse community contexts. New Orleans serves throughout as the benchmark implementation context — a city whose cultural knowledge is simultaneously among the richest and most extracted in the world, and whose communities demonstrate that when the methodology works here, it works anywhere.

The paper concludes with an ethical framework and a future research agenda, arguing that the preservation of community knowledge is not a supplemental scholarly activity but a form of community protection — and that institutions seeking to serve communities honestly must develop the capacity to recognize and honor the knowledge communities have always carried.

detail.abstract: As industries increasingly adopt AI-driven solutions, scalable and secure infrastructures become essential to manage data-intensive operations. This paper presents a modular design for scalable AI infrastructure that integrates advanced security protocols with cloud-native technologies. The proposed architecture ensures data integrity, protects sensitive information, and adapts to evolving workload demands. Applications in healthcare and finance are analyzed to demonstrate the model's versatility, highlighting improvements in scalability, reliability, and compliance. This framework serves as a blueprint for deploying secure AI systems in high-stakes industries.

title:
Arbitrage-Free Bootstrapping of Instantaneous Forward Rate Curves: Piecewise Constant, Piecewise Linear, and Monotone Convex Cubic Schemes 
A Unified Framework with Machine-Precision No-Arbitrage Guarantees
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Arbitrage-Free Bootstrapping of Instantaneous Forward Rate Curves: Piecewise Constant, Piecewise Linear, and Monotone Convex Cubic Schemes 
A Unified Framework with Machine-Precision No-Arbitrage Guarantees
detail.abstract: We present a unified framework for bootstrapping the instantaneous forward rate curve from observed par swap rates, implemented through three progressively richer interpolation schemes: piecewise constant forwards (S1), piecewise linear forwards (S2), and monotone convex cubic forwards (S3). All three schemes are derived from first principles under the no-arbitrage condition that discount factors implied by the bootstrapped forward curve exactly reproduce market discount factors. The S3 scheme constructs a C 1 piecewise cubic forward rate function by enforcing value continuity, derivative continuity, and span-integral no-arbitrage constraints simultaneously, without the case distinctions required by the Hagan-West Monotone Convex method. The forward curve produced by S3 starts exactly at the observed short rate, is differentiable at all maturities, and satisfies no-arbitrage to machine precision (≲ 10-6 basis points round-trip error). A key feature of the framework is the treatment of the instantaneous forward rate function f (0, T) as the primitive object of term structure modeling, from which discount factors, zero rates, and par rates are derived-rather than the reverse. This perspective simplifies both calibration and downstream modeling, as the function f (0, T) is the natural state variable for Heath-Jarrow-Morton style analysis. The implementation uses only freely available public data from the U.S. Treasury Constant Maturity yield series and is fully reproducible.

title: How Community Finance Builds Entrepreneurial Performance: Longitudinal Evidence from Women Microentrepreneurs in Kinshasa

detail.title: How Community Finance Builds Entrepreneurial Performance: Longitudinal Evidence from Women Microentrepreneurs in Kinshasa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author report no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The survey protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee for Psychological Sciences of the Department of Psychology, University of Kinshasa, on January 24, 2022 (Ref: No. 0139/2022/LMK/DPSY/UNIKIN).

detail.abstract: Where financial inclusion remains limited, community-based savings and credit arrangements represent an important driver of entrepreneurial development. This study examines how community finance builds entrepreneurial performance among women-owned microenterprises in Kinshasa. Drawing on a three-wave longitudinal design conducted over eighteen months with 261 women microentrepreneurs, the study combines ordinary least squares regressions, sequential mediation analyses and moderation tests. The findings show that greater participation in community finance strengthens investment, improves the quality of goods and services, and fosters sustained entrepreneurial performance. More importantly, these effects operate through a capability-building process in which financial resilience enhances cash-flow stability, which subsequently supports entrepreneurial development over time. Community social capital further reinforces these mechanisms by strengthening trust, cohesion and resource circulation within savings groups. Beyond providing robust longitudinal evidence from an underrepresented Francophone Central African context, the study advances a processual understanding of community finance by showing that its contribution extends beyond access to liquidity to the gradual development of entrepreneurial capabilities. The findings also provide practical insights for financial inclusion policies seeking to combine community-based financial mechanisms, entrepreneurial capability development and stronger complementarities with formal financial institutions.

title: Energy-Agriculture Commodity Linkages across Investment Horizons: A Frequency-Band VARMA-Machine Learning Forecasting and Causality Framework

detail.abstract:
Commodity markets are shaped by mechanisms operating at different speeds. Speculative trading can affect futures prices within days, energy-cost pass-through may operate over weeks or months, while storage, fertilizer costs, transport disruptions, crop substitution and food-security pressures may unfold over longer horizons. Recent geopolitical crises, including the war in Ukraine and tensions in the Middle East, have reinforced the need to understand how energy shocks propagate toward agricultural markets through fuel prices, fertilizer costs, freight rates, insurance costs, exchange rates and food-import bills. This paper develops a frequency-resolved hybrid econometric–machine learning framework for forecasting and interpreting energy–agriculture commodity linkages. Daily log-returns of eight commodity futures—Brent crude, natural gas, cocoa, arabica coffee, sugar, corn, soybeans and wheat—from January 2010 to December 2025 are decomposed using a Daubechies discrete wavelet transform. Each wavelet band is interpreted as an investment and economic decision horizon. Within each band, a multivariate VARMA model captures linear cross-market dynamics, while a machine learning residual corrector captures nonlinear dependence left unexplained by the VARMA component. Band-level forecasts are then recombined through the exact wavelet reconstruction identity. The framework is complemented by band-specific  Granger causality tests, permutation importance measures and crisis-period robustness analyses. 
The empirical results show that the DWT–VARMA–Gradient Boosting model substantially outperforms raw-series VARMA and direct machine learning benchmarks. The main 80/20 hold-out evaluation yields an RMSE of 0.00764 and a directional accuracy of 91.23%, corresponding to a 70% RMSE reduction relative to the standalone VARIMA baseline. Raw-series Granger tests detect only five significant directed links among the 56 possible pairs, whereas band-specific tests reveal substantially richer energy–agriculture causal structures, especially at monthly, quarterly and long-run horizons. The results indicate that energy–food linkages are weak or invisible at the daily aggregate level but become economically interpretable once decomposed across investment horizons. The paper contributes to hybrid forecasting, frequency-domain causality and the economics of commodity market interdependence under global shocks.

title: The Economics of Tax Increment Financing: A Quasi-Experimental Analysis of Efficiency, Equity, and Urban Development in Chicago

detail.title: The Economics of Tax Increment Financing: A Quasi-Experimental Analysis of Efficiency, Equity, and Urban Development in Chicago

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it relies entirely on the secondary analysis of publicly available, aggregate administrative and demographic data. The research involved no human subjects, clinical trials, or private participant information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The study was conducted as an independent academic project.

detail.abstract: Tax Increment Financing (TIF) is one of Chicago's most pervasive-but contested-development tools. Using a newly built panel that merges every 2017-2023 TIF annual report with community-area socioeconomic snapshots, this honors thesis evaluates whether Chicago's program is (i) efficient-does it pass the "but-for" test by catalyzing development that would not otherwise occur?-and (ii) equitable-are benefits and burdens shared fairly across neighborhoods and residents. Employing OLS, fixed-effects, difference-indifferences , spatial regression-discontinuity, and an Invest South/West-based instrumental-variables design, we find five central results. First, TIF fund balances and cumulative spending are strongly but non-linearly related to neighborhood income: both the poorest and the richest areas hold the largest per-capita balances, while middle-income communities hold the least. Second, causal estimates show no significant reduction in unemployment among district residents, echoing Czurylo (2023) who finds that job gains recorded inside Chicago TIF blocks accrue mainly to commuters rather than local households. Third, in PTELL-capped Cook County the existence of a TIF district does not cut Chicago Public Schools revenue below what the Property-Tax Extension Limitation Law would otherwise allow; instead, the increment can raise aggregate tax rates faced by all property owners, shifting the equity debate from school funding to taxpayer incidence. Fourth, since the launch of Invest South/West in late 2019 the City has drawn down excessive downtown balances and increased expenditures in historically disinvested South-and West-Side neighborhoods, although the program's net distributional impact remains modest. Finally, robustness checks scaling balances by frozen equalized assessed value (EAV) rather than population leave all qualitative conclusions intact. Together, the evidence suggests that while TIF can finance large capital projects, its record in Chicago shows limited efficiency gains and persistent inequities. We discuss policy implications, including stricter adherence to the "but-for" criterion, improved transparency and oversight, and complementary investments (like Invest South/West) to ensure TIF contributes to inclusive urban development.

title: Between Deterrence and Rivalry: The Evolving Military Competition Between Turkey and Israel in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East
affiliations: Lebanese University

detail.title: Between Deterrence and Rivalry: The Evolving Military Competition Between Turkey and Israel in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Middle East
detail.abstract:
Purpose:
This study examines the transformation of Turkish-Israeli relations from a limited diplomatic dispute into a multidimensional strategic rivalry shaped by maritime competition, military modernization, intelligence confrontation, and competing visions of regional order. It analyzes how geopolitical shifts, security doctrines, and regional power dynamics have altered the nature of interaction between the two states.

Design/methodology/approach:
The research employs a geopolitical and strategic analysis framework, combining primary strategic sources, official doctrines—including Turkey’s Blue Homeland (Mavi Vatan) doctrine—military assessments, intelligence analyses, and multi-theatre mapping of developments across the Eastern Mediterranean, Syria, and Lebanon. The study evaluates strategic capabilities, operational patterns, and regional alignments to explain the evolution of Turkish-Israeli competition beyond conventional diplomatic tensions.

Findings:
The study finds that while a direct conventional military confrontation remains unlikely due to mutual deterrence, institutional constraints, and strategic calculations, a persistent “shadow war” has emerged. This competition involves intelligence operations, cyber activities, maritime signaling, military posturing, and indirect rivalry through regional arenas. Syria and Lebanon have become particularly significant theatres where competing security interests, proxy dynamics, and regional influence campaigns intersect. The findings demonstrate that maritime disputes, energy competition, and shifting alliances have transformed bilateral friction into a broader struggle over regional power and order.

Originality/value:
This research provides a comprehensive analysis of the militarization of Turkish-Israeli rivalry and contributes to broader debates on Middle Eastern security dynamics. It argues that the primary danger does not stem from an imminent conventional war, but from the gradual normalization of strategic confrontation. The accumulation of persistent tensions, military competition, and indirect engagements may ultimately reshape regional security structures as profoundly as an open conflict.

title: Authority Accretion and the Crystallization Threshold: A Cross-Sector Theory of AI Safeguard Failure

detail.title: Authority Accretion and the Crystallization Threshold: A Cross-Sector Theory of AI Safeguard Failure
detail.abstract: AI safeguard failures across industries exhibit divergent surface characteristics but a recurrent underlying mechanism. Drawing on institutional theory, organizational silence research, principalagent theory, and safety science, this paper develops a three-stage model of that mechanism: (1) advisory entry, in which AI systems are classified as decision support and thereby exempted from decision-grade governance; (2) authority accretion, in which human review degrades into ratification through individually rational, undocumented adjustments under throughput pressure, inflating the system's operational mandate while its documented mandate remains fixed; and (3) a crystallization threshold, at which the accumulated divergence between documented and behavioral authority can no longer be reconciled quietly and surfaces through incident, audit, or litigation. The paper explains why event-triggered governance structurally fails against this gradient-static risk classification, efficiency metrics that reward oversight erosion, and suppressed practitioner voice-and synthesizes evidence patterns from twelve sectors, including security operations, financial services, healthcare, energy, manufacturing, public administration, and supply chain. Three cross-sector safeguard instruments are proposed: behavioral authority audits that re-derive actual decision authority from interaction telemetry; paired counter-metrics under independent ownership; and voice channels validated by visible outcomes. The framework yields falsifiable propositions, principally that AI-related incidents are disproportionately preceded by measurable divergence between documented and behavioral authority, testable retrospectively within single organizations. The paper contributes a mechanism-level account of AI governance failure that unifies sectoral observations and converts safeguard design from compliance enumeration into gradient measurement.

title: Institutional Maintenance: Why Coherence Requires Ongoing Care
affiliations: Hoopoe Holding Ltd.

detail.title: Institutional Maintenance: Why Coherence Requires Ongoing Care
detail.abstract: Institutions do not remain coherent by default. Coherence is not a static asset that organizations possess once and for all. It is an ongoing achievement that must be preserved, repaired, and renewed. This paper argues that institutional maintenance is the practical counterpart to institutional drift. If drift describes the slow erosion of meaning, authority, memory, and responsibility, maintenance describes the work through which these four domains are kept connected over time. In healthcare clinics, franchise systems, and other high-stakes service organizations, maintenance becomes visible when organizations continue functioning without losing interpretability to themselves. This requires more than oversight or compliance. It requires the continuous upkeep of shared language, legible decision rights, institutional memory, and accountable ownership. Existing accounts of organizational resilience often emphasize adaptation, flexibility, or crisis response. While these are important, they do not fully explain how institutions preserve coherence during ordinary operations, when no crisis is present yet erosion continues quietly. This paper develops a conceptual argument that reframes maintenance as the hidden labor of organizational durability. Drawing on earlier work on structural blindness, structural DNA, invisible governance, and institutional drift, the article suggests that organizations remain healthy not because they avoid change, but because they maintain the internal conditions that make change legible and governable (Barzegar, 2025a, 2025b, 2025c, 2025d). The contribution is theoretical. It identifies maintenance as the everyday practice that keeps institutions from becoming unintelligible to themselves.

title: The Health Innovation Corridor: An Operating System for Moving Health Innovation from Science to Scale between Europe and the Gulf

detail.title: The Health Innovation Corridor: An Operating System for Moving Health Innovation from Science to Scale between Europe and the Gulf

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author serves as Regional Director of the Galien Foundation Middle East & Central and Eastern Europe and is involved in the development of Galien Foundation initiatives in the regions discussed in this paper. This institutional role may be perceived as relevant to the subject matter. The author declares no other personal or financial conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a strategic policy analysis and does not involve human participants, patient data, clinical interventions or animal research.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for the preparation of this paper.

detail.abstract:
Europe and the Gulf possess complementary strengths but also mirrored structural deficits in health innovation. Europe combines world-class science, clinical research, regulatory expertise and a dense biotechnology and medical-technology ecosystem, yet repeatedly fails to move promising innovations from validated science to commercial and clinical scale. The Gulf, by contrast, has capital, execution speed, national-scale health systems, advanced genomic infrastructure and the political capacity to deploy innovation rapidly, while still importing much of its health technology, intellectual property and specialist knowledge.

This paper proposes the Health Innovation Corridor as a permanent institutional mechanism connecting European scientific and clinical capacity with Gulf capital, validation environments, procurement systems and deployment scale. Rather than another dialogue platform, the Corridor is designed as an operating system for adoption. Its core components include a shared Innovation Qualification Framework, access to clinical pilots, mapped regulatory pathways, blended capital, procurement mechanisms, a data and sovereignty compact, and an independent public-private operator accountable for measurable outcomes.

The paper argues that Central and Eastern Europe should serve as the Corridor’s principal European entry point because the region combines strong scientific and clinical capabilities with one of Europe’s most acute scale-up deficits. It identifies precision medicine and AI-enabled diagnostics as leading pilot sectors and proposes a narrow 24-month implementation programme focused on moving qualified projects from selection through clinical validation to procurement and co-production.

The central thesis is that the scarce resource in Europe-Gulf health cooperation is neither science nor capital, but the institutional machinery capable of converting one into the other.

title: Resilience-oriented Strategic Stocking and Capacity Planning: Hedging against Rare Disruptions
affiliations: , School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - Department of Decision Sciences & Managerial Economics

detail.title: Resilience-oriented Strategic Stocking and Capacity Planning: Hedging against Rare Disruptions
detail.abstract: Occurrence of unexpected disruptions (e.g., natural disasters, wars and conflicts, and tariff wars) in recent years has made an increasing number of enterprises aware of the importance of supply chain resilience. Unlike traditional operational risks, these disruptive events cannot be predicted using probabilistic methods because their likelihood of occurrence is almost negligible. Consequently, how to balance operational efficiency and supply chain resilience remains a challenge for practitioners and scholars. Considering that a disruptive event may or may not occur, we propose to model the objective of a firm as minimizing a weighted summation of two-dimensional regrets, with the ``efficiency regret" being the gap between the actual profit and the ``hindsight" optimal profit, conditioning upon the absence of the disruptive event, whereas the ``resilience regret" being the corresponding gap conditioning upon the presence of the disruptive event. Building on this decision criterion, we analyze two canonical operational settings, in which a firm procures from an outside supplier and produces product using its own facilities, respectively. For the first scenario, considering the potential supply disruption and demand surge, we investigate the firm’s strategic stocking strategy in order to build resilience. For the second scenario, considering that existing production facility may be forced to shut down (or demand may surge significantly), we study the firm's capacity decision associated with facility backup (or capacity redundancy), together with the pre-stocking decision. Analysis on the structure properties of the optimal decisions, the efficient frontiers that are composed of the two-dimensional regrets, and results from numerical experiments yield several insightful managerial implications, which offer practical guidance for firms seeking to build robust, forward-looking operations in an era of heightened uncertainty.

title: Strategic Intelligence Systems and Competitive Advantage: A Resource-Based Perspective on Emerging Economies
affiliations: Islamic Azad University

detail.title: Strategic Intelligence Systems and Competitive Advantage: A Resource-Based Perspective on Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: In today's world, strategic information systems (SIS) are recognized as an essential tool for achieving competitive advantage in organizations. These systems allow organizations to use information resources effectively and make better strategic decisions. However, effective use of SIS requires the exploitation of organizationspecific resources. The Resource Based Perspective (RBV) believes that resources Internal organizations, including human resources, technology, and organizational knowledge, can act as a key factor in creating a sustainable competitive advantage. This research examines the role of SIS and various organizational resources in creating a sustainable competitive advantage in emerging economies.The present study analyzes the issue of how organizations in emerging economies can use their internal resources and strategic information systems to achieve competitive advantage. The findings show that non-material resources such as human resources and organizational relations are of particular importance and can play an effective role in strengthening strategic information systems and improving organizational performance.The results of this research also emphasize that the use of new technologies, especially in information systems, can help organizations react quickly to environmental and competitive changes. Strategic information systems can help organizations optimize operational processes and identify innovation opportunities in emerging economies, which face specific challenges. Faced with infrastructural constraints, lack of financial resources and manpower, effective use of these systems can significantly improve the performance of organizations.This research shows that organizations should pay special attention to organizing their internal resources and using SIS effectively to achieve strategic goals. It is suggested that organizations focus on their intangible resources in this process and implement information systems in line with business strategies.

title: Peer Group Comparisons and Pay Spillovers in the CEO Labor Market
affiliations: University of Massachusetts at Amherst - College of Social and Behavioral Sciences - Department of Economics and

detail.title: Peer Group Comparisons and Pay Spillovers in the CEO Labor Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines the peer benchmarking process in executive compensation and its effects on CEO pay. Previous studies have shown that firms manipulate the benchmarking process to raise CEO pay by selecting high-paying peer firms. We study whether this peer group manipulation by one firm has effects on CEO pay at other firms. Using data on disclosed compensation peer groups from 2006 to 2023, we decompose peer compensation into a fundamentals component, captured by predicted peer-group pay, and a deviation component, captured by the peer pay effect (PPE). We then instrument average peer pay with the average PPE of those peers, isolating the component of peer compensation driven by their own strategic benchmarking. We find that pay changes at one firm propagate through the benchmarking network to other firms. Dyadic tests show that effects are significantly stronger for actual disclosed peers than for predicted but non-selected peers, consistent with transmission through the formal benchmarking network. Results are robust across first-differences, spatial autoregressive, and alternative peer-prediction specifications. Even firms with strong corporate governance and no apparent peer group manipulation see their CEO pay inflated by the actions of other firms. This implies that peer group manipulation need not reflect opportunistic rent-seeking to generate externalities: firms selecting higher-paying peers for arguably legitimate reasons, such as rewarding a well-performing manager, may inadvertently contribute to pay increases elsewhere in the network. The findings illustrate how benchmarking in imperfectly competitive markets can systematically raise compensation levels overall.

title: Algorithmic Communitas: Simulated Nomadism and the Extraction of Symbolic Capital in Tech-Boho Culture

detail.title: Algorithmic Communitas: Simulated Nomadism and the Extraction of Symbolic Capital in Tech-Boho Culture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent researcher tracing long-term transformations of bohemia, cultural autonomy, and symbolic power in modernity.

detail.abstract: This article examines the transformation of the phenomenon of bohemia in the first third of the twenty-first century through the evolution of the Burning Man festival and the emergence of the tech-boho class. The author critically analyzes the dominant narrative of Burning Man as a space of radical counterculture and escapism. Drawing on Victor Turner's anthropology of ritual, Herbert Marcuse's concept of repressive desublimation, and Pierre Bourdieu's theory of the field of cultural production, the article interprets contemporary corporate rebellion through the concept of double simulation: digital simulation (continuous internet connectivity destroys the ritual's temporary autonomy) and labor simulation (economic risk and creative labor, once borne by the bohemian subject, are now carried by a separate, less protected class-artists and crafters-while symbolic profit is appropriated by a risk-free class). The empirical basis of the study consists of data from the Black Rock City Census, publicly available financial reports of the Burning Man Project, the author's qualitative field observations during personal participation in the festival, and a discourse analysis of participant communication in digital communities.

title: Price Risk Management Framework for Smallholder Farmers: A Real-World Forward Contract Model

detail.title: Price Risk Management Framework for Smallholder Farmers: A Real-World Forward Contract Model
detail.abstract: This paper addresses a systemic vulnerability in agricultural economics: the high price volatility faced by smallholder farmers at harvest due to production time lags. Unlike speculative digital assets and subprime-style financial instruments that lack tangible security, this study proposes a practical, asset-backed Forward Contract Model. By designing a dual-incentive structure that legally binds local farmers and large-scale agro-processors, the framework "locks in" a guaranteed floor price at the time of planting. This mechanism stabilizes the velocity of money within rural communities, mitigates the risk of sudden liquidity bankruptcies, and secures the agricultural supply chain against speculative shocks.

reference: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/iKIET/223; i-KIET Issues & Analysis, No. 223
title: The US Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals (ATCM): Reshaping Critical Minerals Supply Chains and Korea’s Strategic Response
affiliations: and

detail.title: The US Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals (ATCM): Reshaping Critical Minerals Supply Chains and Korea’s Strategic Response

keywords: Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/iKIET/223
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The United States is pursuing the Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals (ATCM) with five principal objectives: diversifying critical minerals supply chains, reducing dependence on China, building a preferential trading bloc among allies, establishing a price stabilization mechanism, and setting rules for investment and trade. Washington has designed the agreement as a legally binding plurilateral framework for industrial policy cooperation, intended to sustain and expand the critical minerals production capacity and industrial base of partner countries. The instruments under consideration include a price floor, a common external tariff, minimum import prices, and reference pricing powered by artificial intelligence (AI). 

Each is meant to counter low-price offensives and overcapacity in specific countries while preserving investment incentives and production capacity among allies. Taken together, they amount to an attempt to build a new allied critical minerals market for critical minerals. Many other countries also see China's domination of critical minerals supply chains as a major risk, distorting prices and creating major dependency risks, and that diversification is necessary. But not all are on board with Washington's interventionist instruments: the price floor, the common external tariff, and AI-based pricing are likely to become central points of contention in negotiations. 

Korea faces a dual dependence: on China for processed critical minerals and on the United States and the European Union as export markets for derivative products. Should the ATCM build a "friendly" supply chain and establish a preferential trading system, Korea stands to diversify its sources of processed critical minerals and to secure steadier access to US and EU markets. But if major suppliers remain outside the agreement, any gains could be offset by new supply chain risks. This study argues that Korea should weigh participation in ATCM as a question of industrial competitiveness and supply chain resilience rather than one of resource diplomacy alone. It recommends a principle of selective and conditional participation in the price floor and the AI-based reference pricing system, coupled with diversification of supply through platforms such as FORGE, expanded recycling and domestic production capacity, and complementary domestic measures covering statistics, monitoring, and strategic stockpiling.

This paper was translated using the Claude Opus 5 large language model (Max effort). The paper was professionally edited and reviewed by the authors prior to publication.

title: Political Economy, Resources, and State Fragility
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Political Economy, Resources, and State Fragility
detail.abstract: This article tests the Fraser Theory of Post-Colonial Intervention's (FTPI) claim that intervention is also a political-economic project, in which material interests shape both the decision to intervene and the character of the post-conflict order left behind. It examines whether strategic resources, military basing, reconstruction contracting, and aid or trade dependency align with the postwar trajectories identified in this research programme's companion articles, using four cases selected for variation in resource exposure and institutional control: Iraq, where the oil sector was restructured after 2003 through service contracts rather than ownership transfer; Libya, where the National Oil Corporation has remained the central, contested prize in a fragmented state; Afghanistan, where an estimated $1-3 trillion in mineral wealth went almost entirely untapped during two decades of Western presence, only to be aggressively developed by China after the 2021 withdrawal; and the Sahel, where France's decades-long uranium and counterterrorism presence in Niger was reversed within months by a 2023 coup and a 2025 nationalisation. The comparison finds that the simplest version of a resource-extraction thesis, namely that Western intervention is undertaken chiefly to seize material assets, is not well supported by the evidence: the case with the largest known resource endowment saw the least extraction, and Iraq's actual oil contracts constrained rather than rewarded the Western companies that pursued them for over a decade. What the material record does support is a subtler claim consistent with FTPI: that an intervening power's material engagement with a transformed state tracks the same responsibility gap identified in this programme's companion articles, and that material relationships persist or collapse largely independent of whether the original intervention achieved its stated humanitarian or security aims.

title: Recognition Without Autonomy: Indigenous Development Zones and Identity Formation in Chile
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Political Science

detail.title: Recognition Without Autonomy: Indigenous Development Zones and Identity Formation in Chile
detail.abstract: Countries around the world have increasingly recognized indigenous communities and created development policies tailored to them. How do these policies shape indigenous identity? I examine this using a quasi-experiment in Chile, where the government delineated indigenous development zones and channeled resources into them. Using a geographic regression discontinuity that compares similarly situated Mapuche communities on both sides of a zonal boundary that did not exhibit pre-existing differences in identity or socioeconomic conditions, I find that active programming produced a considerable and durable positive shift in Mapuche self-identification. A nearby zone designated but never activated produced no such shift, ruling out symbolic recognition as the driver. What drove the shift was programmatic implementation and the organizational and social change it stimulated. The findings speak to debates over constrained recognition and partial policymaking that defines neoliberal multiculturalism: rather than producing assimilation or conflict, these arrangements can reinforce indigenous identity in unanticipated ways. * I thank Felipe Jordán for fruitful feedback and insights. Agustin Duarte and Jason Lin provided excellent research assistance. Lautaro Cella collaborated on an early iteration of the paper.

title: ESG Label or Just the Index? Causal Evidence on Institutional Flows Around ESG-Index Inclusion

detail.title: ESG Label or Just the Index? Causal Evidence on Institutional Flows Around ESG-Index Inclusion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial or personal relationship with any organization that could be perceived to have influenced this study. In particular, the author has no affiliation with, and no financial interest in, any ESG rating provider, index provider, asset manager, or ETF issuer referenced in the paper. All data used are publicly available regulatory filings. The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or private personal data. It relies solely on publicly available regulatory filings (SEC Forms 13F and N-PORT) and public market data, so no ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Does an ESG label move money, or does the index it sits on do the moving? When a stock enters an ESG index, institutional capital visibly arrives. But capital arrives when a stock enters any index, so the inflow by itself proves nothing about the label. Using SEC Form 13F institutional holdings (2019Q1– 2026Q1) and a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design with heterogeneity-robust estimators (Callaway–Sant'Anna 2021; Sun–Abraham 2021), I estimate the effect of inclusion in the MSCI USA (Extended) ESG Leaders index, proxied through iShares ESG-ETF N-PORT holdings, on how many institutions hold a stock (breadth) and how much of it they hold (depth). The identification device is a placebo: run the identical estimator on generic S&P 500 additions, and whatever survives the subtraction is the ESG-specific effect. Not much survives. ESG inclusion is associated with roughly +28 additional 13F filers; a generic S&P 500 addition draws about +149; the contrast is −121 filers (p = 0.001). The breadth design is well-powered (minimum detectable effect ≈104 filers at 80% power), and the 95% CI rules out a positive ESG premium even a quarter the size of a generic add. Depth, and a post-2022 “legitimacy decay” split, are underpowered — I report them as open questions rather than dressing them up as nulls. Pre-trends fail for the ESG arm; that failure is treated as load-bearing. And an honest-DiD analysis (Rambachan–Roth 2023) shows the negative point estimate is itself fragile, so the conclusion rests on power, not sign. For SFDR, SDR, and SEC disclosure regimes premised on ESG ratings leading capital, the steering is not where it should be.

title: Job Displacement and Household Consumption Patterns: Evidence from South Korea
affiliations: and

detail.title: Job Displacement and Household Consumption Patterns: Evidence from South Korea
detail.abstract: This paper provides evidence on the effects of job loss on household consumption behavior. Although prior research consistently shows that job loss reduces total household earnings and consumption, there is limited evidence regarding which specific spending categories are affected. Using representative household-level data, we find evidence that job displacement reduces household earnings and spending across several specific categories. Specifically, our findings show that job displacement reduces household expenditure on food and allowances for household members. Although job loss does not change large consumption commitments for housing and vehicles, we find that job loss results in smaller consumption commitments for communication expenses. Overall, our findings show that household consumption declines in essential and flexible spending categories following job loss, while large, fixed commitments remain unchanged.

title: Equilibrium Non-Monotonicity in Bank Regulation: A Newton-Strang Mean Field Game with Jump-Diffusion Dynamics

detail.title: Equilibrium Non-Monotonicity in Bank Regulation: A Newton-Strang Mean Field Game with Jump-Diffusion Dynamics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. No funding was received for this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or any data requiring ethical approval. The study is entirely theoretical and numerical, based on mathematical modeling and computational simulations.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This paper establishes a non-monotonicity in bank regulation: the relationship between borrowing penalties and systemic default risk is U-shaped, implying an interior optimal penalty rate. We demonstrate this within a mean field game (MFG) framework where a continuum of banks, facing jump-diffusion reserve dynamics with strategic interaction, optimally borrow from a central bank facility. The coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman and Fokker-Planck equations are solved using Newton-linearized implicit time stepping with analytical Jacobian, Strang splitting, and adaptive fixed-point iteration, achieving near machine-precision convergence (5.81 × 10-9) in 15 iterations. Grid convergence confirms first-to-second order accuracy (p = 1.27), with 0.76% relative L ∞ error. We identify four mechanisms. Default probability is U-shaped in κ, minimized at κ ≈ 0.3 (26% below κ = 0.1), reflecting discipline vs. smoothing. Interaction strength θ amplifies default risk 31.1-fold. Volatility increases risk 2.47-fold. Higher jump intensity reduces default probability by 5.8%, reversing partial-equilibrium predictions. A Systemic Risk Index reveals a default-inequality trade-off invisible to single-metric analysis.

title: Trust, Transparency, and the Fragile Promise of Data Governance in the Era of Modernization

detail.title: Trust, Transparency, and the Fragile Promise of Data Governance in the Era of Modernization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics, volume 54, issue S1, 2026[10.1017/jme.2026.10234]
Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Public health data modernization in the United States has accelerated since COVID-19 exposed systemic weaknesses in fragmented data infrastructure and governance. Technical solutions have advanced, but legal and relational barriers still complicate data sharing across jurisdictions. Traditionally, interjurisdictional data sharing has relied on individually negotiated Data Use Agreements (DUAs), a process that is both resource-heavy and often opaque. To address this, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have proposed a Core DUA to standardize terms and reduce administrative burden. However, its success depends on trusta fragile foundation increasingly strained by politicization, perceived lack of transparency, and controversial federal actions involving sensitive data. Jurisdictional concerns about compliance, security, and misuse underscore the need for governance frameworks that prioritize clarity, reciprocity, and accountability. Coercive approaches risk deepening fragmentation and undermining collaborative governance. Ultimately, modernization efforts will fail without supporting trust as the cornerstone of public health data governance. This article examines legal variation, transactional friction, and evolving jurisdictional perspectives to illuminate the critical role of trust in shaping the future of public health data systems.

title: When the City Gate Catches Fire, the Fish in the Moat Suffer: Supplier Violations and the Financing Constraints of Firms
affiliations: Baoji University of Arts and Sciences and Baoji University of Arts and Sciences

detail.title: When the City Gate Catches Fire, the Fish in the Moat Suffer: Supplier Violations and the Financing Constraints of Firms
detail.abstract: Understanding the cross-tier spillover effects of environmental misconduct is critical for sustainable supply chain finance and resilience. Drawing on signaling theory and resource dependence theory, this study investigates whether and how upstream supplier environmental violations exacerbate downstream customer firms’ financing constraints, using a sample of Chinese A-share non-financial listed firms from 2010 to 2023. The results show that supplier environmental violations significantly tighten customer financing constraints, primarily through two channels: elevated operational risk and eroded reputational capital. Notably, we identify corporate ESG performance as a critical moderator; superior ESG practices effectively buffer firms against these negative spillovers. Heterogeneity analysis further reveals that the contagion effect is more pronounced among firms with CEO–chairperson separation and higher supplier concentration. By uncovering an exogenous, supply-side driver of financing constraints, this study extends the literature on environmental violation externalities and provides empirical evidence for ESG-driven risk governance in global supply chains.

detail.abstract:
Background: Women consistently receive more psychotropic medications than men in high-income countries, yet whether these differences reflect clinical need or gender-related variation in clinical decision making remains unclear. Whether sex independently influenced psychotropic prescribing and referral to specialised mental health services among adults managed in Spanish primary care were investigated.

Methods: A retrospective cross-sectional study was conducted using routinely collected electronic health records from six urban primary care centres managed by Badalona Serveis Assistencials (Spain). Adults aged 15 years or older with an active diagnosis of anxiety, depression, insomnia, trauma-related disorders, or persistent mood disorders between Jan 1 and Dec 31, 2025, were eligible. Psychosis, bipolar disorder, postpartum depression, eating disorders, and substance-use disorders were excluded. Primary outcomes were psychotropic treatment intensity and referral to specialised mental health services. Multivariable logistic and multinomial regression models adjusted for age, socioeconomic status, diagnosis, healthcare utilisation, and pharmacological burden.

Findings: Among 33 575 participants, 65·1% were women and the mean age was 55·5 years (SD 18·1). Anxiety was the most frequent diagnosis (61·5%), followed by depression (19·3%). After adjustment, women had lower odds of referral to specialised mental health services than men (adjusted OR 0·63, 95% CI 0·57–0·69; p<0·0001). Women were also less likely to remain untreated (adjusted OR for no psychotropic medication vs four medications 0·50, 0·43–0·58), indicating greater treatment intensity. Individuals born outside Spain had lower odds of a recorded mental health diagnosis than those born in Spain (adjusted OR 0·73, 0·59–0·89).

Interpretation: Sex independently influenced clinical management after adjustment for demographic, socioeconomic, diagnostic, and healthcare utilisation variables. Women were more likely to receive multiple psychotropic medications but less likely to be referred to specialised mental health services, suggesting sex-related differences in therapeutic pathways. These findings support incorporating a gender-sensitive perspective into prescribing, referral protocols, and mental health service planning.

detail.abstract:
Background: Sex- and gender-related inequities in access to specialist kidney care remain insufficiently characterised in low- and middle-income countries despite the substantial burden of chronic kidney disease (CKD). We evaluated differences in utilisation of tertiary nephrology services by sex over a 10-year period in North India.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using electronic health records from a high-volume tertiary nephrology referral centre in North India. All nephrology visits between Jan 1, 2010, and Dec 31, 2020, were included. Patient-level data were linked with district-level demographic and socioeconomic indicators from the 2011 Census of India. The primary outcome was utilisation of nephrology services by sex. Secondary outcomes included utilisation of kidney replacement therapies (haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and kidney transplantation), post-transplant survival, temporal trends, and geographical patterns of access.

Findings: A total of 492,857 nephrology visits from 104,512 unique individuals were analysed. Women accounted for 152,136 (30.9%) visits and 35,254 (33.7%) unique patients. The lower representation of women was consistent across administrative divisions and throughout the study period, including after a marked expansion in service utilisation in 2014 (30.9% after vs 31.1% before; p=0.24). Women were also less likely than men to receive kidney transplantation. Among 1,205 transplant recipients, 151 (12.5%) were women; transplantation rates among patients receiving nephrology care were 2.45% for women and 6.86% for men (p<0.0001). Post-transplant survival was similar between women and men (log-rank p=0.38). Districts located farther from the study centre contributed fewer patients, whereas greater female socioeconomic advantage at the district level was associated with higher utilisation by women.

Interpretation: Women had consistently lower utilisation of tertiary nephrology services over a decade despite comparable post-transplant survival, suggesting that inequities occur primarily before access to specialist kidney care is achieved. Strategies that improve timely referral, equitable access to diagnostic and therapeutic services, and financial protection may help reduce sex- and gender-related inequities in kidney care in resource-constrained settings.

title: Nominal and Real Cigarette Price Trends from a Global Dataset, 2008-2024 and Implications for the World Health Organization's 3 by 35 Initiative: A Longitudinal Study and Forecasting Analysis

detail.title: Nominal and Real Cigarette Price Trends from a Global Dataset, 2008-2024 and Implications for the World Health Organization's 3 by 35 Initiative: A Longitudinal Study and Forecasting Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
